1/S0/F0.text: The full forms of the abbreviations are extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and mixed reality (MR), respectively.

1/S0/F1.text: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

1/S1/F0.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

1/S1/F1.text: The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

1/S1/F2.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

1/S2/F0.text: The reality-virtuality continuum is a scale whose extremes are a completely real environment with nothing virtual and a completely virtual environment with nothing real.

1/S2/F1.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

1/S2/F2.text: Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.

1/S2/F3.text: Mixed reality, in a broad sense, is the entire space between the real environment extreme and the virtual environment extreme of the reality-virtuality continuum, containing different degrees of augmentation of the real environment with virtual content and of the virtual environment with real content.

1/S3/F0.text: A 2022 forecast estimated the share of content related to extended reality technologies in different application domains as video games 34 percent, healthcare 15 percent, engineering 14 percent, live events 12 percent, video entertainment 9 percent, real estate 7 percent, retail 5 percent, and military 4 percent, and these figures may now be larger.

1/S3/F1.text: A market study reports that the extended reality market size was about 20.5 billion US dollars in 2021 and is expected to be about 860 billion US dollars by 2030, an exponential increase.

1/S3/F2.text: The hardware market in the extended reality market is about 60 percent of the market size, and the software market is about 40 percent.

1/S3/F3.text: In India, the extended reality industry was estimated at about 1.83 billion US dollars in 2020 and is expected to be about 14 billion US dollars in 2027.

1/S3/F4.text: The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.

1/S3/F5.text: The metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology, while one broad view is that it reimagines the way humans interact with the digital world.

1/S3/F6.text: In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction with digital content, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions with occasional three-dimensional interaction.

1/S3/F7.text: The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software.

1/S3/F8.text: The growth of extended reality creates a need for more knowledgeable and skilled manpower who can develop and deploy systems based on the technology.

1/S3/F9.text: The extended reality field is one of the major emerging areas identified by many national governments, along with artificial intelligence (AI), large language models, generative artificial intelligence, drones, and nanomaterials.

1/S5/F0.text: The seminal reference for the reality-virtuality continuum is the 1994 paper 'A Taxonomy of Mixed Reality Visual Displays' by Paul Milgram and Fumio Kishino, one of the earliest papers in the field of mixed reality visual displays, which significantly influenced the development of that field.

2/S0/F0.text: Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

2/S0/F1.text: The major current application domains for virtual reality (VR) discussed are gaming and entertainment, healthcare, education, the automobile industry, travel and tourism (including virtual tourism and digital heritage preservation), real estate and architecture, and defense.

2/S0/F2.text: Gaming and entertainment is an early and current virtual reality (VR) application domain; recent immersive gaming products use immersive technologies to make gaming more acceptable and popular, adding value to the gaming industry, and players are expected to wear headsets or other VR devices to experience immersion.

2/S0/F3.text: Healthcare is a prominent virtual reality (VR) application domain, primarily for medical education and training, and mixed reality (MR) is also used; in it, potential doctors can learn about body organs, how they work, how they look, and their different parts, and immersive simulations help when obtaining cadavers is difficult.

2/S0/F4.text: Education is an emerging application domain for immersive technologies from primary to tertiary levels; appropriate exposure to immersive technologies can improve learners' engagement and learning outcomes compared with standard teaching and learning methods, although excessive duration may create problems; examples include classroom education at primary or secondary level and higher-education institutes developing immersive topic-specific teaching and learning solutions.

2/S0/F5.text: Although it is not yet very popular, the automobile industry is an evolving virtual reality (VR) application area in which companies create immersive experiences of newly launched car models without showroom visits or actual driving to increase customer satisfaction and experience; although primarily intended for potential buyers, it can also be used in automobile design and development.

2/S0/F6.text: Travel and tourism is an emerging application area for immersive technologies, including virtual tours and virtual tourism, which let users visit faraway places without physically going there and save money and physical effort.

2/S0/F7.text: Digital heritage preservation and heritage tourism are emerging immersive-technology applications for heritage places that cannot be physically visited by large numbers of users or in all parts for preservation reasons; they let users explore each part virtually, preserve the space digitally despite physical decay, and increase the space's lifespan and potential to be visited by more users.

2/S0/F8.text: Real estate and architecture is a prominent virtual reality (VR) application area in which potential buyers can explore upcoming properties, including properties that do not yet exist, without visiting the place, enabling them to make informed purchase decisions before spending large amounts on real estate.

2/S0/F9.text: Defense is a major virtual reality (VR) application area for training, including specialized military training that simulates vehicles, soldiers, and combat environments with constraints; virtual boot camp and combat training using head-mounted displays (HMDs) with motion trackers, full-body tracking systems, and wireless weapon controllers; training for military medical personnel; and maintenance and assembly technician training, with applications catering to these needs already existing.

2/S1/F0.text: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

2/S1/F1.text: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

2/S1/F2.text: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

2/S1/F3.text: A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world.

2/S1/F4.text: Non-immersive virtual reality (VR) includes specifically gaming applications, such as games on PlayStation, Xbox, or similar systems and games like World of Warcraft or similar games, that rely on computer or video game console displays and input devices such as keyboards, mice, and handheld controllers.

2/S1/F5.text: Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals.

2/S1/F6.text: Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) can be a three-dimensional virtual environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, a VR box, or a VR headset, with a VR headset being the common example; users typically have no real physical movements, and examples include virtual tours using only a headset, which can be device-based or web-based.

2/S1/F7.text: Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

2/S1/F8.text: A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

2/S1/F9.text: Fully immersive virtual reality (VR) systems, such as dedicated virtual shooting game zones, use many devices such as helmets, gloves, body connectors with sense detectors, and body suits, so users view the virtual environment through a helmet or head-mounted display and their actual movements, such as running, jumping, crouching, shooting, and throwing, their reactions, and even a blink of an eye are detected and translated into actions in the virtual world while the user cannot sense anything in the real world.

2/S1/F10.text: Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

3/S0/F0.text: Extended reality (XR) technologies have huge application potential in domains including video games, healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military.

3/S0/F1.text: Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.

3/S0/F2.text: Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.

3/S0/F3.text: In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.

3/S0/F4.text: In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.

3/S0/F5.text: The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.

3/S0/F6.text: Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

3/S1/F0.text: The Gatwick Airport passenger app used more than 2,000 beacons placed at different points in the passenger terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal, and such apps are helpful in large terminals.

3/S1/F1.text: Augmented reality (AR) customer-experience applications that let a customer preview a product before purchase include the IKEA Place app, which lets a user scan a room and place IKEA objects in the digital image of the room to see how the room would look, and a Dulux visualizer app, which lets a customer digitally paint walls on a screen and see the effect before deciding whether to buy the paint.

3/S1/F2.text: An augmented reality (AR) virtual tape measure application can measure the heights and lengths of objects inside or outside a room using a mobile phone, so a physical tape is not needed.

3/S1/F3.text: Augmented reality (AR) customer-experience try-on applications before purchase include the Sephora app, which lets a customer virtually try different cosmetic looks on a digital face and choose the product color that satisfies the most, and a Rolex app, which lets a customer try different watch models on a digital representation of their hand and decide whether to buy based on look and feel.

3/S1/F4.text: In healthcare, augmented reality (AR) applications include medical training, telemedicine options that enable medical professionals to interact with patients, and real-time information to treatment areas that supports diagnosis, surgery, and treatment plans.

3/S1/F5.text: AccuVein is a handheld device with augmented reality (AR) applications that scans a patient's vein network, can indicate the patient's condition, can lead to a 45% reduction in escalation, and, by being pointed at the skin surface, allows the internal vein network to be visualized so the treatment course can be decided.

3/S2/F0.text: Augmented reality (AR) applications are categorized by technology rather than by psychological or immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based augmented reality applications and markerless augmented reality applications.

3/S2/F1.text: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications can have four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, and outlining-based.

3/S2/F2.text: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.

3/S2/F3.text: Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.

3/S2/F4.text: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications are easier to build but difficult to maintain because markers are prone to damage, and a damaged marker may make the application not work.

3/S2/F5.text: Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

3/S2/F6.text: Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

3/S2/F7.text: Superimposition-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications recognize one or multiple physical objects using computer vision techniques and superimpose digital content on the real-world scene depending on the recognized objects.

3/S2/F8.text: Projection-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use light projectors to project digital graphics, digital characters, or other digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space, such as in holographic projection.

3/S2/F9.text: Outlining-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications use object recognition to recreate the user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view, for example by showing cars around a driver that are not clearly visible in low-light conditions.

3/S3/F0.text: Virtual reality (VR) system categories are based on the experience or psychological aspect, and comprise non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems.

3/S3/F1.text: Augmented reality (AR) system categories are based primarily on the technology used to develop and deploy the systems rather than on the psychological aspect, and broadly comprise marker-based and markerless systems.

3/S3/F2.text: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) systems are easier to make because they rely on simple algorithms, but their markers are difficult to maintain unless the environment is very sanitized, such as inside a museum; without a well-attended environment, markers in outdoor settings are prone to damage.

3/S3/F3.text: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques are used to overcome the difficulty of maintaining markers in marker-based systems.

3/S3/F4.text: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) sensors, in location-based applications.

3/S3/F5.text: Computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) applications include superimposition-based and outline-based applications.

3/S3/F6.text: Projection-based techniques, such as holographic projection, can be used in augmented reality (AR) application development.

3/S3/F7.text: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) have broadly similar application domains, but VR applications are characterized as immersive, whereas AR applications emphasize augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than immersive applications.

4/S0/F0.text: The term virtual means, according to Webster's New Universal Dictionary, being in essence or effect but not in fact, that is, something that is there but cannot be attributed to any factual things.

4/S0/F1.text: The term reality is defined in dictionary terms as the state or quality of being real, as something that exists independently of ideas concerning it, or as something that constitutes a real or actual thing as distinguished from something merely apparent.

4/S0/F2.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

4/S1/F0.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

4/S1/F1.text: The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

4/S1/F2.text: An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

4/S1/F3.text: The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

4/S1/F4.text: The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

4/S2/F0.text: A system is a virtual reality (VR) system if it satisfies all three characteristics of a VR system—virtual environment, immersive experience through sensory organs, and interaction—and it is not a VR system if it does not satisfy at least one of them.

4/S2/F1.text: A computer-aided design (CAD) system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it supports a virtual environment and interaction, it does not support an immersive experience, since the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

4/S2/F2.text: A video conferencing system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it is interactive, it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience, since it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen and the user remains in the real world, with the screen only aiding interaction.

4/S2/F3.text: A three-dimensional (3D) movie experience is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it is not interactive, as the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.

5/S0/F0.text: Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

5/S0/F1.text: The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

5/S0/F2.text: An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

5/S0/F3.text: A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.

5/S1/F0.text: Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

5/S1/F1.text: A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

5/S1/F2.text: An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

5/S2/F0.text: There is no agreement among practitioners and in the literature on the precise definition of mixed reality (MR).

5/S2/F1.text: The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

5/S2/F2.text: One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

5/S2/F3.text: Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

5/S2/F4.text: Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

5/S2/F5.text: In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

5/S2/F6.text: Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

5/S3/F0.text: In this course, mixed reality (MR) is assumed to be the same technology and idea as augmented reality (AR), a view shared by many if not all practitioners and adopted for simplicity in the course's subsequent discussion.

6/S0/F0.text: The historical evolution of virtual reality is broadly divided into four mostly distinct, sometimes overlapping phases: the early era, which existed before the advent of digital computers, the formative years from roughly 1950 to 1990, the modern phase from 1991 to 2015, and the current growth phase from roughly 2016 onwards.

6/S1/F0.text: The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

6/S1/F1.text: Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 demonstration of a stereoscopic device established, for the first time in recorded history, that the human brain can process two-dimensional (2D) images as three-dimensional (3D) objects, and this demonstration is roughly considered a first step toward immersive experience.

6/S1/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

6/S1/F3.text: David Brewster's 1860 compact-sized stereoscope was an early form of stereoscopic display that created the illusion of depth in viewed images and, as an advancement over Sir Charles Wheatstone's 1838 stereoscopic device, is roughly considered another step toward practical immersive experiences.

6/S1/F4.text: The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

6/S2/F0.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

6/S2/F1.text: In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.

6/S2/F2.text: In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.

6/S2/F3.text: In 1962, Morton Heilig introduced Sensorama, which can be considered the first immersive virtual reality system under the modern definition of virtual reality.

6/S2/F4.text: Sensorama was publicized as having 3D, wide vision, motion, color, stereo sound, smell, wind, and vibrations (haptics), and it stimulated all sensory organs by letting a user feel pre-recorded vibrations, sounds, smells, and wind.

6/S2/F5.text: In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).

6/S2/F6.text: In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

6/S2/F7.text: In 1967, Fred Brooks at the University of North Carolina developed a haptic feedback system that used a force feedback device to let a user feel, through touch, objects shown on a screen while manipulating them.

6/S2/F8.text: In 1973, Krueger used the term artificial reality, an early term that eventually evolved into the modern term virtual reality.

6/S2/F9.text: In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

6/S2/F10.text: In 1987, two papers appeared in Scientific American, one on the data glove, an input device, and these papers helped shape and popularize the field of virtual reality.

6/S2/F11.text: In the late 1980s, Jaron Lanier proposed the term virtual reality, which became the term used to refer to immersive technologies.

6/S3/F0.text: The modern phase of virtual reality (VR) is the period roughly from 1990 to 2015, about 25 years.

6/S3/F1.text: The CAVE system, invented in 1992 at the University of Illinois at Chicago's Electronic Visualization Laboratory, used a single Silicon Graphics computer to render images in a surrounding setting that made a user feel surrounded by holograms and provided an immersive experience.

6/S3/F2.text: In 1992, the company Sense8 developed the WTK software package for higher-level application development in virtual reality (VR), which helped in building virtual reality systems.

6/S3/F3.text: Virtual reality modeling language (VRML) was presented in 1994, and other modeling languages for virtual reality (VR), such as X3D and Java 3D, also started in 1994.

6/S3/F4.text: White 5 is a head-mounted display (HMD) with a 150-degree field of view (FOV) created in 2006 by Mark Bolas of the University of Southern California's MXR lab and Ian McDowall of Fakespace Labs.

6/S3/F5.text: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) evolved from the bulky appearance of late-1950s models, through Sutherland's HMD and NASA HMDs, into a more portable, less bulky, and more usable form.

6/S3/F6.text: Oculus Rift is an inexpensive virtual reality (VR) headset created by Palmer Luckey in 2012.

6/S3/F7.text: Facebook purchased the Oculus Rift virtual reality (VR) headset in 2014, and with that purchase it tried to popularize the headset and made virtual reality affordable for the masses.

6/S3/F8.text: The availability of inexpensive headsets, such as the Oculus Rift, greatly spurred interest in virtual reality (VR) towards the end of its modern phase.

6/S4/F0.text: In the evolution of virtual reality (VR), the growth phase is the last and continuing phase and began roughly in 2016, when many well-known companies released commercial virtual reality (VR) headsets that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population and spurred growth in the field.

6/S4/F1.text: The commercial virtual reality (VR) headsets released by well-known companies in 2016 include Oculus Rift version 1 from Facebook, HTC Vive from HTC, PlayStation virtual reality headset from Sony, and HoloLens from Microsoft.

6/S4/F2.text: The term Metaverse had existed in the research community since the 1990s, but nobody paid much attention to the term; in 2021, Zuckerberg of Meta popularized the term, after which people began taking an interest in Metaverse and interpreting Metaverse in different ways, spurring further activity in the field.

6/S4/F3.text: Apple released the Apple Vision Pro virtual reality (VR) headset in 2023.

6/S4/F4.text: The virtual reality (VR) growth phase is a continuing phase because more developments, including better headsets, better immersive displays, and better input devices, will happen, will continue, and may accelerate because there is going to be huge demand.

6/S5/F0.text: A book by LaValle is available online and covers the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) in detail.

7/S0/F0.text: The historical evolution of augmented reality (AR) can be broadly divided into four phases that may sometimes overlap, unlike the phases of virtual reality: the experimental phase before the 1980s, the basic research phase from the 1980s to the mid-1990s, the tools or applications phase from the mid-1990s to 2007, and the commercial application phase from 2007 to the present.

7/S0/F1.text: The phases of augmented reality (AR) evolution are characterized as follows: the experimental phase involved early experimentation that defined the concepts and showed the types of technology required for AR; the basic research phase involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices; the tools or applications phase involved developing or exploring early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques, usability of such applications, and design theory for AR; and the commercial application phase involved widespread AR availability and newer applications appearing in domains such as gaming, medicine, mobile, commerce, and marketing.

7/S1/F0.text: Ivan Sutherland and Bob Sproull created the first truly computer-generated augmented reality (AR) prototype in 1968.

7/S1/F1.text: The first Sutherland-Sproull augmented reality (AR) prototype combined a cathode ray tube (CRT)-based optical see-through head-mounted display (HMD) with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system connected to a PDP-11 computer and custom graphics hardware; the tracking system registered head movements in three dimensions on the see-through display, and the mechanical tracker was later replaced by an ultrasonic tracker.

7/S1/F2.text: Tom Furness at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base began research on the United States (US) Air Force super cockpit program, which was a major research program that produced technologies relevant to augmented reality (AR).

7/S1/F3.text: In the super cockpit prototype, a pilot wearing a head-mounted display (HMD) in the aircraft cockpit saw computer-generated imagery superimposed over the real-world view in daylight and saw computer-generated imagery replace the real-world view at night or in bad weather.

7/S1/F4.text: The early augmented reality (AR) experiments led to head-mounted augmented reality displays used in modern aircraft, to virtual reality (VR) displays such as the VIVED head-mounted display (HMD), and to input and tracking hardware.

7/S2/F0.text: The basic research phase of augmented reality (AR) came after the experimentation phase and included much influential work in the 1990s that shaped the field of augmented reality.

7/S2/F1.text: Tom Caudell is often credited with coining the phrase augmented reality (AR) because he published the first academic article containing the term AR in 1992.

7/S2/F2.text: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research projects at the University of North Carolina included registration tracking techniques in 1993 and 1994, early research in 1995 and 1996 on see-through head-mounted displays typically used in AR, and several applications developed alongside the basic research.

7/S2/F3.text: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at Columbia University included one of the first academic papers on AR describing the KARMA system in 1993, work in 1993 on AR interaction methods, that is, how to interact with augmented digital content, and some publications on mobile AR systems in 1997.

7/S2/F4.text: During the basic research phase of augmented reality (AR), research at the University of Toronto included overlaying virtual cues on stereoscopic video from 1991 to 1993 and work on AR applications from 1992 to 1993.

7/S2/F5.text: Chameleon was an early handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1993 that allowed a user to move a liquid-crystal display (LCD) over a piece of paper and see virtual content.

7/S2/F6.text: NaviCam by Rekimoto was a handheld or mobile augmented reality (AR) system developed in 1995 that superimposed virtual tags on real objects using handheld and head-mounted displays.

7/S2/F7.text: Chameleon and NaviCam were true augmented reality (AR)-type applications and precursors to the kind of AR applications seen today.

7/S3/F0.text: Notable works during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included research on key enabling technologies for augmented reality, such as tracking, display, and interaction.

7/S3/F1.text: Work during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included systems that allowed people in the same location to see and interact with shared augmented reality content.

7/S3/F2.text: Medical applications developed during the mid-1990s tools or applications phase of augmented reality (AR) included visualization of laparoscopic surgery, X-ray visualization in a patient's body, and image-guided surgery.

7/S3/F3.text: From the mid-1990s, wearable computing using head-mounted displays (HMDs) emerged as a related research area in augmented reality (AR), although it had existed earlier and people began paying more attention to such head-mounted displays.

7/S3/F4.text: In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

7/S3/F5.text: In 1997, wearable computers with global positioning system (GPS) tracking produced outdoor augmented reality (AR) interfaces that showed information in place in the real world, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.

7/S3/F6.text: In 2002 and 2003, outdoor wearable augmented reality (AR) applications included terrestrial navigation, on-site viewing and creation of computer-aided design (CAD) models, and game playing.

7/S3/F7.text: The wearable augmented reality (AR) systems being developed in 2002 and 2003 were bulky and difficult to use because of the size of their custom computer hardware, batteries, tracking sensors, and display hardware, and their setups were technically wearable computers with a headset, a computer carried in a backpack, and different input devices.

7/S3/F8.text: Viewpoint tracking was one of the most significant challenges of augmented reality (AR), and it was addressed so that three-dimensional registration of content could happen accurately.

7/S3/F9.text: In 1996, Rekimoto developed a simple computer-vision tracking system based on a printed matrix that evolved into the cyber code system, as part of software that could enable an augmented reality (AR) system to track a user's viewpoint.

7/S3/F10.text: In 1999, Kato and Billinghurst developed the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit tracking library, which was released in 2000 as open-source software, provided real-time computer-vision tracking of a square marker, and could enable an augmented reality system to track a user's viewpoint.

7/S3/F11.text: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

7/S4/F0.text: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) began in October 2007 with the release of the Sony PlayStation 3-based game The Eye of Judgment, one of the first widely used consumer AR experiences, and with its launch such AR experiences started becoming very popular after AR had previously been neither very popular nor easily available.

7/S4/F1.text: In 2009, augmented reality (AR) moved from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology.

7/S4/F2.text: The main factors behind the move of augmented reality (AR) from research laboratories and specialist applications to widely available commercial technology in 2009 were Adobe Flash-based AR authoring tools that made experiencing AR through web browsers possible from 2008, smartphone-based AR because the era of smartphones had begun by then, and the use of AR in global marketing campaigns to increase sales and make products popular.

7/S4/F3.text: Starting in 2017, Apple launched the augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) ARKit for AR system development, and Google released ARCore for Android operating system (OS) or Android platforms; these launches further stimulated AR growth by enabling many developers to create AR applications and increasing the number of AR applications from simple to complex ones.

7/S4/F4.text: The commercial application phase of augmented reality (AR) is still ongoing and is expected to continue growing, with more AR applications and tools, hardware improvements in wearable devices, mobile devices, and holographic projection-based devices, and the development of algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and computer vision technologies making three-dimensional (3D) tracking and registration more feasible on low-end devices.

7/S5/F0.text: The 2015 article by Billinghurst et al. is a recommended source for a more detailed account of the historical evolution of augmented reality (AR).

8/S0/F0.text: The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

8/S0/F1.text: There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

8/S0/F2.text: The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.

8/S1/F0.text: In the definition originally proposed by Slater and Wilbur, immersion is the objective degree to which a virtual reality (VR) system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive, and plot-informing.

8/S1/F1.text: Extensive, as a quality of immersion, refers to the range of sensory modalities presented to the user, with examples including visual, auditory, physical force perception, smell, taste, and touch, and the more sensory organs are stimulated by computer-provided stimuli, the more extensive the immersion is.

8/S1/F2.text: Matching, as a quality of immersion, refers to congruence between sensory modalities, especially a match between a user's physical movement and movement in the virtual world, such as immediate visual change when the head moves or virtual reflection of walking or hand movement.

8/S1/F3.text: Surrounding, as a quality of immersion, is the extent to which cues are panoramic, such as the extent of visual field of view or the extent of auditory source perception, and a wide field of view produces a more surrounding experience than a narrow field of view.

8/S1/F4.text: Vivid, as a quality of immersion, refers to the amount of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality and is related to factors such as resolution, lighting, frame rate, and audio bit rate, with higher resolution or audio bit rate improving visual or auditory perception and making immersion more vivid.

8/S1/F5.text: Interactivity, as a quality of immersion, is the user's capability to make changes to the virtual world, receive responses from virtual entities to user actions, and influence future events, not merely one-way interaction.

8/S1/F6.text: Plot-informing, as a quality of immersion, means the experience is a scripted story, and the more the user can understand, comprehend, or predict the consequences of actions and the overall story, including its consistent portrayal, dynamic unfolding, and behavior of the world and its entities, the more plot-informing the experience is.

8/S1/F7.text: In virtual reality (VR), immersion is the technological issue and presence is the psychological issue.

8/S2/F0.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

8/S2/F1.text: Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

8/S2/F2.text: Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

8/S2/F3.text: Perfect presence is the inability to distinguish between the virtual world and the real world.

8/S3/F0.text: Immersion is an objective and quantifiable description of what a particular system can provide or does provide, and that description can be measured or comprehended.

8/S3/F1.text: Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

8/S3/F2.text: Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

8/S3/F3.text: Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

8/S3/F4.text: The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.

8/S3/F5.text: Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

8/S4/F0.text: Slater and Wilbur's 1997 paper is one of the earliest papers related to virtual reality (VR) immersion and presence, and it is one of the references from which the terms and definitions of immersion and presence were taken.

9/S0/F0.text: The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

9/S0/F1.text: For some people, reality is the gold standard, meaning that what is perceived and sensed in the real world is reality, so for them the goal of a virtual reality (VR) system is to match real-world experience as closely as possible.

9/S0/F2.text: For some people, the concept of reality in a virtual reality (VR) system should be something beyond or surpassing their lived day-to-day reality, not an exact mimicry of the real world, so for them the goal of a VR system is to surpass their idea of reality.

9/S0/F3.text: Different conceptions of reality make the evaluation of a virtual reality (VR) system ambiguous: a VR system that matches one group's sense of reality may not be considered good by another group, and a VR system that surpasses reality may seem creepy or difficult to comprehend to some.

9/S1/F0.text: The uncanny valley effect is a finding from a scientific study of human perception of artificial objects, originally robots and extendable to digital representations, that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first.

9/S1/F1.text: In the plot illustrating the uncanny valley effect, with human likeness on the horizontal axis (x-axis) and familiarity on the vertical axis (y-axis), as an artificial object or digital object in virtual reality (VR) becomes more human-like, familiarity first increases for both moving and stationary objects, then decreases, more sharply for moving objects, reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region, typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness, and then increases again.

9/S1/F2.text: When creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the uncanny valley effect means that trying to match reality exactly with human-like figures or realistic objects may not produce a good experience if their human-likeness falls in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.

9/S2/F0.text: In virtual reality (VR), presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects; other cues may be equally useful for achieving higher presence.

9/S2/F1.text: A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity, along with immersion and presence.

9/S2/F2.text: Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual reality (VR) experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth.

9/S2/F3.text: The highest representational fidelity is indicated by very good photorealistic immersive film content, such as 360-degree video or images of the real world in a virtual environment, while extremely low representational fidelity is indicated by purely abstract and non-objective worlds that are unfamiliar in real-world experience.

9/S2/F4.text: Interaction fidelity is the degree to which the physical actions for a virtual task correspond to the physical actions for an equivalent real-world task, and it exploits real-world experience.

9/S2/F5.text: High interaction fidelity involves intense realistic physical actions for virtual tasks, in which real-world physical activities are translated into virtual activities, while very low interaction fidelity involves no physical motion, such as sitting while moving forward in the virtual world by button press.

9/S2/F6.text: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the virtual reality (VR) creator.

9/S2/F7.text: Low experiential fidelity occurs when a free roaming virtual world with endless possibilities leads every usage to a different experience, because that is not what happens in the real world, while higher experiential fidelity results when real-world constraints are placed on virtual navigation, movement, and interaction, making the virtual experience closer to the real world.

9/S2/F8.text: A virtual reality (VR) system developer or content creator should be aware of the uncanny valley effect and maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience.

9/S3/F0.text: The challenges of augmented reality (AR) systems are mostly technological rather than psychological because immersion is not a major concern and psychological effects are less important in augmented reality than in virtual reality (VR).

9/S3/F1.text: The definition of augmented reality (AR) used to identify AR challenges was given by Azuma in 1997.

9/S3/F2.text: Combining real and virtual content in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on the device, and the same display issue also exists in virtual reality (VR).

9/S3/F3.text: Real-time interaction in augmented reality (AR) requires suitable forms of interaction, including different input devices and input modalities, so that the user can interact with digital content overlaid on a representation of the real world.

9/S3/F4.text: Three-dimensional (3D) registration in augmented reality (AR) means anchoring virtual content in the real world at a suitable place so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

9/S3/F5.text: To register virtual content in augmented reality (AR), the pose of the viewer relative to an anchor in the real world must be determined, where pose means position and orientation; without proper pose estimation, three-dimensional (3D) registration is difficult or impossible.

9/S3/F6.text: Conceptually, pose determination in augmented reality (AR) has two parts, the registration phase and the tracking phase, which can be performed in one phase or as separate phases; the registration phase determines the viewer's pose relative to a real-world anchor when the user starts using the system, and the tracking phase updates that pose relative to a previously known pose because the user is likely to move in an AR application, so that virtual and real-world content appear properly mixed.

9/S4/F0.text: The two major concerns in virtual reality (VR) systems are technological and psychological, and they lead to the major concepts immersion, which is tied to technological issues, and presence, which is tied to psychological issues.

9/S4/F1.text: The uncanny valley effect in virtual reality (VR) is the phenomenon in which making environments as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience can cause uneasiness or creepiness in the user's mind.

9/S4/F2.text: To avoid the uncanny valley effect while building virtual reality (VR) systems, one should be aware of representational fidelity, experiential fidelity, and interaction fidelity.

9/S4/F3.text: The major issues in augmented reality (AR) are mostly technological and consist of proper display technology, proper input mechanisms and technology, and pose estimation and updating, which is popularly called tracking, at the beginning and during system use.

10/S0/F0.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

10/S0/F1.text: A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.

10/S0/F2.text: Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

10/S0/F3.text: Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

10/S1/F0.text: Cyber sickness can be understood through three aspects: causes, evaluation, and mitigation.

10/S1/F1.text: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

10/S1/F2.text: Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

10/S1/F3.text: Age is related to cyber sickness susceptibility: children aged 2 to 12 may show increased sensitivity, that tendency decreases as they grow older, older persons are likely to experience higher levels, cyber sickness is generally uncommon among young children, and it is highly unlikely in users aged 12 to 25.

10/S1/F4.text: Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

10/S1/F5.text: The effect of gender on cyber sickness has no conclusive result because studies report contradictory findings: some find that female users have more severe cases, while others find no discernible difference between male and female participants in the presence or severity of cyber sickness.

10/S1/F6.text: Female users who use head-mounted displays (HMDs) are associated with increased cyber sickness.

10/S1/F7.text: A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

10/S1/F8.text: Motion sickness (MS) occurs when the brain receives conflicting signals from various sensory organs, causing symptoms like nausea and dizziness that are similar to cyber sickness.

10/S1/F9.text: Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

10/S1/F10.text: Studies indicate a positive correlation between motion sickness (MS) susceptibility and cyber sickness risk, so individuals with higher MS susceptibility are likely to experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

10/S1/F11.text: Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

10/S1/F12.text: Body awareness, the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, is a physical condition related to cyber sickness; poor sleep quality can affect this awareness and may contribute to or increase the severity of cyber sickness.

10/S1/F13.text: People with greater retinal eccentricity may be more susceptible to cyber sickness.

10/S1/F14.text: Individuals with neurological conditions such as multiple sclerosis may experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms.

10/S1/F15.text: A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

10/S1/F16.text: Emotional conditions at the time of use can increase the likelihood of cyber sickness: negative emotions such as anxiety, stress, and frustration are typically associated with it, and personality traits such as neuroticism may also increase the likelihood.

10/S2/F0.text: In virtual reality (VR), an external factor in cybersickness (CS) is a factor that is not subjective to a user's mental or physical condition, and hardware is one category of external factors.

10/S2/F1.text: Cybersickness (CS) in virtual reality (VR) is not simply a problem of inferior hardware quality; although early users associated it with inferior hardware, many problems persist with advanced technology, so some aspects of devices themselves induce cybersickness.

10/S2/F2.text: Display resolution is a hardware factor that reduces cybersickness (CS) up to a certain point; a study evaluating 1K, 2K, 3K, and 4K resolutions found a substantial reduction in CS induction from 1K to 2K, but no significant further reduction from 2K to 3K or from 3K to 4K.

10/S2/F3.text: Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

10/S2/F4.text: In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR), cybersickness (CS) increases with latency; the more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce cybersickness.

10/S2/F5.text: Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

10/S2/F6.text: Latency jitter causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery and can lead to inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness (CS).

10/S2/F7.text: Display type is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness (CS), with users using head-mounted display (HMD)-based or virtual reality (VR) headset displays experiencing more CS than users using conventional monitors or non-immersive VR systems; in one study comparing stereoscopic three-dimensional (3D) videos on flat screens, panoramic screens, and VR headsets, VR headset users experienced more CS.

10/S2/F8.text: Users with higher-end head-mounted displays (HMDs) experience less cybersickness (CS) than users with lower-end HMDs, a difference related to display qualities such as resolution, brightness, clarity, and contrast.

10/S2/F9.text: In virtual reality (VR), the type of input method used, such as hand controllers, treadmills, and motion sensors, can influence the level of cybersickness (CS).

10/S2/F10.text: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

10/S3/F0.text: The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.

10/S3/F1.text: Virtual reality (VR) content is an external factor among the causes of cybersickness.

11/S0/F0.text: The design of virtual environments can have a significant impact on the likelihood and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

11/S0/F1.text: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

11/S0/F2.text: Visual motion, the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality (VR) environment, is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness (CS), and higher visual motion can increase the risk of cyber sickness while the way the content moves also affects cyber sickness and its severity.

11/S0/F3.text: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).

11/S0/F4.text: The severity of cyber sickness (CS) also significantly increases with larger height and faster speed in a virtual environment.

11/S0/F5.text: The viewpoint during motion is also an important factor for cyber sickness (CS).

11/S0/F6.text: Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cyber sickness (CS), but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cyber sickness.

11/S0/F7.text: Cyber sickness (CS) increases with increasing angular velocity and is more intense when rotation takes place around the x and y axes than around the z axis.

11/S1/F0.text: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

11/S1/F1.text: Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence.

11/S1/F2.text: The type and extent of the control mechanism used in virtual reality (VR) determine the likelihood of cybersickness (CS); research studies find that hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cybersickness than whole-body motion control.

11/S1/F3.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

11/S2/F0.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.

11/S2/F1.text: A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.

11/S2/F2.text: Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

11/S2/F3.text: An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

11/S2/F4.text: The type of content is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and action content, fast movements, and abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment are found to induce more CS than neutral and static content.

11/S2/F5.text: For users with a high preference for adrenaline sports or adventurous things, exposure to action content, fast movements, or abrupt alterations in a virtual reality (VR) environment may not lead to severe cybersickness (CS) compared with users who are not exposed to such sports or adventures, because they are already accustomed to such behavior and environments.

11/S2/F6.text: The genre of a virtual environment affects cybersickness (CS), and content based on horror scenes is likely to induce more CS than pleasant general content.

11/S2/F7.text: The geometry and terrain of a virtual environment affect cybersickness (CS); when a user travels over regular bumps and irregular terrain, CS is more likely than when the same travel occurs over flat terrain without bumpy rides.

11/S2/F8.text: Weather conditions in a virtual environment affect the induction of cybersickness (CS); stormy conditions are more likely to cause higher CS than clear weather conditions.

11/S3/F0.text: Virtual reality (VR) exposure duration is an important factor in cybersickness (CS), and prolonged exposure through head-mounted displays (HMDs) leads to greater cybersickness.

11/S3/F1.text: Cybersickness (CS) increases with virtual reality (VR) exposure time when users use different locomotion controllers during navigation tasks in a virtual environment, and the effect of the locomotion technique used to move from one point to another on cybersickness is further complicated by longer duration.

11/S3/F2.text: Continuous exposure to live-action 180-degree videos results in higher cybersickness (CS), and the increase in cybersickness grows with exposure time.

11/S3/F3.text: Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

11/S4/F0.text: Measurement techniques for cybersickness (CS) rely on three components: the input provided for measurement, the measurement technique itself, and the output generated.

11/S4/F1.text: Inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) can be questionnaire-based, physiological and biometric information, behavioral information, and content-based information.

11/S4/F2.text: The measurement technique or evaluation process for cybersickness (CS) can be manual, automated, machine learning-based, or real-time evaluation while the experience is taking place.

11/S4/F3.text: The output of cybersickness (CS) measurement can be binary classes, multiple classes, or a sickness score that is a number.

11/S4/F4.text: Questionnaire-based input for measuring cybersickness (CS) is a common method that uses self-report questionnaires or scales, generally in the form of ratings, to rate users' discomfort or disorientation on a numerical scale.

11/S4/F5.text: Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are easy to administer and help researchers or practitioners better understand the causes of cybersickness and identify potential interventions.

11/S4/F6.text: Questionnaire-based cybersickness (CS) scales are typically administered before or after an experience, can also be administered during the experience, with before and after being the most common timing and during being occasional.

11/S4/F7.text: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness (CS).

11/S4/F8.text: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) contains 16 items divided into three subscales: the oculomotor subscale, the disorientation subscale, and the nausea subscale.

11/S4/F9.text: In the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ), participants rate the intensity of individual symptoms belonging to the oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea subscales on a scale from 0 to 3, where a higher score denotes more severe symptoms.

11/S4/F10.text: The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) was not originally designed for virtual reality (VR) but was adapted for use in the context of virtual reality.

11/S4/F11.text: Questionnaires specifically designed for virtual reality (VR) include the Virtual Reality Sickness Questionnaire (VRSQ) and the Cyber Sickness Questionnaire (CSQ), which is good for evaluating virtual reality experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).

11/S4/F12.text: Shorter and more concise questionnaires used to assess specific conditions include the Misery Scale (MIS) and the Fast Motion Sickness Scale (FMS).

11/S4/F13.text: Questionnaires used to measure susceptibility to cybersickness (CS) include the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MS-SQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMS or VIMS-SQ).

11/S4/F14.text: Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort include the Nausea Scale and the Motion Sickness Assessment Questionnaire (MSAQ).

11/S5/F0.text: Physiological or biometric inputs can be used to detect cybersickness (CS) because questionnaire-based inputs can be subjective, are prone to inaccuracies, and may not always be reliable.

11/S5/F1.text: Electroencephalogram (EEG) is one of the widely used physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS).

11/S5/F2.text: Physiological or biometric inputs for detecting cybersickness (CS) include heart rate, galvanic skin response (GSR), electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG), electrogastrogram (EGG), electrooculography (EOG), respiration signals, photoplethysmography (PPG), and electromyogram (EMG).

11/S6/F0.text: Behavioral inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include blink rate, head and body movement, the manner of those movements, and postural sway.

11/S6/F1.text: Postural sway can be monitored for measuring cybersickness (CS) during virtual reality (VR) exposure using axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure.

11/S6/F2.text: Postural instability is positively correlated with the severity of cybersickness (CS), so postural sway can indicate CS severity.

11/S6/F3.text: Content-based inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) include optical flow, depth cues, and exceptional motion velocity.

11/S6/F4.text: Optical flow is the apparent motion perceived by virtual reality (VR) users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

11/S6/F5.text: The four categories of inputs for measuring cybersickness (CS) are questionnaire-based inputs, which are subjective; physiological and biometric inputs, which are objective; behavioral inputs; and content-based inputs.

11/S7/F0.text: Cybersickness (CS) measurement techniques based on input are broadly of two types: manual evaluation, which is based on human intervention, and machine learning-based (ML) or automated evaluation, which uses automated algorithms on input to measure cybersickness.

11/S7/F1.text: Manual evaluation for cybersickness (CS) is entirely based on human intervention and typically uses questionnaire-based assessment, in which a person distributes the questionnaire, collects feedback, and reviews the responses to decide the severity, onset, or possibility of cybersickness.

11/S7/F2.text: Machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) can use psychological, physiological, or biometric inputs to train models that automatically determine cybersickness.

11/S7/F3.text: One way to perform machine learning-based (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) is to use transparent models, which provide clear insight into the decision-making process and whose inner workings can easily be understood.

11/S7/F4.text: Stepwise regression analysis can be considered a transparent model that is utilized to measure cybersickness (CS) using a variety of physiological signals or physiological inputs.

12/S0/F0.text: Cybersickness (CS) evaluation strategies can be organized into three aspects: input, process, and output.

12/S0/F1.text: In machine learning (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS), interpretable models are similar to transparent models, offer more flexibility in customization and in how the model is used, and provide more precise details about the relationships between the input and the output.

12/S0/F2.text: Interpretable machine learning (ML) algorithms used to measure cybersickness (CS) include CN2 rule induction, bagged decision trees, Naive Bayes classifiers, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), and long short-term memory (LSTM) regression analysis.

12/S0/F3.text: Combinations of machine learning (ML) techniques have also been used to identify and provide insight into cybersickness (CS); for example, explainable boosting machine (EBM), decision tree, and logistic regression were combined using biophysiological and subjective measurements as input.

12/S0/F4.text: Black-box models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation are models that cannot be easily understood or explained; they take an input and produce an output without revealing how or why that output is generated from the input, unlike transparent or interpretable models.

12/S0/F5.text: Black-box models studied for cybersickness (CS) evaluation include long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural network (CNN), and support vector machine (SVM) models.

12/S0/F6.text: In a study comparing long short-term memory (LSTM), convolutional neural network (CNN), and support vector machine (SVM) models for cybersickness (CS) measurement, LSTM achieved the best results.

12/S0/F7.text: Black-box models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation generally provide higher prediction accuracy than transparent and interpretable models, but unlike those other models they require large amounts of data and processing power.

12/S0/F8.text: Hybrid models in machine learning (ML) evaluation of cybersickness (CS) are combinations of different machine learning (ML) models, designed to provide high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process.

12/S0/F9.text: Hybrid models used to predict or classify cybersickness (CS) include a combination of a deep embedded self-organizing map (DESOM) and an autoencoder designed from EEGNET, a specialized convolutional neural network (CNN) for electroencephalography (EEG) prediction, and a voting classifier combining random forest, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression, and a multilayer perceptron neural network for binary and three-level classification.
