12/S0/F10.text: Hybrid models in cybersickness (CS) evaluation can combine the strengths of transparent and black-box models by providing good predictive accuracy and some interpretability, making them useful in application domains where both high accuracy and transparency are essential, such as medical diagnosis.

12/S1/F0.text: Classification based on the event of measurement is a category of cybersickness (CS) evaluation technique that distinguishes detection, which uses input generated after the experience to determine whether cybersickness has occurred, from prediction, which occurs before the experience to determine whether cybersickness will occur.

12/S1/F1.text: Most cybersickness (CS) evaluation work focuses on detection rather than prediction, but prediction is important because it can enable mitigation measures before cybersickness occurs.

12/S1/F2.text: Limited research on predicting cybersickness (CS) uses physiological signals and video features, baseline measurements before virtual reality (VR) immersion, and machine learning (ML) studies that predict susceptibility to cybersickness or impending cybersickness episodes.

12/S1/F3.text: The outputs of self-report questionnaires for cybersickness (CS) are generally scores or ratings on rating scales, and these scores or ratings can be used to assess the severity of cybersickness.

12/S1/F4.text: Machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation can produce either classification labels or a numerical sickness score as output.

12/S1/F5.text: In machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation, classification labels indicate the likelihood or severity of cybersickness, for example sickness or no sickness, or low, moderate, or acute sickness.

12/S1/F6.text: In machine learning (ML)-based cybersickness (CS) evaluation, a sickness score quantifies the severity of the cybersickness experience and is generally produced by a regression model.

12/S2/F0.text: Because complete prevention of cybersickness (CS) is generally not possible, cybersickness mitigation uses measures to reduce or eliminate cybersickness or at least lessen its impact.

12/S2/F1.text: Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

12/S2/F2.text: Cybersickness (CS) mitigation is considered from two important perspectives, the developer's perspective and the user's perspective, because even a good developer solution may fail to prevent cybersickness if the user does not use the system properly or as expected.

12/S3/F0.text: Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.

12/S3/F1.text: Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.

12/S3/F2.text: Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.

12/S3/F3.text: Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

12/S3/F4.text: A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.

12/S3/F5.text: A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

12/S3/F6.text: An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

12/S3/F7.text: A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.

12/S3/F8.text: A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

12/S3/F9.text: Dynamic visual blur is a technique for reducing the possibility of cybersickness (CS) in which blurring means obscuring or reducing clarity, and it has two types: depth-of-field blur, which uses well-known depth cues in human vision, and peripheral blur, also called dynamic non-salient region blurring.

12/S3/F10.text: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, and rest frames attached to the head reference frame are known as independent visual backgrounds, with examples including clouds, grids, and a virtual nose.

12/S3/F11.text: Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.

12/S3/F12.text: Hardware-level alterations can reduce or eliminate cybersickness (CS) by modifying existing hardware to different degrees or by proposing completely new hardware.

12/S3/F13.text: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a sparse peripheral display that expands a head-mounted display (HMD) periphery with a colorful LED matrix, and miniature LED screens placed in the HMD.

12/S3/F14.text: Hardware-level alterations for reducing cybersickness (CS) include a Noble camera setup twin cam that reduces motion blur and cybersickness, and a hybrid 360 panoramic video camera rig that can be used to reduce cybersickness.

12/S3/F15.text: Phantom legs is a hardware-level alteration that applies alternating haptic cues synchronized to users' footsteps using additional hardware, and it was found to reduce cybersickness (CS) to a great extent.

12/S3/F16.text: Floor vibrations are a hardware-level alteration for reducing cybersickness (CS) that uses vibration-driven whole-body tactile feedback to match the vibrations of the virtual environment.

12/S3/F17.text: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration is a hardware-level alteration that has been tried for reducing cybersickness (CS), for example in a walking vibe system that uses two small vibration motors behind the ears for vibrotactile feedback during a walking experience.

12/S3/F18.text: Modified motion platforms are a hardware-level alteration in which short bursts of rotational acceleration matching visual forward acceleration were found quite effective in reducing cybersickness (CS), and the platforms can be modified to produce this effect.

12/S3/F19.text: Locomotion techniques can play a crucial role in preventing cybersickness (CS), and they can be modified or new techniques can be proposed to reduce its effect.

12/S3/F20.text: Locomotion modifications for reducing cybersickness (CS) include novel walking methods instead of natural walking, teleportation rather than steering-based locomotion, dynamic steering speed that skips certain locations when going over long distances to reduce the duration of virtual exposure, viewpoint snapping that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation, and invisible ramps placed on top of stairs.

12/S4/F0.text: Cybersickness (CS) is subjective and individual susceptibility to cybersickness varies, so a one-size-fits-all approach or developer-side interventions alone may not be sufficient and users need their own countermeasures to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

12/S4/F1.text: To reduce the risk of cybersickness (CS), users may be advised to avoid continuous or long-duration exposure to a virtual environment, and studies suggest that the generally safe maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) session for the majority of users likely to suffer from cybersickness is between 55 and 70 minutes, although the exact duration may vary with device, content, and other factors, and longer exposure is risky.

12/S4/F2.text: Habituation is the gradual decrease in the intensity of cybersickness (CS) after repeated experience in a virtual environment.

12/S4/F3.text: Users can attempt habituation to a virtual environment through a two-stage approach in which users first use repeated short-duration exposures until undesirable symptoms appear, then use repeated longer-duration exposures after full recovery from cybersickness (CS) symptoms.

12/S4/F4.text: Users can try slow diaphragmatic breathing, or controlled breathing patterns, to delay the onset, reduce the severity, and, to a large extent, reduce the possibility of cybersickness (CS).

12/S4/F5.text: Playing pleasant background music and ensuring adequate external air flow are user-side strategies that can calm or soothe the mind and reduce cybersickness (CS).

13/S0/F0.text: A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

13/S0/F1.text: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

13/S0/F2.text: In a complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, the organism component, which typically refers to the human user, is equally important to account for as the VR hardware component and cannot be omitted because the user is always present.

13/S1/F0.text: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

13/S1/F1.text: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

13/S2/F0.text: The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

13/S2/F1.text: The surrounding physical environment is considered part of the virtual reality (VR) system because the user may respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, and may not be completely detached from the real world, so the environment may affect the user's behavior while interacting with the virtual world.

13/S2/F2.text: A user's physical movement while interacting with the virtual world may change the surrounding physical environment.

13/S2/F3.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience.

13/S2/F4.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

13/S2/F5.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware is not limited to only the computer, head-mounted display (HMD), or controller used by the user; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment.

13/S3/F0.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays (output devices), sensors (input devices), and computers (processing devices).

13/S3/F1.text: In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a display or output device is used in a broad sense to mean any device that produces output that stimulates the user's sensory organs, not only a visual display.

13/S3/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.

13/S3/F3.text: In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a computer or processing device is used in a broad sense to mean a device that processes inputs and produces outputs for the user to perceive the world.

13/S4/F0.text: Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

13/S4/F1.text: Hand input devices in virtual reality (VR) fall into five broad categories: world-grounded devices, non-tracked handheld controllers, tracked handheld controllers, hand-worn devices, and bare-hand inputs.

13/S4/F2.text: World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area.

13/S4/F3.text: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

13/S4/F4.text: Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence because the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the position of the virtual hands in the virtual world, creating discomfort about whether the user is performing the task appropriately and affecting the perception of presence in the virtual world.

13/S4/F5.text: Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

13/S4/F6.text: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

13/S4/F7.text: Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

13/S4/F8.text: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

13/S4/F9.text: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

13/S4/F10.text: The advantages of hand-worn hand input devices are natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction, comfortable hand positions, no line-of-sight issue unlike some controller-based input, and the ability of the user's hands and fingers to fully interact with real objects, making different sorts of perception possible.

13/S4/F11.text: Issues with hand-worn hand input devices are that recognizing many gestures requires users to recalibrate often or to learn and remember many gestures, which can create problems for different user categories, and that long exposure time can become uncomfortable because the hands may become sweaty.

13/S4/F12.text: Bare-hand inputs are the most natural hand input interactions: the system tracks the user's bare hand using computer vision techniques, the user does not need to wear anything or use any external device, and computer vision algorithms detect the user's gestures and translate them into commands in the virtual environment, leaving the user's hands completely free.

13/S4/F13.text: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

13/S4/F14.text: The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.

13/S4/F15.text: The Leap Motion device has problems: fatigue may occur from holding hands in front of its sensor or camera, the hand must be in the line of sight of its camera, and consistent recognition of gestures across a wide range of users may be an issue.

13/S5/F0.text: Non-hand-based input devices are input devices that capture input from parts of the body other than the hand, including head movement, eye gaze, voice, and body movement.

13/S5/F1.text: Head-tracking-based input devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically use head motion for input, and a head-mounted display (HMD) worn by the user can double as a head tracking device with sensors that detect yaw, roll, and pitch and infer the input to change the view.

13/S5/F2.text: Eye tracking devices are non-hand-based input devices that typically come integrated with headsets and track eye movements, including where the user is looking and how the eyes are moving, helping the system understand the user's eye movement and infer what action to take.

13/S5/F3.text: The Midas touch problem in eye tracking-based input is the inability to differentiate an intentional gaze meant to select an object from a habitual blank gaze, so the system may select an object or perform an action even though the user did not intend to.

13/S5/F4.text: Multimodal input, which uses other forms of input in addition to eye tracking, is generally preferable over only eye tracking-based input for interacting with a system because eye tracking alone can cause objects to be selected or actions to be performed from unintentional gazes.

13/S6/F0.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware must be understood from the overall system point of view, considering the multiple components of the system, not only the hardware part, and how those components interact with the hardware, so that the requirements and the hardware to look for are known.

13/S6/F1.text: The three major hardware components of any virtual reality (VR) system are input, output, and processor.

14/S0/F0.text: Non-hand input techniques in virtual reality (VR) consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

14/S0/F1.text: Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method in virtual reality (VR) that tracks full-body movement, more than the head, hands, and eyes.

14/S0/F2.text: Full-body tracking can add to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in a virtual world because its output can show the user a fuller representation of themselves.

14/S0/F3.text: There are two broad approaches to full-body tracking: a motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.

14/S0/F4.text: In a motion capture suit (MOCAP) approach to full-body tracking, sensors in the suit capture and transmit raw movement data, which are combined and converted into full-body position and movement; for example, the Perception Neuron suit uses straps with inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors on the legs, hands, arms, and head.

14/S0/F5.text: In camera-based full-body tracking, multiple surrounding cameras observe an actor wearing a suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, and infer the actor's overall body movement from the markers' movement; OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect are examples of such camera-based full-body tracking systems.

14/S0/F6.text: Sound-based tracking is a non-hand input technique in virtual reality (VR) that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in a 360-degree environment.

14/S1/F0.text: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the processing part or computer is a device that processes data from input sensors and, based on that processing, activates or actuates output devices.

14/S1/F1.text: The processing element or computer in a virtual reality (VR) system may be a standard personal computer (PC), a high-end workstation with a high-quality graphics processing unit (GPU), a distributed computer system interconnected through a high-speed communication network, or a smartphone, and its selection depends on the application, the target users, the assumed input and output devices and their availability, and the required level of immersion.

14/S1/F2.text: The major components of a computer used as the processing element in a virtual reality (VR) system are the graphics processing unit (GPU), the central processing unit (CPU), and random access memory (RAM).

14/S1/F3.text: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is used to speed up the rendering process because of its inherent parallel processing abilities and the inherent parallelism in the rendering process, and it is therefore very useful for rendering complex graphics and complex scenes that are part of realistic virtual reality (VR) experiences.

14/S1/F4.text: Multi-GPU-enabled systems are typically used for building virtual reality (VR) applications, and a good-quality graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled graphics card or GPU-enabled environment is preferable, especially for rendering.

14/S1/F5.text: In virtual reality (VR) processing, multicore processors greatly increase computational capacity compared with non-multicore or unicore processors, and nowadays processors are multicore by default.

14/S1/F6.text: Modern central processing unit (CPU) processors are quite powerful, but they have many other tasks to do, so a CPU-only virtual reality (VR) processing system with minimal graphics processing unit (GPU) support can have performance issues, and GPU support is preferable.

14/S1/F7.text: An extended reality (XR) engine is middleware required to support, develop, and render virtual reality (VR) experiences.

14/S1/F8.text: Each extended reality (XR) engine has its own minimum random access memory (RAM) requirement, and at least 8 GB of RAM is typically preferable in a virtual reality (VR) system's hardware for a good user experience.

14/S2/F0.text: Output devices for virtual reality (VR) experience include visual displays, audio output, haptics, motion platforms and treadmills, and other sensory outputs that stimulate the taste and smell sensory organs, namely the tongue and nose.

14/S2/F1.text: Other sensory output systems for taste and smell in virtual reality (VR) are premature, not widely used, available, or popular, and are mostly confined to highly specialized environments or research domains.

14/S2/F2.text: Visual displays are displays meant to stimulate the visual sense, that is the eyes.

14/S2/F3.text: The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.

14/S2/F4.text: Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.

14/S2/F5.text: A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

14/S2/F6.text: A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.

14/S2/F7.text: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

14/S2/F8.text: Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

14/S2/F9.text: A world-fixed display renders graphics onto a surface or screen that is fixed and does not move with the user's head; the display is not moving, while the user can move within a physical space.

14/S2/F10.text: World-fixed displays range from standard monitors to displays that completely surround the user, typically called a cave.

14/S2/F11.text: The fish tank display, developed in 1993, is an early world-fixed virtual reality (VR) display that uses a fixed cathode-ray tube (CRT) monitor as the output and an optical head tracker and a haptic device as inputs, so that the stereo perspective view of a 3D scene changes as the user's head moves.

14/S2/F12.text: A more recent world-fixed display example is the surround screen, or cave system, which typically has three to six large screens around the user for visual immersion and is usually driven by a single or group of powerful graphics engines and requires elaborate tracking of the user's movements.

14/S2/F13.text: Regular displays, which can be mobile or stationary, refer to common tablets or smartphones, are not specialized, are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality (VR), and are mostly used for augmented reality (AR).

14/S3/F0.text: Audio output is an output device typically used in a virtual reality (VR) setup, and it can provide specialized three-dimensional (3D) audio for a sense of where sounds are coming from, with speakers fixed in space or moving with the head, and headphones are preferred for a fully immersive system because the sound source can change with head movement.

14/S3/F1.text: Haptic rendering systems are outputs that activate touch sensation and explore touch perception, and haptic outputs can be categorized as passive versus active, tactile versus proprioceptive, and self-grounded versus world-grounded devices.

14/S3/F2.text: Passive haptic devices are static real-world physical objects that match the shape of virtual objects and are not controlled by the computer, whereas active haptic devices are physical objects or physical feedback controlled by the computer that provide a sense of touch when interacting with virtual objects.

14/S3/F3.text: Tactile haptics are haptic devices that provide touch sensations through the skin, and they include vibrotactile stimulation, which uses mechanical vibration of the skin, and electrotactile stimulation, which uses electrodes that pass current through the skin.

14/S3/F4.text: Proprioceptive force-based haptics use forces that activate joints or muscles and provide a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance by providing corresponding signals to the muscles and joints.

14/S3/F5.text: Self-grounded haptic devices are worn or held by the user and move with the user, with handheld controllers as examples, whereas world-grounded haptic devices are physically attached to the real world, cannot be moved, and can provide the sense of fully solid objects that do not move.

14/S3/F6.text: Motion platforms are hardware output devices that move the entire body to produce a sense of physical motion and gravity, conveying a sense of orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.

14/S3/F7.text: Use of motion platforms may result in motion sickness, which can be reduced by decreasing the conflict between visual motion and the perceived motion in the real world.

14/S3/F8.text: Motion platforms can be active, meaning they are controlled by computer simulation, or passive, meaning they are controlled by the user with no direct computer control, and passive platforms are likely to result in less motion sickness than active platforms.

14/S3/F9.text: Treadmills are output devices that provide the sense of walking or running while staying in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

14/S3/F10.text: Omnidirectional treadmills are common in virtual reality systems and can be active, with computer-controlled mechanically moving parts that create the sensation of walking or moving, or passive, containing no computer-controlled mechanically moving parts and controlled by the user.

15/S0/F0.text: Augmented reality (AR) devices can be categorised into headsets and glasses, handheld devices, projection-based systems, spatial augmented reality (spatial AR), head-up displays, and AR contact lenses.

15/S0/F1.text: Examples of augmented reality (AR) headsets, smart glasses, and handheld devices include Microsoft HoloLens as a headset, Google Glass and Vuzix Blade Glasses as smart glasses, and smartphones, tablets, and Nintendo devices as handheld devices.

15/S0/F2.text: Examples of augmented reality (AR) projection-based systems include projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems, while examples of spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) include interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, projection mapping software, laser projectors, and projection keyboards, with interactive projectors and projection keyboards appearing under both categories.

15/S0/F3.text: Augmented reality (AR) head-up displays are typically found in cars.

15/S0/F4.text: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by Google, Innovega, Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens, and Innovega's iOptic system.

15/S0/F5.text: The application domains of augmented reality (AR) device categories include headsets and smart glasses in education, retail, healthcare, tourism, and manufacturing; handheld devices in education, retail, e-commerce, tourism, and real estate; projection-based systems and spatial augmented reality (spatial AR) in industrial design, healthcare, training, retail, gaming, education, art and design, medical training, industrial applications, and entertainment; head-up displays in gaming experiences, medicine, wearables, and sports; and AR contact lenses in medical development.

15/S1/F0.text: Generally, augmented reality (AR) headsets are larger and more immersive, present more content in the form of real-world content and augmented digital content, and provide a wider field of view.

15/S1/F1.text: Augmented reality (AR) headsets typically include built-in sensors, often cameras and depth sensors, and some of these sensors may or may not also be present in virtual reality (VR) headsets.

15/S1/F2.text: The Microsoft HoloLens is one example of an augmented reality (AR) headset, and other such headsets are available.

15/S1/F3.text: The Microsoft HoloLens includes two depth cameras, one noise-cancelling microphone, a speaker, a port for attaching headphones, special glasses that project digital content onto the regular real-world view, a tilt mechanism, nose pads, one camera, one projector, sensors, a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) optical head-mounted display (HMD), and spatial audio capabilities.

15/S1/F4.text: Virtual reality (VR) headsets may not include some advanced features of augmented reality (AR) headsets and typically have fewer components than an AR headset such as the Microsoft HoloLens, because VR does not need to provide a real-world view.

15/S1/F5.text: The Microsoft HoloLens integrates high-definition holograms or digital content with the real-world view obtained through its special glasses.

15/S1/F6.text: Interaction in the Microsoft HoloLens takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions, and the device is equipped with detection of eye movements, voice commands, and hand gestures.

15/S2/F0.text: Compared with augmented reality (AR) headsets, AR smart glasses are lighter, less immersive, wearable devices that resemble standard eyeglasses, usually have a smaller field of view, are less powerful, and are more comfortable to wear for extended periods, whereas AR headsets are more powerful wearables.

15/S2/F1.text: Augmented reality (AR) smart glasses provide simpler heads-up display-type AR digital content overlays rather than the full 3D holograms provided by AR headsets, because AR headsets contain more components, sensors, and projectors than AR smart glasses.

15/S2/F2.text: Google Glass is an earlier example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that presents data in a format similar to a smartphone, operates hands-free, and supports interaction through natural-language voice commands, with built-in detection of those commands.

15/S2/F3.text: Google Glass includes a gyroscope, accelerometer, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, speaker, trackpad, microphone, camera, and projector, but its projector and camera are less powerful than similar components in an augmented reality (AR) headset.

15/S2/F4.text: Vuzix's Blade is another example of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses that includes tracking sensors and output actuators, including dual haptic feedback components, a display engine, a see-through display, noise-cancelling microphones, Android operating system (OS), memory storage, a camera, universal serial bus (USB) connectivity, a touchpad, and a place to store batteries.

15/S2/F5.text: Additional examples of augmented reality (AR) smart glasses include Epson glasses and Magic Leap glasses.

15/S2/F6.text: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices are familiar devices such as smartphones or tablets and are the most common and accessible devices used in AR.

15/S2/F7.text: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices use their own camera to capture a live real-world image that is displayed on the device screen, then overlay digital content on top of that live real-world view.

15/S2/F8.text: Handheld augmented reality (AR) devices typically rely on two main augmented reality technologies: marker-based AR and markerless AR.

15/S3/F0.text: Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices are the third category of augmented reality devices, also known as room-scale augmented reality or tabletop augmented reality, and they typically use projectors to display graphical information on physical objects; unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, they overlay digital content on physical objects in the real world rather than on the user's view of the real world.

15/S3/F1.text: A defining feature of spatial augmented reality (AR) devices is that their display element is not tied to or held by the user, unlike headsets, glasses, or handheld devices, and they can provide more natural and intuitive interfaces than these other device categories.

15/S3/F2.text: Spatial augmented reality (AR) devices allow multiple users to interact simultaneously with digital content augmented onto a physical object, whereas with headsets, glasses, or handheld devices each user interacts only with the content on that user's own device and others cannot interact with it.

15/S3/F3.text: Major application areas for spatial augmented reality (AR) devices and systems include education, art and design, medical training, industrial applications, museums and exhibits, and entertainment.

15/S3/F4.text: The fundamental principle of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system is that it augments the physical environment by adding virtual objects that seem to coexist in the same space as real objects, so the digitally augmented content appears to coexist with the physical space surrounding the user.

15/S3/F5.text: Implementing a spatial augmented reality (AR) system requires understanding the geometry and lighting conditions of the physical environment for seamless mixing, which can be achieved using advanced depth sensors or computer vision techniques typically included in the system.

15/S3/F6.text: Projection-based augmented reality (AR) systems and spatial augmented reality systems generally refer to similar ideas.

15/S3/F7.text: Examples of spatial augmented reality (AR) systems discussed as major categories include interactive projectors, air sandboxes, projection keyboards, and projection mapping.

15/S3/F8.text: An interactive projector is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects images or interfaces onto any surface, turning the surface into an interactive display; for example, a projector can project an interface onto a tabletop, making the tabletop an interactive display and an augmented reality experience, and Sony Xperia Touch is an example.

15/S3/F9.text: An air sandbox is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that uses a projector and a sensor, such as a three-dimensional (3D) camera like Microsoft Kinect, to project a topographic map onto a physical box of sand and update the map in real time when users move the sand or gesture, allowing two to three users to interact simultaneously.

15/S3/F10.text: A projection keyboard is an example of a spatial augmented reality (AR) system that projects a virtual keyboard onto a flat surface, converting that surface into an interactive keyboard, and it may use infrared sensors to detect finger positions, which is the more common way to handle key-press interaction.

15/S3/F11.text: Projection mapping technology is a software-based application of spatial augmented reality (AR) in which software solutions such as TouchDesigner, MadMapper, or HeavyM are used with standard projectors to create complex projections onto three-dimensional (3D) space without a surface, for example projecting a map or a model of the Earth in air.

15/S3/F12.text: Projection mapping displays can be interacted with by rotating, pinching, zooming in, or zooming out.

15/S3/F13.text: Projection mapping is commonly used in entertainment and gaming industries.

15/S4/F0.text: A head-up display (HUD) is an augmented reality (AR) display category that projects images onto a transparent surface, usually a screen or visor; ideally the surface is invisible and only the content is visible, but borders or shades may be visible.

15/S4/F1.text: Head-up displays (HUDs) are commonly used in cars and aircraft.

15/S4/F2.text: In augmented reality (AR) hardware, head-mounted displays (HMDs), glasses, handheld devices, and spatial AR systems are bulky or require elaborate setups, and smartphones and tablets can be difficult to hold for a long time.

15/S4/F3.text: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses are an emerging display category and a future wearable technology; they are very small, can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens, are not visible to outsiders, and are still in the realm of the future.

15/S4/F4.text: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses superimpose digital images or information onto the wearer's field of vision directly on the lens.

15/S4/F5.text: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can contain miniaturized components placed on the lens, including imagers made on complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, a display, wireless components, motion sensors, and other sophisticated components.

15/S4/F6.text: Augmented reality (AR) contact lenses can be used to show information such as flight and seat information in front of the wearer while the wearer sees the real world, and may provide ways to interact with or change that information.

15/S4/F7.text: Examples of current activities developing augmented reality (AR) contact lenses include Google's smart contact lens project, InnoVega's eye optic system, and Mojo Vision's Mojo Lens.

15/S4/F8.text: The effect of augmented reality (AR) contact lenses on the user is not well known or researched; seeing a lot of changing information directly in front of the eyes may affect normal behavior or cause some sort of sickness.

16/S0/F0.text: Tracking is an integral hardware component of an extended reality (XR) system.

16/S0/F1.text: Keeping track of motion in the physical world is a crucial part of any extended reality (XR) system, more importantly in virtual reality (VR) systems.

16/S0/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracking is primarily about tracking the user's physical motion or input so that it can be translated into virtual motion in the virtual world.

16/S0/F3.text: In augmented reality (AR), tracking is primarily about registering virtual content in three-dimensional (3D) space with respect to an anchor in the real world, and it requires tracking the user's pose, position, and orientation as well as tracking moving real-world objects in the field of view.

16/S0/F4.text: Tracking is also commonly called sensing; tracking is the more popular term, but the devices that enable tracking are more often called sensors than trackers.

16/S1/F0.text: Tracking can be categorized by what is being tracked into three categories: tracking the user's sense organs, tracking the user's other body parts, and tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user.

16/S1/F1.text: Tracking of the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, is needed because they have body-controlled degrees of freedom and a display attached to them must be perceived as attached to the surrounding world, so their position and orientation are tracked to update the virtual world or user experience.

16/S1/F2.text: In virtual reality (VR), sense-organ tracking mostly focuses on head tracking, which is sufficient for the visual and aural components related to the eyes and ears.

16/S1/F3.text: In virtual reality (VR), eye tracking may be required if rendering and display technology require compensating for eye movements, and eye tracking may be part of head tracking.

16/S1/F4.text: Tracking of the user's other body parts is required when the user wants a representation of the body in the virtual world, such as avatars or virtual hands, and it may involve facial expressions or hand gestures for interaction, so the motion can be reproduced in the virtual world's matched zone.

16/S1/F5.text: For tracking of the user's other body parts, perfect matching is not required; approximate movement or an approximate representation of the body-part movement in the virtual world can provide a good experience.

16/S1/F6.text: A limiting case of tracking the user's other body parts is to send a simple explicit input signal, such as pressing a button, to change to a predetermined body configuration, such as making a virtual hand grasp an object, without elaborate or further tracking.

16/S1/F7.text: Tracking the surrounding environment not related to the user may involve tracking physical objects in the real world around the user; it is more important in augmented reality (AR), but also important in virtual reality (VR).

16/S1/F8.text: In augmented reality (AR), a moved physical object must be tracked in the real-world view so that digital content can be appropriately registered in three-dimensional (3D) space.

16/S1/F9.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracking the surrounding environment can alert the user to physical objects not represented in the virtual world, such as a wall, to reduce harm; for this, tracking the user is not useful, and the environment itself must be tracked.

16/S1/F10.text: In virtual reality (VR), tracked physical objects may be matched in the virtual world so that the user receives touch feedback while interacting with them, giving a better, more natural experience.

16/S1/F11.text: In telepresence applications, a large part of the physical world can be brought into the virtual world through live capture, augmenting the virtual world with a live capture of the real world; this is generally classified as augmented virtuality and is a form of tracking the surrounding environment.

16/S2/F0.text: The choice of how to track, and which tracking method or technique to apply, depends on tracker position, tracking process, and tracker types.

16/S2/F1.text: Based on the position of the tracker or sensor that provides input for tracking, tracking is categorized into outside-in tracking and inside-out tracking.

16/S2/F2.text: In outside-in tracking, the user's experience device does not contain the tracking sensors or trackers; instead, external trackers or sensors in the real world, such as cameras or markers, provide data that helps the system attached to the user identify and track the user's motion, pose, and orientation.

16/S2/F3.text: Most virtual reality (VR) headsets today that use external sensors fall under outside-in tracking.

16/S2/F4.text: Outside-in tracking is restricted to the specific area where its external sensors are placed and works only when the user is in that environment within the sensor range, whereas inside-out tracking has no such restriction because the user wears the sensors or the sensors are attached to the user.

16/S2/F5.text: Inside-out tracking is a tracking type in which the cameras or other sensors required for tracking are located within the device used for the experience, such as the head-mounted display (HMD) in virtual reality (VR), which is more common, so no other external devices are needed.

16/S2/F6.text: Examples of inside-out tracking are Microsoft HoloLens, Intel Project Alloy, and Qualcomm VR820.

16/S3/F0.text: There are two broad ways to obtain input for tracking: inside-out and outside-in.

16/S3/F1.text: The tracking process broadly consists of four steps: calibration, registration, integration, and drift correction.

16/S3/F2.text: In the tracking process, calibration is the step that transforms the output of imperfect sensors so that it behaves as closely as possible to the natural or real value, reducing sensor error.

16/S3/F3.text: In the tracking process, registration estimates or determines the initial position and orientation of the sensor, so that the starting point is known before movement can be tracked.

16/S3/F4.text: In the tracking process, integration aggregates sensory measurements from multiple sensors or input data sources at discrete time points to combine the values and track sense organs, body parts, or the environment.

16/S3/F5.text: In the tracking process, drift correction compensates for the difference between the estimated and actual position and orientation of the user, the user's sense organs, body parts, or objects in the environment, reducing estimation error.

17/S0/F0.text: An inertial measurement unit (IMU) is a composite hardware unit that mainly contains a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer, and is typically part of many modern devices, including mobile phones and head-mounted displays (HMDs).

17/S0/F1.text: In an inertial measurement unit (IMU), a gyroscope captures angular velocity, an accelerometer captures linear acceleration along the x, y, and z axes, and a magnetometer captures magnetic field strength along the x, y, and z axes.

17/S0/F2.text: Inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor tracking relies mainly on gyroscope readings of angular velocity, while the accelerometer and magnetometer do not directly contribute to the tracking estimation but can be used to detect drift errors and take corrective measures.

17/S1/F0.text: In the calibration of inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, a gyroscope provides angular velocity, and the measured angular velocity (omega_g) can differ from the actual angular velocity (omega_a) because the devices and measurement technique are imperfect, so the measurement error is omega_g minus omega_a.

17/S1/F1.text: In the calibration stage for inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, the objective is to make the measured angular velocity (omega_g) and the actual angular velocity (omega_a) as close as possible, which means reducing the measurement error to as small a value as possible.

17/S1/F2.text: One simple calibration model assumes a linear relationship between measured angular velocity (omega_g) and actual angular velocity (omega_a), for example omega_g = a + b omega_a, where the ideal condition omega_g = omega_a corresponds to a = 0 and b = 1, but this ideal condition never happens in practice and the linear relationship is not the only possible relationship.

17/S1/F3.text: The presented calibration uses many, sometimes thousands, paired samples from two sensors: a cheap, inaccurate inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor that produces the measured values (omega_g), and an expensive, highly accurate benchmark sensor that produces the actual values (omega_a), although the benchmark is very close rather than exact or ideal.

17/S1/F4.text: A simple calibration method compares the paired samples by computing, for n pairs, the sum of the squared differences between the expression C1 + C2 omega_g and the actual values omega_a, and it finds the constants C1 and C2 that minimize this sum; this classical optimization is linear least squares regression, one of many techniques that is used here for simplicity.

17/S1/F5.text: After the constants C1 and C2 are determined, calibration mathematically transforms the cheap sensor reading into a calibrated value omega_cal, defined as omega_cal = C1 + C2 omega_g, mapping the inexpensive measured angular velocity omega_g to the closest possible match with the actual value rather than by using an actually expensive or highly accurate sensor.

17/S2/F0.text: Registration is the step that finds the initial pose or initial orientation of the sensor or user and sets the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented as theta at t = 0.

17/S2/F1.text: A simplifying assumption for understanding registration is that the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on is taken as the initial orientation, with the initial alignment set to the forward direction.

17/S2/F2.text: Registration can be aided by fiducial markers, reflectors, or tags; it can also be performed without them using computer vision techniques, and the process is simpler when such aids are present.

17/S2/F3.text: Integration is the stage that computes the current sensor orientation theta_t at time t = k delta_t by adding to the initial orientation estimated during registration, theta_0, the sum of calibrated angular velocity samples W_cal_i times the sampling interval delta_t over the elapsed samples; the sensor data stream usually arrives at regular discrete intervals, and k is an integer.

17/S2/F4.text: A calibrated angular velocity sample W_cal_i is the angular velocity sample from a gyroscopic sensor at instant i, and it indicates a change in orientation equal to W_cal_i multiplied by the sampling interval delta_t.

17/S3/F0.text: Drift correction is usually done with the help of extra sensors and, in general, requires at least two sensors whose values are blended to estimate and correct drift.

17/S3/F1.text: For drift correction, a gyroscope may be used together with other sensors such as cameras, and in an inertial measurement unit (IMU), accelerometer and magnetometer readings can be used in addition to gyroscope values.

17/S3/F2.text: A classic approach to drift correction combines the two individually computed orientations at the same time instant using the expression theta_dk = alpha theta_gk + (1 - alpha) theta_ck, where theta_gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant, theta_ck is the orientation obtained with a camera at the kth instant, theta_dk is the drift-corrected orientation, and alpha is the gain parameter, a normalized value between 0 and 1.

18/S0/F0.text: Tracking technologies used in virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are categorized into electromechanical, electromagnetic, acoustic or ultrasonic, vision-based, inertial, and others, where the others category includes location-based and hybrid tracking technologies.

18/S1/F0.text: Electromechanical trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

18/S1/F1.text: Electromechanical trackers are of two types: world-fixed trackers and wearable trackers.

18/S1/F2.text: A world-fixed electromechanical tracker is a setup that is quite cumbersome, with a display attached to an electromechanically tracked setup that has mechanical pivoting, tracking sensors, and a counterbalance to make it stable.

18/S1/F3.text: Wearable electromechanical trackers are worn on a person's body and track and translate the movements of that person into animated avatar movement in a virtual world.

18/S1/F4.text: Wearable electromechanical trackers include products such as IGS 190, Gypsy 6, Gypsy Gyro, and exoskeleton tracker.

18/S1/F5.text: Wearable electromechanical trackers are not very comfortable to wear, are quite cumbersome, and are used in limited, highly specialized setups.

18/S2/F0.text: Electromagnetic trackers are non-contact position measurement devices in which a stationary transmitter in the environment produces a magnetic field, and a receiver attached to the headset moves with the head, and the receiver's real-time position is obtained from the magnetic field direction.

18/S2/F1.text: In an electromagnetic tracker, the transmitter generally has three antennas that produce three orthogonal magnetic fields, and these fields generate alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC) in the receiver; the resulting currents help track the head's position relative to a fixed position in the environment.

18/S2/F2.text: Acoustic tracking, also called ultrasonic tracking, uses ultrasonic signals from stationary transmitters, which can be called speakers, to determine the real-time position of receivers, which can be called microphones, that are attached to a head-mounted display (HMD), so the head's position or orientation can be tracked.

18/S2/F3.text: Electromagnetic tracking and acoustic or ultrasonic tracking both use stationary transmitters and receivers that move with the head or the user's body.

18/S2/F4.text: Acoustic or ultrasonic tracking requires line of sight between the transmitter and receiver, with no obstacle in between, whereas electromagnetic tracking does not require this line of sight.

18/S3/F0.text: Vision-based trackers are more prevalent trackers that determine poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras.

18/S3/F1.text: The three main categories of optical sensors that can be deployed to detect or track a pose are infrared sensors, visible light sensors, and three-dimensional (3D) structure sensors.

18/S3/F2.text: Infrared tracking is considered to be among the earliest vision-based tracking techniques developed and used in virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

18/S3/F3.text: Infrared tracking uses targets that emit or reflect light, which makes detection easy due to high brightness compared with the surroundings.

18/S3/F4.text: Infrared tracking is robust to adverse illumination effects such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows because it relies on infrared sensing rather than visible light sensing.

18/S3/F5.text: Infrared tracking can be done in two ways: outside looking in and inside looking out.

18/S3/F6.text: In outside looking in infrared tracking, cameras placed in the environment rather than on the tracked object detect targets attached to the object and use them to determine the object's pose and position.

18/S3/F7.text: In inside looking out infrared tracking, the camera is mounted with the user and detects external targets, from which it estimates poses.

18/S4/F0.text: Visible light tracking uses visible light sensors or optical cameras; optical cameras are the most common optical sensor type and are available in almost all consumer-grade electronic devices, including laptops, smartphones, and tablet personal computers (PCs), and in wearable devices, giving an abundant supply of such sensors.

18/S4/F1.text: Visible light tracking is classified into three tracking techniques: fiducial tracking, natural feature tracking, and model-based tracking.

18/S4/F2.text: Fiducial tracking adds fiducials, which are artificial landmarks in the environment, to aid registration and tracking of the object being tracked.

18/S4/F3.text: The complexity of fiducial tracking depends on the kind of fiducial used, such as small colored light-emitting diodes (LEDs) or pieces of paper, multi-ring fiducials for detection at greater distances, proportional width ring fiducials whose appearance changes with distance, or constant width ring fiducials whose ring width remains constant.

18/S5/F0.text: Natural feature tracking is the second category of visual light-based sensing that registers camera pose in real time using features already present in the natural environment, and it requires advanced image processing or computer vision techniques.

18/S5/F1.text: In natural feature tracking, the advanced image processing algorithms or computer vision techniques detect features that are unique to the surroundings with respect to the object to be tracked, such as points, corners, and line intersections.

18/S5/F2.text: In natural feature tracking, unique descriptors are calculated for each detected feature, and their role is to identify and differentiate one feature from other features.

18/S5/F3.text: In natural feature tracking, camera pose is estimated by using the calculated feature descriptors to match features detected in the scene with features detected in the object to be tracked.

18/S5/F4.text: Popular natural feature detection and description algorithms used for natural feature tracking include scale invariant feature transform (SIFT), speeded up robust features (SURF), binary robust independent elementary features (BRIEF), and binary robust invariant scalable key points (BRISK).

18/S6/F0.text: Model-based tracking is the third category of visible light-based sensing.

18/S6/F1.text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it, and as time passes the map is updated with the object's changing position, enabling real-time tracking.

18/S6/F2.text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) was originally developed for robot navigation and subsequently adapted for augmented reality.

18/S6/F3.text: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) allows drift-free tracking of unknown environments.

18/S6/F4.text: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is a further optimization of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) that allows tracking of the camera and mapping of the environment as separate activities.

18/S6/F5.text: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) was specifically designed for augmented reality.

18/S6/F6.text: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) improved both the accuracy of tracking and the overall performance.

18/S6/F7.text: Parallel Tracking and Mapping (PTAM) is more suitable for smaller environments because the computational requirements for larger environments are quite high.

18/S7/F0.text: 3D structure tracking (3D structure sensing) is a recent tracking technique that uses commercial sensors to obtain the 3D positions of points in the scene and creates 3D models of the structures in the environment for augmentation of the real-world view.

18/S7/F1.text: Commercial sensors capable of detecting 3D structure information from the environment became affordable in recent years, a trend that started with the introduction of the Microsoft Kinect device, and similar devices are available.

18/S7/F2.text: Kinect Fusion, an augmented reality (AR) system by Microsoft and an example of 3D structure tracking, uses data from the Kinect's structured light depth sensor to create high-quality 3D models of real objects and environments, and the models are also used for tracking the pose of the Kinect.

18/S8/F0.text: Inertial trackers are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration, and they measure only changes rather than absolute values.

18/S8/F1.text: Inertial trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and are part of the device that the user is using, for example most smartphones and head-mounted displays (HMDs) nowadays, so they have no range limitation and can be readily used for tracking.

18/S8/F2.text: Hybrid software-level sensors can be designed using the primary inertial sensors (a gyroscope, an accelerometer, and a magnetometer) and can be part of the device.

18/S8/F3.text: Basic types of tracking sensors typically used include electromechanical, electromagnetic, inertial, three-dimensional (3D) structure sensing, and light-based sensing.

18/S8/F4.text: Sensing approaches that do not directly fit into the basic tracking sensor categories include acoustic sensing and the global positioning system (GPS).

18/S8/F5.text: The global positioning system (GPS) is a positional tracking device that is particularly useful in outdoor environments.

18/S8/F6.text: The global positioning system (GPS) generally offers low accuracy, particularly in indoor environments, and allows only positional tracking.

18/S8/F7.text: Real time kinematic (RTK) technology can be used with a basic global positioning system (GPS) sensor to improve detection accuracy by using global positioning system signal carrier waves for measurement, providing further accuracy than the basic global positioning system.

18/S8/F8.text: The global positioning system (GPS) is typically utilized when accurate position registration is not important, when an approximation is good enough, or as part of a hybrid tracking system with other tracking systems.

18/S9/F0.text: Motion capture is a technique for digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans, and it can be based on any tracking method, so it is not a fundamentally new tracking method.

18/S9/F1.text: Motion capture is packaged as wearable suits that include tracking sensors, typically using one or two facial trackers and four or five full body tracking devices that can be cameras, and it records the movements of users who wear the suits and make movements.

18/S9/F2.text: Motion capture need not be real-time tracking; it can be non-real-time tracking as well.

18/S9/F3.text: Eye-tracking systems can be part of other trackers and can be head-mounted or remotely attached to a display or an external display.

18/S9/F4.text: Eye-tracking systems use optical tracking with a high-resolution camera-based tracking device, and they can also use techniques such as infrared lighting-based eye tracking, electro-oculography (EOG), and video-oculography (VOG).

18/S9/F5.text: Eye-tracking systems typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

18/S9/F6.text: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that uses two or more basic tracking systems or approaches, formed by combining basic tracking methods, and emotion capture is an example of a hybrid tracker.

18/S9/F7.text: Typically, hybrid trackers have been found to perform better than single-technology-based tracking.

19/S0/F0.text: The role of virtual reality (VR) software is to drive virtual reality hardware or augmented reality (AR) hardware, not merely to drive the hardware, so that the hardware generates appropriate stimuli that are appropriately received to stimulate human sense organs, creating a virtual reality experience that utilizes human senses.

19/S1/F0.text: In a virtual reality (VR) system, bidirectional data flows occur between the virtual reality hardware, the surrounding physical world, and the user (organism), with tracking and stimulation occurring between the user and the virtual reality hardware.

19/S1/F1.text: The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware works by the user operating input devices to generate data that is sent to and processed by the virtual reality system, and by sending the processed data back to output devices that generate stimuli to suitably affect the user's sense organs.

19/S1/F2.text: The data flow between a user and virtual reality (VR) hardware requires proper interaction design and modeling for the user's interaction with input devices, perceptual design and modeling so that stimuli generated by output devices suitably stimulate the user's sense organs, and software to process input data and generate output data.

19/S1/F3.text: The software part of the virtual reality (VR) data-flow diagram is represented by two components: the virtual reality engine and a software-and-database component.

19/S2/F0.text: Creating a virtual reality (VR) experience involves three activities: creating the virtual environment, which can also be called environment modeling or object modeling; creating the stereoscopic output view, which can also be called rendering; and incorporating interactions, which involve tracking hardware.

19/S2/F1.text: In the context of creating a virtual reality (VR) experience, the terms view or rendering are used in a broad sense to refer not only to visual output but also to output for other senses.

19/S2/F2.text: From the developer's point of view, virtual reality (VR) software should allow the developer to create a VR application by providing assistance in the three activities of creating the virtual environment, rendering the stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.

19/S2/F3.text: Ideally, virtual reality (VR) software should let a developer provide only high-level descriptions from which all low-level details are automatically determined; the developer can then use middleware between the developer and the hardware, following well-known patterns and calling well-designed software libraries to avoid micro-level activities; and the software should also allow the developer to design functions from scratch for original work rather than depending on middleware.

19/S2/F4.text: In practice, a virtual reality (VR) developer may need to implement much functionality from scratch instead of providing only high-level descriptions that software automatically converts to low-level details.

19/S2/F5.text: In practical virtual reality (VR) development, a developer may use a software development kit (SDK) for a particular headset or platform to handle lowest-level, platform-specific operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output; SDKs are platform dependent, with a platform being a combination of hardware and operating system (OS), and the developer may not handle the lowest-level operations directly but must understand the SDK that handles them.

19/S2/F6.text: A game engine can be used as middleware for virtual reality (VR) application development; game engines are generally developed for games, which need not be immersive VR games, and can be adopted for VR development or specific VR engines can be developed.

19/S2/F7.text: Using a game engine as middleware can avoid substantial initial effort but may be cumbersome for implementing ideas not part of standard video games, and if the engine is not specifically a virtual reality (VR) engine, the developer loses some flexibility.

19/S3/F0.text: The virtual world generator (VWG) is an abstraction of the whole virtual reality (VR) software system, treated as a black box whose internal operation is not considered.

19/S3/F1.text: The virtual world generator (VWG) receives input from low-level systems such as a head tracker that estimates the user's head position and orientation, a keyboard, a mouse, and a game controller, and other input devices, and simultaneous input events are arranged in a queue so that they can be processed systematically.

19/S3/F2.text: The virtual world generator (VWG) must maintain an internal reality that appears real to the user, convert incoming input into output so that renderers can extract information and calculate outputs for their displays, and keep output devices synchronized with the input data to maintain an input-output match.

19/S3/F3.text: The virtual world generator (VWG) can use several output renderers, including a visual renderer that generates a visual display, an aural renderer that generates an aural display sensed by the ears, and a haptic renderer that generates a haptic display sensed by the skin, along with other possible renderers.

19/S3/F4.text: A completely synthetic virtual world requires defining a triangular mesh in a three-dimensional space and maintaining material and physical surface properties that indicate how the surfaces interact with light, sound, and forces.

19/S3/F5.text: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models, and the software that helps a developer build a virtual reality (VR) experience should support computer-graphics operations.

19/S3/F6.text: A virtual world can also be a recorded physical world, made realistic by capturing the real world with cameras and using computer-vision and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) techniques, so virtual reality (VR) software may require support for SLAM or computer-vision techniques.

19/S3/F7.text: One possibility for creating a virtual world is texture mapping, in which camera images of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object; this is a common computer-graphics operation that virtual reality (VR) software should ideally support.

19/S4/F0.text: Matched motion in virtual reality (VR) is the maintenance of correspondence between a user's motions in the real world and the virtual world.

19/S4/F1.text: A matched zone is a place where the real world and the virtual world perfectly align; it corresponds to the safe real-world region where a user's physical movement is restricted, although the virtual world is not similarly confined, and movement within that region is translated to movement in other parts of the virtual world.

19/S4/F2.text: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) application that is not carefully implemented, an obstacle mismatch can occur when a virtual obstacle blocks the user without a corresponding physical obstacle in the matched zone, or when a physical obstacle exists in the matched zone without a corresponding virtual obstacle.

19/S4/F3.text: In virtual reality (VR), the real-world motions reflected in the virtual world vary among virtual reality experiences: head motions must be matched so the visual renderer uses the correct viewpoint, and other body parts require tracking and matched motion when the user needs hand-eye coordination or looks at those body parts during the experience.

19/S4/F4.text: Virtual reality (VR) software should include developer support for resolving matched-motion challenges, such as deciding which real-world motions to reflect and creating a correspondence between a user's physical motion in the matched zone and a different virtual motion.

19/S4/F5.text: User locomotion in virtual reality (VR), which is closely related to matched motion, is moving oneself in the virtual world while one's physical motion in the real world is not matched; it is motivated because users often want to move well outside the matched zone.

19/S4/F6.text: Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

19/S4/F7.text: A popular option for user locomotion in virtual reality (VR) is operating a game controller, mouse, or keyboard so the user's avatar can walk, run, jump, swim, climb, board a vehicle, and operate its controls while the user remains seated; the vehicle option is a vehicle metaphor.

19/S4/F8.text: Virtual reality (VR) locomotion operations that let the user avoid physical movement may lead to cyber sickness, which increases with exposure duration and other factors.

19/S4/F9.text: Support for user locomotion, including different sorts of locomotion so that cyber sickness can be addressed, should be part of virtual reality (VR) software.

20/S0/F0.text: Physics support is a required key support in a virtual world generator, in addition to computer graphics and computer vision support for rendering, locomotion support, and matched motion support.

20/S0/F1.text: A virtual world generator usually implements some physics, depending on the kind of generator and the extent of support it can provide.

20/S0/F2.text: The basic purpose of physics support in a virtual world generator is to make the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, so that events observed in the real world have similar events in the virtual world.

20/S0/F3.text: In most cases, object motion in a virtual world generator should be governed by basic laws of mechanics; support for basic laws should be good enough, while support for advanced laws can make motion more realistic, which sometimes may be desirable.

20/S0/F4.text: Physics support in a virtual world generator should make a dropped ball accelerate toward the ground due to gravity rather than move it at constant speed.

20/S0/F5.text: Collision support in a virtual world generator should ideally include collision detection, which determines whether two or more bodies intersect, and collision response, which determines how they should behave after a collision occurs.

20/S0/F6.text: Physics support in a virtual world generator should also replicate other physical-world phenomena, such as how light propagates, how light interacts with different surfaces, the effects generated, the sources of light and resulting illumination effects, and how sound and smell propagate.

20/S1/F0.text: A networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is a collaborative virtual reality experience created over a network, in which a shared virtual world is maintained by a system or a server, although such a network experience may not be required everywhere.

20/S1/F1.text: In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, each user has a distinct matched zone; matched zones may overlap in the real world, but most often they are disjoint and distributed around the Earth, so unwanted physical collision must be avoided when users are close, while users spread around the globe have no possibility of physical collision.

20/S1/F2.text: Within the shared virtual world of a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience, user interactions, including collisions, must be managed by the virtual reality system whether users are close or spread around the world.

20/S1/F3.text: In a networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) setting, the virtual world generator (VWG) should support eye movements, facial expressions, and body language when social interaction is important, and the burden of matched motion may increase as users meet each other.

20/S2/F0.text: To build a virtual reality (VR) experience, a developer can either build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch using a basic software development kit (SDK) for a specific headset, device, or platform, or use a ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) customized by choosing menu options and writing high-level scripts.

20/S2/F1.text: A basic software development kit (SDK) for a headset, device, or platform is typically expected to provide basic drivers to drive the hardware, interfaces or application programming interfaces (APIs) to access tracking data, and application programming interfaces (APIs) to make calls to graphical rendering libraries; in a virtual world generator (VWG), basic drivers and tracking cover some aspects and rendering covers other aspects, but not every aspect of locomotion or matched motion, physics, or networked collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience is typically taken care of by the software development kit (SDK).

20/S2/F2.text: When building a virtual world generator (VWG) from a basic software development kit (SDK), the developer must build, at the very least, the physics support of the virtual world from scratch, handling problems such as movement of an avatar, collision detection, occurrence of collision and the response to it, lighting models, and audio support; sometimes collaborative virtual reality (VR) experience support is also required.

20/S2/F3.text: Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch gives the developer maximum control and the ability to optimize performance because the developer can choose and implement the algorithms for physics support according to performance, rather than being forced to use whatever comes with a package.

20/S2/F4.text: Using a basic software development kit (SDK) to build a virtual world generator (VWG) from scratch imposes a difficult implementation burden and requires a lot of effort to understand and implement the overall system from scratch.

20/S2/F5.text: OpenSimulator and Unity3D can provide ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) support; OpenSimulator is an open-source alternative to Second Life designed to support developers in building a virtual society of avatars, and Unity3D is a popular game engine adapted to work for virtual reality (VR).

20/S2/F6.text: A ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) or higher-level engine makes it easy for developers to create a virtual reality (VR) experience in little time because it comes with supports, including support for collisions or physics, so the developer does not have to build things from scratch.

20/S2/F7.text: A ready-made virtual world generator (VWG) or engine is harder to use for highly original experiences not imagined by the engine builder because it comes with its own function supports and algorithm implementations that the developer must use, which restricts the developer, although it reduces effort.

20/S3/F0.text: A virtual reality (VR) engine, also called a game engine, is middleware that sits between hardware and higher-level application software, abstracts hardware functionalities for developers of extended reality (XR) applications, and provides support for hardware abstractions.

20/S3/F1.text: A game engine is a software development environment for building extended reality (XR) experiences, and a developer can build their own application on top of it.

20/S3/F2.text: A game engine can be thought of schematically as comprising multiple components, for example a physics engine, a rendering engine, an audio engine, and a user interface.
