20/S3/F3.text: An authoring tool for a game engine lets a developer access the different functionalities supported by the game engine in order to develop their own software that runs on top of the game engine.

20/S3/F4.text: An authoring tool for a game engine may provide loading options, feature-setting options, and logic-setting options, and its logic setting can sometimes be done through scripting, which can be part of a game engine development environment.

20/S3/F5.text: A development environment that comprises a game engine plus other components can include the entire authoring tool, and Unity three-dimensional (3D) Development Environment or Unity Hub is an example of such a development environment.

20/S3/F6.text: Typically, game engines have core functionalities that include rendering support, physics support, audio support, scripting for customizing various features, networking support primarily for multiplayer collaborative virtual reality (VR) experiences, and low-level support for platform-specific tasks, including memory management and other activities, with threading and localization support being part of memory management.

20/S4/F0.text: A rendering engine in a game engine helps generate animated three-dimensional (3D) graphics by rendering methods such as rasterization or ray tracing, a particular rendering engine may support a particular rendering method, and the rendering method adopted may depend on the sophistication level of the engine or platform.

20/S4/F1.text: Rasterization is less computationally intensive than ray tracing.

20/S4/F2.text: A rendering engine is typically built on one or multiple rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), such as Direct3D, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), or Vulkan, which provide software abstractions of the graphics processing unit (GPU).

20/S4/F3.text: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the hardware component that is used for speeding up the rendering process.

20/S4/F4.text: In a typical virtual reality (VR) system that uses a game engine as middleware, the layers from lowest to highest are hardware, rendering application programming interfaces (APIs), game engine, and application software, and the hardware layer includes a graphics processing unit (GPU), a central processing unit (CPU), and memory.

20/S4/F5.text: An audio engine is a part of basic game engine support that consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

20/S4/F6.text: An audio engine can perform its calculations on a central processing unit (CPU) or on a dedicated application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC), so it does not require a graphics processing unit (GPU), and audio engines are not typically associated with a GPU because a GPU is generally associated with graphics or rendering.

20/S4/F7.text: An audio engine can be built on top of abstraction application programming interfaces (APIs) such as Open Audio Library (OpenAL), Simple DirectMedia Layer (SDL) audio, X audio 2, and Wave audio.

20/S4/F8.text: A physics engine is one of the crucial components of a game engine and is responsible for emulating the laws of physics realistically within the application by providing a set of functions for simulating physical forces and collisions acting on various objects within the scene at runtime.

20/S4/F9.text: The rendering, audio, and physics engines are often basic components of a game engine, but not all game engines contain all of these components.

20/S4/F10.text: Unity 3D, Unreal Engine 4, CryEngine, Godot, Lumberyard, and Amazon Sumerian are examples of game engines.

20/S4/F11.text: Based on the latest market-share statistics, Unity 3D and Unreal Engine are the most popular game engines, with Unity 3D occupying almost 51% of the game-engine market share, Unreal Engine occupying 28%, and all other game engines together occupying the rest.

20/S4/F12.text: Unreal Engine's major features are freely available, whereas Unity 3D is proprietary, has a free version with limitations, and offers more flexibility in its proprietary versions.

20/S5/F0.text: Deployment of a virtual reality (VR) application can be native application deployment, which requires software development kits (SDKs) tailored to the platform and hardware, or web application deployment, which allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

20/S5/F1.text: In deployment, a platform typically means the operating system (OS) plus the hardware, with Windows or Mac OS for desktop platforms and Android or iOS for mobile platforms.

20/S5/F2.text: A software development kit (SDK) is a collection of software development tools in one installable package specific to a hardware and operating system (OS) combination, providing fundamental tools to design, build, and test virtual reality (VR) experiences for specific platforms.

20/S5/F3.text: Native deployment software development kits (SDKs) can be categorized in two ways: by application type, as virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) applications, and by availability, as proprietary or open source.

20/S5/F4.text: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are the most popular device types for virtual reality (VR) experiences.

20/S5/F5.text: Different head-mounted displays (HMDs) use different virtual reality (VR) software development kits (SDKs): the HTC Vive system can use the OpenVR SDK by Valve, the SteamVR SDK, or the VRTK SDK; the Oculus Rift uses the Oculus SDK; the Samsung Gear VR uses the Oculus Mobile SDK; the Sony PlayStation uses the PSVR SDK; and Google Daydream View or Google Cardboard uses the Google VR SDK.

20/S5/F6.text: The Google virtual reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) is open source but is no longer very much supported.

20/S6/F0.text: Web deployment tools can be broadly categorized as cloud hosting and rendering over a network tools, libraries for development support for deployment over the web, complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web, generic development editors for writing code for web-based deployment, and software development kit (SDK) support, including native software development kits and software development kits primarily meant for web deployment.

20/S6/F1.text: Cloud hosting and rendering support tools for web deployment only provide hosting and rendering over a network.

20/S6/F2.text: Examples of cloud hosting and rendering support tools include Azure Remote Rendering for three-dimensional (3D) rendering, NVIDIA CloudXR, Immersive Stream for extended reality (XR), which works on Google Cloud, Eco3D, and Arbor XR.

20/S6/F3.text: Some popular libraries for development support for deployment over the web include WebXR, Three.js, augmented reality (AR).js, three.xr.js, WaveXR, AFrame, Babylon.js, and ReactXR.js, and there are many more such libraries.

20/S6/F5.text: Three.js makes WebGL easier and is used for rendering.

20/S6/F7.text: Complete development and deployment tools for applications on the web include ZappAir, 8thWall, MyWebAR, VRDirect, GmetriXR, InstaVR, PlugXR, Amazon Sumerian, and other such tools.

21/S0/F0.text: Augmented Reality (AR) software tools can be categorized by developer skill, target application platform (desktop AR applications or mobile AR applications), or tracking technology (computer vision (CV)-based tracking or other sensors such as Global Positioning System (GPS) sensors).

21/S0/F1.text: In a skill-based hierarchy, Augmented Reality (AR) software tools are arranged in four categories according to decreasing programming skill: low-level software libraries or frameworks, rapid prototyping tools, plugins for existing developer tools, and standalone AR authoring tools.

21/S0/F2.text: The skill requirements for the four skill-based Augmented Reality (AR) software tool categories are: low-level software libraries or frameworks require strong programming or coding ability and understanding of how to call the library functions; rapid prototyping tools require some programming ability, lower than for low-level tools, and may require design prototyping skills; plugins require skill with the original developer tool with which the plugin is used; and standalone AR authoring tools assume no programming ability and can be used without any knowledge.

21/S0/F3.text: Examples of Augmented Reality (AR) software tools for each skill-based category are: AR Toolkit, OSG Art, StudiersTube, and MXR Toolkit for low-level software libraries or frameworks; FLAR Manager and OpenFrameworks for rapid prototyping tools; AR media plugins, Vuforia, MetaIO Unity plugins, and Dart for plugins for existing developer tools; and BuildAR, MetaIO Creator, and Wikitude for standalone AR authoring tools.

21/S1/F0.text: Low-level libraries and frameworks are the augmented reality (AR) software category that requires the maximum skill from the developer because they provide access to the core tracking and display functionality used to build an AR application.

21/S1/F1.text: ARToolKit is one of the most widely adopted software libraries for developing augmented reality (AR) applications; it is written in C and supports platforms such as Windows, Linux, and macOS.

21/S1/F2.text: ARToolKit provides marker-based tracking in its open-source version, while its commercial version, available from ARToolWorks, also supports tracking natural features on an arbitrary image using computer vision techniques.

21/S1/F3.text: ARToolKit is primarily a tracking-support library: it provides functions that enable a developer to perform tracking and then carry out a related activity.

21/S1/F4.text: ARToolKit provides only low-level OpenGL-based rendering support, with very primitive rendering and no built-in support for interaction techniques or complex realistic graphics, so using it alone yields a rudimentary system in which the developer must write interaction from scratch, making a complete realistic augmented reality (AR) application difficult and time-consuming.

21/S1/F5.text: Many standard augmented reality (AR) toolkits or low-level libraries primarily provide tracking support but lack the features needed for realistic rendering of digital content over the real-world view and for interaction support.

21/S1/F6.text: To overcome the limitations of ARToolKit or other tracking-focused low-level libraries, a framework for augmented reality (AR) system development can be created by combining multiple libraries, especially libraries that provide interaction and realistic graphics support.

21/S1/F7.text: A scene graph is a node-based graph, essentially a tree of nodes and links, that represents a computer graphics scene, allowing selective work with nodes to manipulate the scene, create realistic effects, and support interaction, thereby providing a way to manage the functionality of a complex graphics application.

21/S1/F8.text: Scene graph-based representations support operations that are part of a three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, including sorting objects according to visibility (visible surface detection), removing objects outside the camera field of view (clipping), state management, and higher-level abstractions of functionality.

21/S1/F9.text: When ARToolKit is combined with a scene graph library, the scene graph library can take care of low-level object rendering, so the developer can focus on interaction between virtual objects while ARToolKit remains responsible for tracking.

21/S1/F10.text: Open Scene Graph (OSG) is an open-source scene graph library, Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) is an open-source successor of OSG, and both are widely used.

21/S1/F11.text: Open Scene Graph (OSG) and similar scene-graph libraries are written in C++ and are built on top of OpenGL, which accesses lower-level hardware.

21/S1/F12.text: Open Scene Graph (OSG) supports a large number of plugins for additional functionality such as model loading, shadow rendering, and physics, which are primarily relevant for virtual reality (VR) and partly relevant for augmented reality (AR).

21/S1/F13.text: In an augmented reality (AR) example in which a phone detects a marker on a table and a three-dimensional (3D) cow object appears on the screen, the operation involves tracking, which recognizes the marker and its position, and three-dimensional (3D) registration, which creates and renders the cow at that position.

21/S1/F14.text: In the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, combining ARToolKit with Open Scene Graph (OSG) or Vulkan Scene Graph (VSG) can perform the operations: ARToolKit handles tracking and three-dimensional (3D) registration, while OSG handles creation of the AR scene with the rendered cow.

21/S1/F15.text: In a scene-graph representation of the marker-cow augmented reality (AR) example, the whole activity is represented as a node graph containing nodes for video input, tracking, a root node, a virtual camera whose parameters can be manipulated, projection, other related concepts, the three-dimensional (3D) object, and transformations represented as a single node or individual nodes; video input comes from the input device, tracking uses device sensors such as a camera, and graphics-rendering nodes include transformation, three-dimensional (3D) object representation, and orthographic projection, making the scene easier to visualize and manipulate to create the desired effect.

21/S1/F16.text: Examples of frameworks that combine tracking and rendering libraries include the Open Scene Graph (OSG) ART 3 library, which links ARToolKit for tracking support with OSG for real-time rendering features; Goblin XNA, which combines the ART tag tracking library with the Microsoft XNA game platform; and Metaio SDK plus OSG, in which the Metaio SDK provides augmented reality (AR) tracking technologies and OSG provides rendering support.

21/S1/F17.text: Mobile-specific augmented reality (AR) frameworks include ARToolKit for mobile, DroidAR, and Vuforia; DroidAR uses other sensors for tracking support, while Vuforia uses computer vision for tracking support.

21/S1/F18.text: ARToolKit for mobile is a version of ARToolKit available for mobile platforms including iOS and Android, integrated with Open Scene Graph (OSG) but developed for mobile.

21/S2/F0.text: Low-level augmented reality (AR) libraries and frameworks provide maximum development flexibility, but implementing an AR application with them requires knowing the library or framework and writing programs, so it is time-consuming and requires significant programming skill.

21/S2/F1.text: Rapid prototyping and development tools are used to visualize an augmented reality (AR) idea with simple means before major development and show it to end users or clients, so an unsuitable idea does not require further coding.

21/S2/F2.text: Adobe Flash is a popular authoring tool for creating prototypes with multimedia content for web and desktop platforms and can be used, through augmented reality (AR) plugins such as FLAR Toolkit or Flash AR Manager (FLAR Manager), to prototype desktop and mobile augmented reality experiences.

21/S2/F3.text: FLAR Toolkit is a version of the augmented reality (AR) Toolkit ported to Adobe Flash and allows an AR experience to be run from within a web browser.

21/S2/F4.text: FLAR Toolkit lets a user, with a few lines of code, activate a camera, track augmented reality (AR) markers in the camera view, and load and overlay virtual content onto the tracked image for three-dimensional (3D) registering.

21/S2/F5.text: FLAR Toolkit makes it possible for anyone with a Flash-enabled web browser and a camera connected to a computer to have or develop an augmented reality (AR) experience with minimal effort because the required tracking and overlay activities can be done with a few lines of code.

21/S2/F6.text: Flash augmented reality (AR) Manager (FLAR Manager) is a framework that combines various augmented reality tracking and graphics libraries, primarily for prototyping.

21/S2/F7.text: In Flash augmented reality Manager (FLAR Manager), an augmented reality tracking library such as FLAR Toolkit or FLAR Tracker can be combined with a three-dimensional (3D) graphics library such as Alternative 3D, Away 3D, Away 3D Lite, Paper Vision 3D, or Sandy 3D, and such combinations are used primarily for prototyping rather than full-fledged development.

21/S2/F8.text: Non-Flash-based authoring tools for augmented reality prototyping exist, but they may be less popular than Flash-based tools because Flash-based tools have greater market penetration.

22/S0/F0.text: Non-flash-based browser tools for augmented reality (AR) rapid prototyping can avoid third-party browser plugins by letting a developer with mastery of HyperText Markup Language (HTML), Web Graphics Library (WebGL), or similar web component technologies write their own code to create a fast prototype.

22/S0/F1.text: Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware framework and library that is a non-web-based authoring tool for desktop and mobile platforms, combining multiple libraries.

22/S0/F2.text: For augmented reality (AR) application development, Open Frameworks provides support for tracking, rendering, and interaction, and can combine more than two libraries, for example a tracking library such as augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for hand tracking, a three-dimensional (3D) scene graph for rendering, and audio playback libraries, to generate different effects.

22/S0/F3.text: Wikitude is a free augmented reality (AR) browser application that runs on mobile devices as a useful mobile prototyping tool.

22/S0/F4.text: Wikitude treats the mobile device primarily as a client or rendering device only, and the application connects to backend servers for content and specification of user interface elements, with computation not taking place on the mobile device but possibly taking place on the backend server.

22/S0/F5.text: Wikitude makes prototyping easier or faster when developers have their own content; without content, developers depend on default content provided by the tool, which may reduce flexibility but is still usable.

22/S1/F0.text: Plugins to existing tools are a category of augmented reality (AR) software in which a plugin is added to an existing interactive two-dimensional (2D) or three-dimensional (3D) content authoring tool that may not itself support AR content or system development, and the plugin adds AR-specific functions such as tracking, visualization, and 3D registration of digital content over the real-world view, while relying on the main authoring tool for content authoring.

22/S1/F1.text: Plugins to existing tools provide an easy and quick method for developing augmented reality (AR) applications when the developer already knows the host authoring tool, because the developer can rely on knowledge of the original tool and only needs to understand the plugin, reducing the required understanding of the system; if the developer does not know the authoring tool, the approach makes no sense because everything must be learned from scratch.

22/S1/F2.text: Many interactive three-dimensional (3D) graphics authoring tools, including Unity, Vizard, and Lumion, are used to create interactive 3D applications, and most of these tools have plugins for augmented reality (AR) visualization; Unity has the widest range of available solutions for AR visualization.

22/S1/F3.text: The augmented reality (AR) Toolkit for Unity from the AR Tool Works is an example of an AR plugin for Unity that provides marker-based tracking, image-based or computer-vision-based tracking, and AR visualization support.

22/S1/F4.text: Vuforia is a tracking library that has an augmented reality (AR) plugin that works with Unity three-dimensional (3D) and can be used to create AR applications, particularly mobile AR applications for iOS and Android platforms.

22/S1/F5.text: Limitations of using plugins to add augmented reality (AR) support to existing content authoring tools are that user interface and interaction design can be limited to what the underlying authoring tool provides, software and hardware configuration depends on that tool, and content produced with the authoring tool usually becomes dependent on proprietary player software in most cases.

22/S1/F6.text: A way to resolve the limitations of higher-level augmented reality (AR) tools or plugins is to use low-level software development tools, such as software libraries, and build the system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool, an approach that applies to any higher-level tool.

22/S2/F0.text: Standalone authoring tools are applications that allow users to create augmented reality (AR) experiences without programming experience.

22/S2/F1.text: Unlike plugins, which require a basic software or basic authoring tool on which augmented reality (AR) support is provided through a plugin, standalone authoring tools are complete packages that include content authoring and augmented reality support and do not require or depend on any other tool.

22/S2/F2.text: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools typically support scene construction, animation, and adding interactive behavior, with capabilities ranging from scene construction only to the full capability of building complex interactive behavior.

22/S2/F3.text: Most standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools provide drag-and-drop graphical user interfaces (GUIs) that allow developers to create applications or experiences without coding, so users with basic personal computer (PC) skills and non-programmers can learn and use them.

22/S2/F4.text: Standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tools can provide scripting-language support for developers who know scripting languages, and applications built with absolute zero coding have limited utility compared with advanced systems that use scripting support for more flexibility.

22/S2/F5.text: Wikitude Studio is an example of a standalone augmented reality (AR) authoring tool; it is a web-based package that allowed users to create rich mobile augmented reality content and deploy it either to the Wikitude augmented reality browser app or as a custom mobile app, and it supported various media, including three-dimensional (3D) models and animations registered to the real world.

22/S3/F0.text: Augmented reality (AR) software tools and packages are available in four categories based on the programming skill required: low-level libraries and frameworks, which require the highest programming skill; standalone authoring tools, which require the least programming skill; and, between these extremes, rapid prototyping tools and plugins to existing systems.

23/S0/F0.text: Extended reality systems belong to the broad class of systems called interactive systems.

23/S0/F1.text: Mark Weiser's 1991 paper 'The Computer for the 21st Century', published in Scientific American, stated that the most profound technologies are those that disappear.

23/S0/F2.text: The statement that the most profound technologies are those that disappear means that a very advanced technology should ideally not be visible to the user, and the user should feel like dealing with any other item rather than a specialized technological item.

23/S0/F3.text: Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

23/S0/F4.text: The earliest computers occupied huge rooms with many wires, programming referred to the idea of reconnecting the wires, and they were accessible only to a very few select people.

23/S0/F5.text: In the development of computer systems, people have tried to make technology disappear from the user's point of view, and the current stage defined by popular technological products such as wearable devices, mobile devices, flexible devices, and connected devices is referred to as Internet of Things (IoT) or ubiquitous computing, in which users are surrounded by multiple connected computers that can communicate with each other without the user separately operating them, moving toward making technology disappear.

23/S1/F0.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.

23/S1/F1.text: In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.

23/S1/F2.text: Technical terms in a system error message, such as event log, security accounts manager, and safe mode, should not be expected to be understood or acted upon by a lay end user, and a hexadecimal status code in such a message is generally incomprehensible to a layperson.

23/S1/F3.text: An error message couched in technical jargon that a layperson is likely to fail to understand can make the user anxious, leave the user not knowing what is wrong or how to get out of it, and may lead to the user refraining from using the system further and to a loss of motivation for further use.

23/S1/F4.text: Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

23/S2/F0.text: The user-centric approach, generally recommended for building interactive systems, is the process of designing computer systems in which users' needs and expectations are taken care of by considering user characteristics, and it starts by understanding user characteristics, what users need and expect, and then designing the system based on that.

23/S2/F1.text: The key characteristics of a user-centric approach are designing interface elements that are acceptable to users, designing layouts that organize elements on the screen or interface to meet user expectations, helping users perceive the system state from their point of view rather than from technical details, and designing interactions that fulfill users' needs by taking them to desired system states, allowing users to get work done by easily transitioning from one state to a goal state.

23/S3/F0.text: Human-computer interaction (HCI) is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding interactive computing systems.

23/S3/F1.text: ACM SIGCHI is the official body that deals with human-computer interaction (HCI) and provides the definition of HCI.

23/S3/F2.text: The core concern of human-computer interaction (HCI) is incorporating humans into the design, which requires first understanding users and then incorporating user characteristics into the design.

23/S4/F0.text: Human factors in system design requires designers to know the users' characteristics and design the system accordingly, because users who perform the same broad task, such as a traveler or agent and a database administrator obtaining railway ticket information, can have different expectations, needs, and query-language skills, and therefore require different interfaces for providing input, seeing the outcome, and acting on the outcome.

24/S0/F0.text: Empirical or field studies of user behavior are typically needed to understand who the users of an interactive system are and how they behave, but they are time-consuming, laborious, and require elaborate setup and planning, so interactive-system designers can rely on the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization instead of always starting with field studies.

24/S0/F1.text: A three-class classification of interactive-system users consists of novice users, who use the system for the first time, intermittent users, who use it occasionally, and expert users, who use it regularly over a long period of time.

24/S0/F2.text: In the novice, intermittent, and expert user categorization, an expert user is not a technology expert but a person who is an expert in using the system and can use it efficiently.

24/S0/F3.text: The novice, intermittent, and expert user classes provide a starting point for understanding users and making interactive-system design decisions when designers assume their potential users belong to one of these classes, because users in different classes are likely to behave differently and designers can broadly understand the behavior of each class.

24/S0/F4.text: A word processing or similar processing application can provide multiple options, such as a hotkey combination and a menu option, for the same task to cater to different user groups.

24/S0/F5.text: For saving a file, the menu option takes longer than the hotkey combination but is suitable for novice first-time users because remembering hotkey combinations is generally difficult for them, while the hotkey combination may be a better alternative for intermittent users and is always preferable for expert users.

24/S0/F6.text: The novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is only one broad way of classifying users; more fine-grained categorizations are possible, and better categorizations can be based on empirical studies of users, but the broad novice, intermittent, and expert categorization is useful when the design process starts.

24/S1/F0.text: The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

24/S1/F1.text: An application software developer building software such as a virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR) system incorporates user characteristics by following a development or design lifecycle that accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations so that the system is easier for the user to use and better matches the users' needs and expectations.

24/S2/F0.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

24/S2/F1.text: The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

24/S2/F2.text: The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

24/S2/F3.text: The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

24/S3/F0.text: User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.

24/S3/F1.text: Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces.

24/S3/F2.text: The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability.

24/S3/F3.text: Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.

24/S3/F4.text: In user-centric software design and software development, the core design concern is the design of usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of lay persons or layman users.

24/S4/F0.text: The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.

24/S4/F1.text: Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.

24/S4/F2.text: The core concern of Extended Reality (XR) software is to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment, and both software and hardware play important roles in building that relationship.

24/S4/F3.text: An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

24/S4/F4.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

24/S4/F5.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

24/S4/F6.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

25/S0/F0.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

25/S0/F1.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

25/S0/F2.text: Creating the best possible illusion of reality is very crucial for virtual reality (VR) because VR aims for total immersion in a virtual environment, whereas in augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) immersion is partial and the real world remains viewable or experienced, so the illusion is less significant but not totally insignificant.

25/S1/F0.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.

25/S1/F1.text: Human bodies and sensory organs are designed to perceive the real world, not a virtual world, and applying artificial stimulation in virtual reality affects biological mechanisms that evolved over a long period in a natural environment.

25/S1/F2.text: Human perception is formed by the combination of physiology and experience stored in long-term memory.

25/S1/F3.text: Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

25/S1/F4.text: One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

25/S1/F5.text: Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

25/S1/F6.text: An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

25/S2/F0.text: Perceptual psychology is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation, received by sensors from the real world, into perceived phenomena.

25/S2/F1.text: Having a little bit of knowledge of perceptual psychology is always advisable for interactive systems in general and is even more important for extended reality (XR) systems because the goal of extended reality systems is to explicitly extend the user's deeply embedded idea of reality.

25/S2/F2.text: Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for building better hardware and for understanding the effects of an extended reality (XR) system on the user by answering questions such as how far away an object appears in a given virtual world, how much video resolution is needed to avoid seeing pixels in a virtual world or virtual object, how many frames per second are enough to perceive motion as continuous, whether the user's head appears at the proper height in the virtual world for the point of view that should correspond to the user's height, where virtual sound appears to come from, why a user feels nauseated, why one system experience is more tiring than another, and what presence is.

25/S2/F3.text: Perceptual psychology requires knowledge of the basic physiology of the human body, including sense organs, neural pathways, and how they are connected to the brain; the key theories and insights of experimental perceptual psychology; and the interference of an engineered extended reality (XR) system with common perceptual processes, with its implications or side effects.

25/S3/F0.text: The term sensor has two related but structurally different meanings: in a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit; in the human body, human bodily sensors are body organs that convert a stimulus into neural impulses.

25/S3/F1.text: The human senses classified by stimulus, receptor, and sense organ are vision (electromagnetic energy, photoreceptors, eye), auditory (air pressure waves, mechanoreceptors, ear), touch (tissue distortion, mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors, skin and muscles), balance (gravity or acceleration, mechanoreceptors, vestibular organs that act as sense organs), taste (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, mouth), and smell (chemical composition, chemoreceptors, nose).

25/S3/F2.text: Among the six human senses, balance is a sense for which there is no specific organ, unlike the other five well-known senses.

25/S4/F0.text: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon in which the receptors in a sense organ are bodily sensors that target particular stimuli and are activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

25/S4/F1.text: The eyes contain photoreceptors, which are activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light and therefore target only visible light.

25/S4/F2.text: The auditory, touch, and balance senses involve mechanoreceptors that sense motion, vibration, or gravitational force.

25/S4/F3.text: The sense of touch additionally involves thermoreceptors that detect changes in temperature.

25/S4/F4.text: The balance sense helps a person know which way the head is oriented, including sensing the upward direction.

25/S4/F5.text: Taste and smell rely on chemoreceptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter, on the tongue for taste and in the nasal passage for smell.

25/S5/F0.text: Some knowledge of perceptual psychology is needed to understand the role of human factors in extended reality systems.

25/S5/F1.text: The physiology of the senses is a part of perceptual psychology.

25/S5/F2.text: The six senses are vision, auditory, balance, taste, smell, and touch.

25/S5/F3.text: For each of the six senses, receptors are part of the sensory organs, and these receptors receive stimuli depending on the sensory organ.

25/S5/F4.text: Different types of receptors include photoreceptors, chemoreceptors, and mechanoreceptors.

25/S5/F5.text: In the human body, the sensory organs are the hardware of sensing.

26/S0/F0.text: The perceptual process proceeds from sensing, which is the lowest level, to perception, which is at a very abstract level, and perception can occur only after sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimulus and convert that input stimulus into neural impulses.

26/S0/F1.text: The human brain contains around 86 billion neurons, and roughly 20 billion of its neurons are devoted to the cerebral cortex, the part of the brain that is responsible for perception and other functions such as attention, memory, language, and consciousness.

26/S0/F2.text: The cerebral cortex is a large, heavily folded sheet of neurons about 3 millimeters thick, folded to fit into the skull.

26/S1/F0.text: Perception and overall cognitive ability depend on the interconnection of neurons.

26/S1/F1.text: A neuron has a nucleus or cell body, dendrites, an axon, branches of the axon, and axon terminals.

26/S1/F2.text: The interconnection of neurons can be thought of as a directed graph or network, the original idea behind neural networks used in machine learning or deep learning, in which the nucleus or cell body is a node that processes input, the dendrites are input edges carrying neural impulses toward the cell body, and the axons are output edges carrying neural impulses away from the cell body.

26/S1/F3.text: A neuron can aggregate information from other neurons, including information that has already been aggregated by other neurons, through the network of dendrites, and the processing that takes place in the nucleus or cell body is transmitted to one or more other neurons through axons.

26/S1/F4.text: For an interconnection between neurons, an axon of one neuron is paired with a dendrite of the next neuron, but the axon and dendrite are not physically connected; communication occurs across a gap called the synapse, through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

26/S1/F5.text: In the human brain, each neuron has on average about 7,000 synaptic connections to other neurons, which results in about 10^15 edges in the brain's neuron-interconnection graph.

26/S2/F0.text: Hierarchical processing is the neural processing performed as signals from sense organ receptors propagate through the neural network to the cerebral cortex.

26/S2/F1.text: Hierarchical processing works by staged aggregation, in which signals from numerous receptors of different types are combined at successive levels by neurons until the cerebral cortex is reached, and aggregated information at each level is higher-level information rather than the same lower-level information.

26/S2/F2.text: Hierarchical processing allows increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

26/S3/F0.text: In perception, once sensory signals reach the cerebral cortex, the interpretation of a stimulus is produced by combining real-time sensory input with life experience or knowledge stored in long-term memory, not by sensory input alone, and this combination produces perceptual phenomena such as face recognition and song identification.

26/S3/F1.text: The interpretation of a stimulus depends on the interpreter's long-term experience, so a person with less experience such as a newborn and a person with long experience such as an aged person can interpret a stimulus very differently.

26/S3/F2.text: Overall perceptual processing is an outcome of hierarchical processing and the combination of real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience.

26/S4/F0.text: Proprioception is another aspect of perception, slightly different from direct perception through sensory organs such as vision, auditory sense, touch, smell, and taste; it is the ability to sense the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort involved in moving them, and because it has no direct sensory organ or receptor it can be called a sixth sense.

26/S4/F1.text: The motor cortex, which controls body motion, sends signals called efference copies to other parts of the brain, including the cerebral cortex, to communicate what motions have been executed, and this information is processed to understand the relative positions of body parts and the amount of muscular effort required to move them.

26/S5/F0.text: The brain processes perception by combining signals from multiple senses and proprioception with experiences learned over a long period and interpreting the inputs in coherent, consistent, and familiar learned ways.

26/S5/F1.text: In an immersive virtual reality (VR) system, interfering with the brain's long-term learned sensory processing can create a mismatch because the brain cannot be retuned to process the new inputs in a short span of time.

26/S5/F2.text: A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

26/S5/F3.text: A mismatch between the brain's sensory inputs and its familiar processing can compromise presence by making the user consciously aware of the conflict and immediately understand that the experience is artificial rather than natural or real.

26/S5/F4.text: Vection is the illusion of self-motion in which a person moving in a virtual environment while physically stationary receives visual input reporting movement or acceleration while the balance sense or proprioception reports no motion, creating a sensory conflict.

26/S5/F5.text: Extended reality design should carefully balance the experiences presented by the various senses, giving an immersive experience by fooling the brain so that it processes the information in the intended way.

27/S0/F0.text: In virtual reality (VR) headsets, light emitted from the displays reaches the retina and is guided by engineered lenses in the headset and natural lenses in the eye, a combined system that helps the user perceive immersive visual content.

27/S0/F1.text: Knowledge of how light propagates through lenses and the human eye is important for understanding how virtual reality (VR) headsets work and how they lead to visual perception.

27/S0/F2.text: Knowledge of the physics of light propagation is used to understand the construction of virtual worlds by modeling light propagation and determining what should be rendered on visual displays.

27/S0/F3.text: Knowledge of how light propagates, how lenses and the eye work, and how cameras work is used to understand camera setups, choose camera positions in virtual worlds for the best experience, and present virtual worlds through panoramic videos.

27/S0/F4.text: Understanding how a camera works helps build tracking hardware and software.

27/S1/F0.text: Light can be described by three views—the photon (particle) view, the wave view, and the ray view—and these views can be used to explain different phenomena related to light.

27/S1/F1.text: The photon (particle) view of light describes light as a large number of photons, tiny energy particles that move through space at a very high speed, often called the speed of light, and it is helpful for understanding or calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

27/S1/F2.text: The wave view of light describes light as waves, ripples through space, and it is helpful for explaining the spectrum of color rather than explaining color in terms of light as particles.

27/S1/F3.text: The ray view of light describes light as rays, which are trajectories or paths assumed to be traces of the motion of a single hypothetical photon, and it is helpful for explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

27/S2/F0.text: When light rays strike a material surface, the possible interactions are transmission, absorption, and reflection, and either one of these interactions or all three can occur.

27/S2/F1.text: In light transmission, some of the light rays that strike a material surface pass through the material and come out of the material.

27/S2/F2.text: In absorption, some of the light rays that strike a material surface are absorbed by the material, terminate inside the material, and do not propagate further outside the material.

27/S2/F3.text: In reflection, a light ray strikes a material surface and is reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating the material.

27/S3/F0.text: In color perception, the perceived color of a surface point is determined by the intensity of the light reaching the viewer's eye.

27/S3/F1.text: Ambient light is light in the environment, reflected from surrounding objects, that reaches the viewer's eye together with light reflected from the object's surface.

27/S4/F0.text: Light incident on the human eye passes in the order cornea, pupil, and lens, and through internal semi-liquid media such as the aqueous humor between the cornea and the pupil and the vitreous humor between the lens and the retina, before reaching the retina at the back of the eye.

27/S4/F1.text: The material that makes up the cornea and the lens of the human eye refracts light so that images are focused on the retina.

27/S4/F2.text: The iris controls the amount of light entering the human eye by dilating or constricting the pupil, typically dilating it in dark surroundings to admit more light and constricting it in bright light to admit less.

27/S4/F3.text: The retina at the back of the eye consists of photoreceptors, which are the bodily sensors required for visual perception, and optic nerve fibers, which are neurons that carry the signal to the brain.

27/S4/F4.text: The human eye contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, in which rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina and cones are mainly located in the small central region of the retina called the fovea.

27/S4/F5.text: Multiple rods can share a single optic nerve fiber, which aids sensitivity to lower levels of light, whereas approximately one optic nerve fiber serves each cone, which aids image acuity.

27/S4/F6.text: Vision accomplished only with cones is photopic vision, which is more related to direct or central vision, and vision accomplished only with rods is scotopic vision, which is more related to peripheral vision.

27/S4/F7.text: Color is perceived only in photopic vision, which is accomplished with cones and gives a sense of color, whereas in scotopic vision weak lights are perceived as a series of grays and color perception is not that good.

27/S5/F0.text: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves, ranging from red light at 4.3 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 700 nanometer wavelength to violet light at 7.5 times 10 to the power 14 hertz and 400 nanometer wavelength.

27/S5/F1.text: Visible light waves can excite cones in the eye, producing photopic vision, which is color perception, while light waves outside the visible light spectrum cannot excite cones and therefore do not produce color perception.

27/S6/F0.text: Human eyes support two types of vision, central vision and peripheral vision, because photoreceptor density across the retina varies greatly.

27/S6/F1.text: The fovea is the central region of the retina with the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, particularly cones.

27/S6/F2.text: The innermost part of the fovea has a diameter of only 0.5 millimeters or an angular range of 0.85 plus or minus 0.85 degrees and contains almost entirely cones.

27/S6/F3.text: Central vision requires the eyes to be focused and pointed straight at an object to perceive a sharp color image.

27/S6/F4.text: Peripheral vision is supported by the peripheral region of the retina, where rays entering the cornea from the sides land, rod density is lower and cone density is very low, and photoreceptor density is lower, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.

27/S6/F5.text: Peripheral vision is better than central vision at detecting movement, but it does not provide effective color perception.

27/S6/F6.text: The blind spot is a region of the retina with no photoreceptors, caused by the retina's inside-out anatomy, which leaves no other way to route neural signals to the brain, and by the optic nerve spreading out around the retina, so light or visual stimuli falling there produce no perception.

28/S0/F0.text: The human eye contains a cornea that acts as a powerful lens with fixed focal depth, a natural lens with variable focal depth, and a non-planar retina that is the image surface where light falls and is converted by photoreceptors into neural pulses transmitted to the brain through optical nerves.

28/S0/F1.text: Compared with an artificially created lens setup, the human eye has no focal plane as such; its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

28/S0/F2.text: The interior of the human eye is liquid, so after transmission through the lens light passes through liquid, whereas in an artificially created lens setup light passes through air after the lens.

28/S0/F3.text: In the human eye, a ray of light passes through five media before hitting the retina—air with refractive index 1.009, cornea with 1.376, aqueous fluid with 1.336, natural lens with 1.413, and vitreous fluid with 1.337—and each medium has its own refractive index.

28/S0/F4.text: Because the outer diameter of the human eyeball is approximately 24 millimeters, a single lens of at least 40 diopters would be required to converge parallel rays onto the center of the retina.

28/S0/F5.text: The human eye effectively contains two convex lenses, the cornea with optical power of approximately 40 diopters and the natural lens with approximately 20 diopters, so their combined optical power is about 60 diopters, which is sufficient to focus images of faraway objects onto the retina.

28/S0/F6.text: A virtual reality (VR) headset places a screen very close to the eyes to fill the view and uses a convex lens, functioning like reading glasses, to focus the screen's light on the retina, after which normal eye operation takes over.

28/S0/F7.text: For the best experience, the screen in a virtual reality (VR) headset is placed at the focal length of its engineered lens, so that the screen appears to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

28/S0/F8.text: In a virtual reality (VR) headset, even though the screen appears as a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and a person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

28/S1/F0.text: Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

28/S1/F1.text: The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

28/S1/F2.text: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, both eyes see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside this region are seen only by the left eye or only by the right eye.

28/S1/F3.text: Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand the relationship between objects in three-dimensional (3D) space.

28/S1/F4.text: Stereoscopy is the process in which two eyes view two images simultaneously, the left eye processes the left image, the right eye processes the right image, and there is a common part seen by both eyes while some parts are seen by only one eye.

28/S1/F5.text: When the left and right two-dimensional (2D) images are processed simultaneously, the processing generates a three-dimensional (3D) view of the objects, so stereoscopic vision, which is aided by binocular vision, helps a person perceive three-dimensional objects.

28/S2/F0.text: A virtual world may allow up to two types of movement in three-dimensional (3D) space: translational movement, used for navigating in that space, and rotational movement, primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

28/S2/F1.text: The concept of degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

28/S2/F2.text: In three-dimensional (3D) space, an object can have a total of six degrees of freedom, consisting of three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes.

28/S2/F3.text: In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

28/S3/F0.text: Basic physiological properties such as photoreceptor density can directly impact the engineering requirements for visual display hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) display should ideally be designed to match the performance of the human visual sense, being good enough to fool the visual sense without needing quality beyond the limits of human receptors.

28/S3/F1.text: To make a display match the performance of the human visual sense, the important considerations are spatial resolution, the needed number of pixels per square area; intensity resolution and range, the number of producible intensity values and their minimum and maximum based on how many can be processed without compromising perceptual quality; and temporal resolution, the frame rates or speed at which display pixels change, which must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter.

28/S3/F2.text: Aliasing in a display is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible, such as when the display is highly magnified or zoomed out.

28/S3/F3.text: The screen door effect is an effect, commonly noticed in images produced by liquid crystal display (LCD) projectors, in which an image appears to have a screen on top of it.

28/S3/F4.text: A retina display is a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi), a threshold claimed by Steve Jobs of Apple in 2010 as sufficient for a retina display.

28/S3/F5.text: Because augmented reality (AR) experiences are typically experienced using displays at a distance from the eye, the 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion, which is suitable for distant displays such as televisions, laptops, and smartphones, can be taken into account when designing such AR experiences.

28/S3/F6.text: For augmented reality (AR) head-mounted displays and virtual reality (VR) headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye, the traditional 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) retina display criterion is not very suitable; a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch (ppi) is probably 7 to 8 times higher than a retina display.

28/S3/F7.text: To avoid or reduce aliasing or the screen door effect in virtual reality (VR) headsets, corrective mechanisms can be used, including adjusting the field of view of the headsets, foveated rendering techniques, and other ways of rendering content, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

28/S3/F8.text: For motion perception in an immersive environment, temporal resolution in a virtual reality (VR) headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second (fps) or 60 fps, with higher frame rates preferred.

29/S0/F0.text: The audio component of virtual reality (VR) is powerful for providing an immersive experience, and technologies exist to bring high-fidelity audio into VR, so using those technologies will clearly improve the immersive experience.

29/S0/F1.text: The objective in dealing with an immersive experience is to include as many senses as possible, because the visual sense alone may not give a full picture of the surroundings, which will affect the immersive experience, and augmenting vision with audio enhances the immersive experience.

29/S0/F2.text: Audio recording, that is recording of sound, speech or non-speech sound, and audio reproduction, that is output generation, can itself be considered a virtual reality (VR) experience even if other senses are missing, and it can provide a better surround sound effect in cave-like VR versions, a surround environment surrounded by display devices, and a better immersive experience in headset VR versions, the wearable display version.

29/S0/F3.text: Combining sound with vision or visual effects affects perception of properties of the virtual environment, such as size, volume, material, intensity, and distance, and although looking alone partly gives an idea of those properties, perception of them is reinforced when vision is augmented with auditory effects.

29/S0/F4.text: Audio reinforces a virtual experience as believable, that is, as closer to reality and everyday experience, and vision coupled with audio helps create or increase an emotional connection with the virtual environment, which vision alone may not be able to achieve.

29/S0/F5.text: Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

29/S1/F0.text: Sound is vibration in a medium, usually air but also water, other gases, liquids, or solids, and it requires a medium to propagate, so there is no sound in a vacuum unlike light, which can propagate without a medium or through a vacuum.

29/S1/F1.text: Sound propagation through a medium is caused by pressure variations created when sound is generated and molecules in the medium are displaced, and these pressure variations range from a compression extreme, where pressure is extremely high, to a decompression extreme, also called a rarefaction extreme, where pressure is very low.

29/S1/F2.text: Pressure variation at the human eardrum is converted into a perceptual auditory experience, because pressure at the human eardrum varies as a function of time.

29/S1/F3.text: Sound can be represented as a sound wave, which is a plot of pressure variation against time with time on the x-axis and air pressure on the y-axis, and the pressure varies from one extreme to another like a sinusoidal wave as time progresses.

29/S1/F4.text: Sound waves are primarily characterized by three properties relevant for dealing with sound waves: frequency, amplitude, and phase, because sound can be represented as a wave.

29/S1/F5.text: Frequency of a sound wave is the number of alterations between one maximum and another maximum per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

29/S1/F6.text: The human audible frequency range, which is a limitation of human physiology, is from 20 hertz (Hz) to 20,000 hertz, and frequencies inside this range are audible to a human ear while frequencies outside this range are not, although other animals can perceive a higher range outside the human range.

29/S1/F7.text: Amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave, measured in decibel (dB) relative to the minimum sound detectable by humans at 1000 hertz (Hz).

29/S1/F8.text: Phase of a sound wave is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin from 0 to 360 degrees, and is measured in degrees.

29/S2/F0.text: The human hearing system contains three parts: the outer ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear.

29/S2/F1.text: In the outer ear, the receiver part receives a sound wave and forces it to propagate through the crucial outer-ear canal, which works as an amplifier by boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

29/S2/F2.text: The complex folds in the outer ear's receiver part and outer-ear canal attenuate high-frequency sound waves.

29/S2/F3.text: In the middle ear, a sound wave passing through the outer-ear canal strikes the tympanic membrane, causing it to vibrate, and the vibration is transferred to three ossicles in an air-filled chamber: the malleus, the incus, and the stapes.

29/S2/F4.text: The inner ear houses the cochlea, which is the sense organ for hearing, in a structure the size of a marble.

29/S2/F5.text: The cochlea is connected to nerves or neurons and converts sound energy into neural impulses that are transmitted to the brain through the neural network.

30/S0/F0.text: Sound perception occurs at three levels—social, warning, and primitive—which together give a person an overall idea of the surroundings.

30/S0/F1.text: Social-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that helps an individual carry out social interactions with other individuals.

30/S0/F2.text: Warning-level sound perception is the level of sound perception that provides an alert or warning about something, such as an event.

30/S0/F3.text: Primitive-level sound perception is the intuitive perception of naive sounds such as background noises that people mostly ignore, and it may not lead to any meaningful action by the individual.

30/S0/F4.text: Identifying the desired sound perception level helps a developer generate suitable auditory effects when generating sound effects for a virtual reality (VR) system; for example, if social-level perception is required, the developer should generate stimuli that support social-level perception rather than stimuli that typically produce primitive-level perception.

30/S1/F0.text: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

30/S1/F1.text: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics and is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

30/S1/F2.text: Stevens' power law is a result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude by the equation P = C M^x, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the original stimulus, P is the perceived magnitude, x is the exponent that relates actual magnitude to perceived magnitude, and C is a constant that depends on units.

30/S1/F3.text: The just noticeable difference (JND) is a result from psychophysics that specifies the amount of change in a stimulus that is required for subjects to perceive it as changed in at least 50 percent of trials.

30/S1/F4.text: Weber's law captures the just noticeable difference (JND), the change in magnitude that is noticeable, by representing it as delta M divided by M equals C, where M is the magnitude or intensity of the stimulus, delta M is the just noticeable difference, and C is a constant; equivalently, delta M equals M times C.

30/S1/F5.text: Weber's law and Stevens' power law are laws from psychophysics that also apply to psychoacoustics, or auditory perception, when physical stimuli are replaced by acoustic stimuli.

30/S1/F6.text: For the perceived loudness of a 3000 hertz (Hz) pure tone, the Stevens' power law exponent x is 0.67, so a much higher pressure level is perceived as only a bit louder because the exponent is less than 1.

30/S1/F7.text: For a change in a stimulus to be perceived, it must be above the just noticeable difference (JND); for it not to be perceived, it must be within or below the JND.

30/S2/F0.text: In pitch perception, the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch.

30/S2/F1.text: For sound frequency, the just noticeable difference (JND) increases as frequency increases: for frequencies less than 1000 Hz, humans can detect a frequency change of less than 1 Hz; at 10,000 Hz the JND is about 100 Hz; in percentage terms, at low frequencies humans can detect frequency differences of 0.1% or less, whereas at higher frequencies a difference of at least 1% is required.

30/S3/F0.text: Sound localization is a main area of psychoacoustics that estimates the location of a sound source by hearing it.

30/S3/F1.text: Sound localization is crucial in virtual reality (VR) because it helps the user perceive the orientation and position of objects relative to the user by matching auditory and visual cues; a mismatch can break presence and cause cybersickness.

30/S3/F2.text: The minimum audible angle (MAA) is the minimum angular variation that can be detected by a human listener, obtained by applying the just noticeable difference (JND) concept to sound localization and represented in a spherical coordinate system with the listener's head as the origin.

30/S3/F3.text: The spherical coordinate system used to represent a sound source location has three parameters: azimuth, the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the projection of the sound source direction, ranging from -180 degrees to 180 degrees; elevation, the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane, ranging from -90 degrees to 90 degrees; and radius, the distance from the listener's head origin to the source.

30/S3/F4.text: The minimum audible angle (MAA) depends on both the frequency and direction of the sound source: at some frequencies and locations it can be as low as 1 degree, while at other combinations localization can be very difficult and the MAA can be extremely high.

30/S4/F0.text: Sound localization cues are either monaural, involving a single ear, or binaural, involving both ears.

30/S4/F1.text: Interaural level difference (ILD) is a binaural sound localization cue that is the difference in sound magnitude heard by each ear, with the ear without obstruction receiving a stronger sound, and the difference can indicate the direction from which the sound is coming.

30/S4/F2.text: An acoustic shadow occurs when a sound wave does not reach one ear, caused by an object in front of the sound source or by the position of the head.

30/S4/F3.text: Interaural time difference is a binaural sound localization cue from different sound arrival times at the ears; in an average human head, the ears are 21.5 centimeters apart, sound travels that distance in about 0.6 milliseconds, and this small time difference can be used to locate the source.

30/S4/F4.text: The auditory component of an extended reality (XR) system should ideally be non-stationary, moving with the user, and interactive, dependent on the listener's actions.

30/S4/F5.text: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) model how a listener receives sound from a location in space, and this model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including extended reality (XR) systems.

30/S4/F6.text: Head-related transfer functions (HRTF) depend on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal, and every person has a unique HRTF.

30/S4/F7.text: Because every person has a unique head-related transfer function (HRTF), it is impractical to determine individual users' HRTFs when building a system, so an HRTF for an average listener is developed and used.

30/S4/F8.text: A pair of head-related transfer functions (HRTF) for both ears can be used to synthesize binaural sound, and by generating sound effects or placing sound receivers according to the HRTF, a localization effect can be implemented in an extended reality (XR) system.

31/S0/F0.text: The human somatosensory system is a sensory system, like the human visual and auditory perceptual systems, that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

31/S0/F1.text: Proprioception, called the sixth sense, is the conscious awareness of the pose and movement of each movable human body part, such as legs, arms, fingers, tongue, mouth, and lips, relative to other body parts.

31/S0/F2.text: Kinesthesis is the awareness of the parameters associated with moving body parts, and it provides information on velocities, accelerations, and forces during movement.

31/S0/F3.text: The human somatosensory system has at least nine major kinds of receptors, of which six are fully devoted to the sense of touch and the remaining three are devoted to proprioception and kinesthesis.

31/S0/F4.text: Touch receptors are embedded in the epidermis and dermis, which are the first and second layers of the skin, and the skin also has a hypodermis layer.

31/S0/F5.text: The touch receptors of the human somatosensory system include at least Merkel's discs, hair follicle receptors, free nerve endings, Ruffini's endings, Meissner's corpuscles, and Pacinian corpuscles.

31/S0/F6.text: The receptors used for proprioception and kinesthesis in the human somatosensory system include muscle spindles embedded in muscles that report changes in muscle length to the brain, Golgi tendon organs embedded in tendons that connect muscles to bones and report changes in muscle tension associated with movement, and joint receptors at joints between bones that coordinate muscle movement and provide information on relative bone positions.

31/S0/F7.text: When a hand touches an object, activated somatosensory receptors transform the input into neural impulses that are transmitted through a neural network from neuron to neuron to the brain, and the brain processes these impulses into touch perception and can send messages back through the same pathway to cause corrective motor actions, such as removing the hand from a hot object, and the same process is equally applicable to the proprioceptive sense.

31/S1/F0.text: Haptic perception is a major part of somatosensory perception, and it is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects as part of touch perception.

31/S1/F1.text: Haptic exploration is the handling or manipulation of geometric objects that is used to infer the overall geometric shape of the object.

31/S1/F2.text: Haptic perception can be thought of at different levels: receptors in the skin receive input from the real world and process the information to perceive something through touch, while higher-level perception requires object manipulations that are called haptic explorations.

31/S1/F3.text: The six types of haptic exploration, each needed for a different object property perception, are lateral motion for texture perception, pressure for hardness perception, enclosure for global shape or volume perception, static contact for temperature perception, unsupported holding for weight perception, and contour following for local shape perception.

31/S1/F4.text: Each haptic exploration used to perceive different properties of objects involves different kinds of receptors and a combination of spatial and temporal information.

31/S1/F5.text: The overall goal of haptic exploration is to integrate somatosensory signals from in-hand manipulation of an object so that a geometric mental model of the object is learned in terms of properties such as shape, size, weight and hardness.

31/S1/F6.text: Haptic perception is important for creating a mental model of the surrounding world, and because mental model creation is an essential part of an immersive experience, haptic perception can improve an immersive experience.

31/S1/F7.text: Haptic perception and haptic exploration offer an extra dimension to virtual reality (VR) by letting users feel the virtual environment through the sense of touch, which gives users a better feeling of the virtual world and helps them feel truly immersed in the virtual world, and because immersion in the real world also involves haptic exploration, adding haptic exploration to a virtual world increases the immersive experience.

31/S1/F8.text: In a virtual desert walking example, visual and auditory perception alone may not give a complete picture of the haptic touch perception of feeling sand glide under the feet, and adding haptic exploration support through proper hardware and software makes the experience far better than an experience using only visual or auditory senses.

31/S2/F0.text: Touch sensation in extended reality (XR) can be provided by engineered devices, and the most popular form is force feedback, typically in the form of vibrations, provided by force feedback devices such as a force feedback mouse, smart gloves, and body suits, which are common in many XR systems, particularly virtual reality (VR) systems.

31/S2/F1.text: The KGS dot view model DV-2 is a haptic pin array with a matrix of pins that a computer controls, and the pins are forced upward, according to signals generated for objects in the virtual world, to simulate the texture of an object surface when the user's fingertip scans across it.

31/S2/F2.text: Controlling a haptic pin array precisely enough to give a realistic feeling of a textured surface is generally difficult and challenging.

31/S2/F3.text: Real-world objects whose virtual avatars appear in a virtual world and that are used in place of computer-controlled haptic devices to provide feedback to the user's somatosensory system are sometimes called tangible user interfaces.

31/S2/F4.text: To give the feeling of touching a real object surface in a virtual world, using real objects to provide touch feedback is generally considered less challenging than creating a computer-controlled haptic device.

31/S2/F5.text: The basic idea for implementing tangible user interfaces is to create the experience by aligning the real world and the virtual world.

31/S2/F6.text: A see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, which is typically good for mixed reality or augmented reality, enables users to see and interact with the physical world around them, and it adds virtual objects to the real world or visually enhances real objects.

31/S2/F7.text: In a see-through display such as Microsoft HoloLens, the computer uses wearable device sensors to detect which real object the user is dealing with and can change the view of that object or add virtual objects to the real world.

31/S3/F0.text: Taste and smell are generally grouped as chemical senses because their chemoreceptors work by chemical reaction with specific molecules or chemical stimuli at appropriate concentrations, and not all chemoreceptors respond to all chemical stimuli.

31/S3/F1.text: There is much less research on integrating smell and taste into extended reality (XR) systems than on visual, auditory, and touch senses, and fewer electronic devices have been made or are being made to provide stimuli to the nose and tongue, the body organs responsible for smell and taste.

31/S3/F2.text: Adding scent or smell to films is an old idea that can be traced back to the early 20th century, and historical systems that included smells include Smell-O-Vision, developed in 1960, which injected 30 different odors into movie theater seats at different points during a film according to the scenery, and Sensorama.

31/S3/F3.text: A smell interface, also called an olfactory display, provides odor stimuli to the nose, usually by using air pumps or micropumps to spray chemical compounds near the nose, with other components that help create the odor.
