31/S3/F4.text: For smell interfaces, delivering odor near the user's nose for a personal experience is relatively easier than delivering it on a room scale for social or larger experiences, because room-scale delivery generally makes it hard to control odor intensity and uniformity and to vary odor concentration over a large area for localization, which is not easy with current research.

31/S3/F5.text: When olfactory displays can generate odor effects, they are shown to induce strong cognitive and emotional responses that make an immersive experience more attractive and more immersive, and pleasant odors can help reduce visually induced motion sickness, also called cybersickness, to some extent.

31/S3/F6.text: A taste interface can place electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation that simulates the main taste types.

31/S3/F7.text: It is generally difficult to develop taste interfaces without causing people to eat food during the experience, which is not a convenient arrangement and is generally quite difficult to achieve in practice.

31/S4/F0.text: The human somatosensory system has several receptors, of which six are dedicated to touch and three are dedicated to proprioception and kinesthesis.

31/S4/F1.text: Research prototypes for generating taste and smell effects are not very popular or commonly used in commercially available virtual reality (VR) systems.

31/S4/F2.text: Chapter 13 of Virtual Reality by LaValle is a reference that can be used to obtain more details on the topics covered in the Other Senses and Full Immersion lecture.

32/S0/F0.text: User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable.

32/S0/F1.text: The core design concern for user-centered software is designing usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.

32/S0/F2.text: The extended reality (XR) application software being developed is interactive software intended for laypersons, who may not know or need to know how the hardware or software works.

32/S0/F3.text: Obtaining usable application software requires following a structured, step-by-step software development lifecycle rather than working in a haphazard or ad hoc manner.

32/S0/F4.text: A software development lifecycle is a systematic, structured set of connected stages for developing and deploying software that comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities needed to build the software.

32/S0/F5.text: Software engineering can be used as a single term that represents the idea of a software development lifecycle, and engineering software means building the software in stages.

32/S1/F0.text: A design space is the set of all possible designs, and when n distinct objects are placed on a screen without repetition, the typical size of the design space is n factorial, with the number of arrangements increasing if repetition is allowed.

32/S1/F1.text: A calendar application has a fixed and large number of elements to be displayed, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year, so it has a very large design space.

32/S1/F2.text: In a calendar application, many possible designs may be invalid because dates must be ordered in a particular way, but in most practical systems a reasonably significant number of valid design choices can remain, such as 10, 15, or 20.

32/S1/F3.text: A software development life cycle (SDLC) is a systematic approach that helps identify the best valid design choice in terms of usability, because intuition may not lead to the single best solution for everyone.

32/S2/F0.text: A software development lifecycle is a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence.

32/S2/F1.text: In interactive system design, users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.

32/S2/F2.text: A highly iterative software development lifecycle is required for a user-centric design approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software, because including users' needs and expectations changes the stage sequence and creates loops where a developer may return to a previous stage instead of proceeding to the next stage.

32/S2/F3.text: In an interactive system development lifecycle, iterations between stages are intended to account for user feedback, where user feedback means involving users in different ways, not only through feedback.

32/S2/F4.text: The iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development comprises feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, a design-prototype-evaluate cycle consisting of design, prototyping, and early evaluation, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study or usability study, deployment and maintenance.

32/S2/F5.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development has iterations between its design, prototyping, and early evaluation stages, and it also has an iteration to the requirement gathering stage.

32/S3/F0.text: In the development of interactive systems, end users must be involved from the requirement-gathering stage onwards, along with the customer or client, whereas typical requirement analysis refers to the requirements of the client.

32/S3/F1.text: Methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage include contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes.

32/S3/F2.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop refines early designs for interactive systems using user feedback through many iterations, in which a design is prototyped, evaluated to identify problems, and refined until not many significantly different problems are identified, after which the design is stabilized and the next stage can begin.

32/S3/F3.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop and each of its stages must be completed quickly so that many iterations can occur within a reasonable time, because otherwise the overall turnaround time will increase significantly.

32/S3/F4.text: The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

32/S4/F0.text: Coding and code testing in interactive system development are carried out in the traditional software engineering way, through code design, then coding and implementation, then code testing.

32/S4/F1.text: In the coding stage, code testing can reveal issues that require returning to code design, creating an iteration; fewer iterations are preferred because code design is a highly skilled, costly process and late problems are costly to rewrite and test.

32/S4/F2.text: The iterative software development life cycle has three evaluation points: early evaluation, which quickly evaluates interface and interaction design ideas with fewer resources and less time as part of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle; code testing, which evaluates the code as part of coding and implementation; and empirical study.

32/S4/F3.text: Code testing tests the executability of code by ensuring that the code is bug-free and executes properly, but it does not establish whether the system is usable from the end user's point of view.

32/S4/F4.text: The empirical study stage is a usability-testing stage that is required to ensure that an interactive system product conforms to usability through systematic testing with end users, which is a different activity from code testing.

32/S4/F5.text: The empirical study stage differentiates interactive system development from other software development and is typically not part of other software development in which end users are not involved.

32/S5/F0.text: In the iterative design of usable extended reality systems, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops, such as the loop between requirement gathering and the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the loop between code design, coding, and code testing, and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, should not be frequent.

32/S5/F1.text: Frequent loops other than the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, particularly the loop between code design, coding, and code testing and the loop between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and coding, implementation, and empirical studies, significantly affect a project's overall outcome and turnaround time, escalate development cost in manpower, time, and resources, and may lead to project abandonment.

32/S5/F2.text: When building usable extended reality systems, the development stages should be completed carefully so that the need to return to previous stages does not arise.

32/S6/F0.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDLC), building interactive software is broadly similar to building regular software, and the differences are in the requirement gathering, design-prototype-evaluate, and empirical study stages.

32/S6/F1.text: The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design discusses the stages of interactive system development life cycles in more detail with respect to broader interactive system development concerns.

33/S0/F0.text: Extended reality systems are examples of interactive systems, so the same system development lifecycle used for interactive systems can essentially be followed to build extended reality systems.

33/S0/F1.text: The Majuli case study is about the digital preservation of the physical heritage of the physical space of the Majuli River Island, focusing on the design, implementation, and evaluation of an extended reality system, specifically a virtual reality system that digitally preserves the ecological and cultural heritage of the Majuli River Island.

33/S1/F0.text: Majuli River Island is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the eastern part of Assam, Northeast India, and it is considered the world's largest inhabited river island and a potential United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site contender.

33/S1/F1.text: Majuli's monsoon season is typically May to September, its non-monsoon season is October to April, and it has an average annual precipitation of 1704 millimeters, an average maximum temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, and a minimum temperature of 7 degrees Celsius.

33/S1/F2.text: Majuli's area was about 1250 square kilometers around 1900, had reduced to about 570 square kilometers in 1975, and had further reduced to about 427 square kilometers by 2021, with 2021 data giving about 427.09 square kilometers, an overall reduction of almost two-thirds and about a 25 percent reduction from 1975 to 2021.

33/S1/F3.text: Majuli has been constantly hit by severe annual floods and erosion, and river erosion is consuming the island and reducing its habitable area, so formerly habitable areas are no longer habitable and have become sandbars, river banks, underwater areas, or barren areas.

33/S1/F4.text: The severe annual floods and erosion of Majuli endanger its cultural resources and its material existence, and although measures are being taken to prevent further erosion, there is a real possibility that the island may disappear.

33/S1/F5.text: Satras are Vaishnavite monasteries on Majuli that are authoritative centers of Vaishnavite faith in Assam and are living workshops of different kinds of visual and performing arts.

33/S1/F6.text: Majuli is home to several tribal communities, including three distinctive tribal communities—Mising, Deori, and Sonowal Kachari—whose distinctive ways of living, rituals, heritage, and culture make them unique.

33/S1/F7.text: Tangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts like masks and musical instruments and the architectural aspects of Satras and traditional tribal homes.

33/S1/F8.text: Intangible heritage of Majuli consists of heritage aspects that cannot be touched and felt but can be sensed, including traditional skills, knowledge, and aesthetic norms in music, dance forms, drama or performing arts, mask making, vernacular architecture, weaving, food, and agricultural practices, and it is typically embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.

33/S1/F9.text: Majuli also has ecological heritage, consisting of the flora and fauna that exist because of the island's unique geology, geography, and topography from natural formation.

33/S1/F10.text: Before Majuli disappears, it is essential to preserve its tangible heritage, intangible heritage, and ecological heritage.

33/S2/F0.text: Traditional methods for preserving cultural heritage include oral traditions, museums, maintenance of historical sites, and documentation.

33/S2/F1.text: Digital preservation is defined by UNESCO as the use of digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources.

33/S2/F2.text: Digital heritage preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve heritage, whether cultural, educational, scientific, ecological, or other, and it involves archiving, digitizing, and using immersive technologies such as virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR).

33/S2/F3.text: In digital heritage preservation, archiving means storing visual and audio files that capture the heritage information of a particular entity, object, space, or place.

33/S2/F4.text: In digital heritage preservation, immersive technologies can recreate a physical space as a virtual world, such as a virtual tour, and, if properly designed, allow users to interact with entities in the virtual world, making the experience more engaging than accessing information through a computer screen.

33/S2/F5.text: Creating digital avatars of the elements and objects of a physical space can preserve fragile artifacts that may not survive the passage of time.

33/S2/F6.text: Virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies permit a global audience to explore heritage sites, artifacts, and intangible aspects of culture remotely from home without visiting the physical site.

33/S2/F7.text: The use of virtual reality (VR) and other immersive technologies in heritage preservation is known to play a pivotal role in promoting the preservation of heritage for the benefit of future generations.

33/S3/F0.text: The virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island has two clear-cut goals: to preserve heritage and to let users anywhere on Earth experience that heritage.

33/S3/F1.text: Heritage preservation in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island means creating an archive of heritage information that is ideally a multimedia archive comprising images, videos, audio, and text, with images and videos in two-dimensional (2D) and 360-degree forms.

33/S3/F2.text: Experiencing heritage in the virtual reality (VR) system for Majuli River Island is intended as an immersive virtual tour or exploration of Majuli River Island that uses the archive of heritage information.

34/S0/F0.text: The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.

34/S0/F1.text: The focus of the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour is mostly on the island's cultural heritage because ecological heritage has similar issues and challenges and is not treated separately.

34/S1/F0.text: The digital heritage preservation system for Majuli island has two components: preservation, which produces the content of the virtual tour, and experiencing the heritage through immersive virtual tours, which allow users to explore the island virtually.

34/S1/F1.text: Majuli island's distinct tribal cultures are present in tribal villages that dot the landscape, its three major tribes are Mishing, Deori, and Sonowal Kacharis, each of which is supposed to have a distinct tangible and intangible cultural identity, and the villages' unique traditions and customs should be reproduced in a virtual tour.

34/S1/F2.text: The intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island includes festivals and rituals that celebrate cultural diversity throughout the year, including the traditional Bihu, the harvest festival of Assam, which takes place on the island with colorful dances, traditional music, and feasts, and the festivals Kati Bihu, Raas Leela, Ali Ai Ligang, and Bhogali Bihu; their timings and forms should be known so that similar experiences can be reproduced in the virtual world.

34/S1/F3.text: The Satras (Vaishnavite monasteries or sattras) on Majuli island are part of both tangible and intangible heritage, are the heart of the island's cultural landscape, and are centers of religious significance and cultural vitality.

34/S1/F4.text: The intangible cultural heritage of Majuli island includes the Mati Akhara dance and the Khol musical instrument, with the Khol being played while the dance takes place, and these elements should be captured and reproduced in a virtual space.

34/S1/F5.text: The traditional crafts of Majuli island residents include pottery, mask making, silk production, and boat building; these crafts are part of professional and daily life, serve as links to tangible and intangible heritage passed down through generations, and lead to trading with the outside world, so they should be captured.

34/S2/F0.text: In the Majuli case study, the island's cultural landscape is represented by a map of the island with 24 hotspots numbered 1 to 24 and spread around the island.

34/S2/F1.text: Capturing the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of the 24 Majuli hotspots is taken to mean that the entire cultural landscape and cultural heritage of the island have been captured.

34/S2/F2.text: The 24 Majuli hotspots include satras, villages, and other places including towns; of the many satras on the island, nine were included, and six villages were also included.

34/S2/F3.text: Among the Majuli hotspots, villages are used to capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of tribal culture, and towns and other places are used to capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of mixed culture.

34/S3/F0.text: The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island comprises two-dimensional (2D) regular images, 360-degree images, 2D videos, 360-degree videos, 2D drone shots, drone videos, three-dimensional (3D) models, and textual descriptions of artifacts, objects, and elements.

34/S3/F1.text: The multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island captures tangible and intangible heritage aspects, including the indigenous architectural heritage of Satras and village life, cultural heritage, and ecological heritage such as the island's unique flora and fauna.

34/S3/F2.text: In the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island, three-dimensional (3D) models were created from captured images to recreate the landscape, preserve ecological heritage, and recreate tangible architectural heritage.

34/S3/F3.text: Two-dimensional (2D) drone shots and drone videos in the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island were used to showcase the landscape and top view of the locations and to digitally recreate and preserve cultural and ecological heritage, including the island's unique flora and fauna.

34/S3/F4.text: The multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is used to recreate a more expansive virtual landscape and a virtual tour of the island.

34/S3/F5.text: After processing a larger captured collection and keeping the minimum required material, the multimodal heritage archive for the 24 locations on Majuli River Island contains about 600 360-degree images, about 25 360-degree images per location, 5 360-degree videos, 11 two-dimensional (2D) regular videos capturing intangible cultural aspects, and 8 drone videos.

34/S3/F6.text: In the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island, the high-definition 360-degree image resolution is 6720 by 3360, the drone 360-degree video resolution is 1920 by 960, and the drone video used for cultural and ecological preservation has resolution 3842 by 1920.

34/S3/F7.text: The average file size in the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is 6.3 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree image, 100 megabytes (MB) for a 360-degree video, 34 megabytes (MB) for a two-dimensional (2D) video used to capture cultural and intangible aspects, and 36 megabytes (MB) for a drone video.

34/S3/F8.text: The average duration in the multimodal heritage archive of Majuli River Island is 4 minutes for a 360-degree video, about 40 seconds for a two-dimensional (2D) cultural video that captures intangible aspects, and 30 seconds for a drone video.

34/S4/F0.text: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was created by recreating Majuli island in virtual space from archival information, with the objective of providing an immersive interactive experience of the island's tangible and intangible heritage.

34/S4/F1.text: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is an interactive system intended for lay persons, who may or may not have technical know-how, so building it is a classical interactive system development challenge.

34/S4/F2.text: The key challenges in building the interactive Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour are understanding the users, understanding their requirements, and converting those requirements into design ideas that can be implemented.

34/S4/F3.text: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is testing whether the design meets user requirements, where testing means usability testing rather than only code testing, although code testing is part of it.

34/S4/F4.text: Another challenge in building the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is combining vast tangible and intangible heritage information into a usable immersive tour that covers the island's large geography, almost 427 square kilometers captured as 24 spots, unlike typical virtual tours of geographically small museums or other places.

34/S4/F5.text: A key challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour is minimizing cyber sickness, because covering the huge island while experiencing the heritage may lead to cyber sickness due to the longer duration and increased interactivity when a user explores the island in depth.

35/S0/F0.text: The requirement gathering stage in the interactive system development life cycle concerns end-user requirements rather than client requirements, and it is aimed at ensuring usability.

35/S0/F1.text: Requirement specification is required for system implementation.

35/S1/F0.text: System-centered design (SCD) is a design approach in which the main concern is the system rather than the user, and development is driven by the developer's skill and interest, by what can be easily built on the platform, what can be created from available tools, and what the programmer finds interesting, rather than by the user's needs and expectations.

35/S1/F1.text: User-centered design (UCD), also called user-centric or human-centric design, is a design approach in which the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view rather than by the programmer's convenience.

35/S2/F0.text: In requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application, a requirement specifically refers to an end-user requirement.

35/S2/F1.text: In requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application, decisions to develop the application for a mobile platform and to use a programming language such as Java or JavaScript are related to the feasibility stage rather than to end-user usability requirements.

35/S2/F2.text: In requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application, deciding how to store information such as reminders and special events, including whether to use a relational database management system (RDBMS) tool such as MySQL, is a code-design decision, not an interface-design decision or an end-user usability requirement.

35/S2/F3.text: In requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application, some developer questions are not necessarily requirements but are part of the design stage, which may involve the interface design or the code design.

35/S2/F4.text: The objective of usability requirement gathering for the user-centered calendar application is to identify end-user requirements that ensure usability and to specify them so they can be converted into plans for system design, implementation, and deployment.

35/S3/F0.text: Requirements are divided into functional requirements and non-functional requirements.

35/S3/F1.text: Functional requirements are the system features and abilities to carry out tasks, expressed as functions treated as black boxes that produce an output from an input once implemented.

35/S3/F2.text: Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions and are typically related to quality attributes of software.

35/S3/F3.text: Usability requirements are a type of non-functional requirement that concerns the design and qualities of the user interface that make the interface usable.

35/S3/F4.text: Categories of non-functional requirements include performance-related requirements, operating constraints, economic considerations, lifecycle requirements, and interface issues.

35/S3/F5.text: Interface issues refer to the design of an interface or the qualities of the interface that make the interface usable, and they concern how the system interfaces with its environment, users, and other systems.

35/S3/F6.text: Interface issues include an external system interface, meaning interfacing between hardware and software, and a user interface, where usability issues arise.

35/S3/F7.text: Usability is important for interactive systems intended to be used by non-experts or users who are unaware of how the system works.

35/S4/F0.text: The first step in gathering end-user requirements is to specify or categorize the users of the system, because end-user requirements cannot be gathered without specified users.

35/S4/F1.text: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) definition of usability requires a usable product to have a specified context of use.

35/S4/F2.text: Knowing how users behave in a specific work context is essential to ensure that the software, product, or system being built is usable, because usability is defined with respect to that specific work context.

35/S4/F3.text: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods for gathering end-user requirements, which in the context of usability requirement gathering are treated as usability requirements.

35/S4/F4.text: Contextual inquiry is a method more than 30 years old, whose importance in user-centered design was highlighted in 1988 under the term phenomenological research method, and by the end of the 1990s it had become well developed and popular.

35/S4/F5.text: Contextual inquiry is often referred to as a semi-structured interview process that consists of both interviews and observations.

35/S4/F6.text: The primary objective of contextual inquiry is to watch and observe users performing tasks in their natural work setting, that is, their work context, in order to gather more insight about user behavior and end-user requirements.

35/S4/F7.text: The interview part in contextual inquiry may involve asking users questions during observations to clarify certain behaviors or activities.

35/S4/F8.text: A well-planned contextual inquiry process generally takes one to two hours.

35/S4/F9.text: Observations and interaction with users in contextual inquiry enable designers to learn about the task domain, work culture, and physical and social constraints at the workplace, which supports design decisions.

35/S5/F0.text: Contextual inquiry is important in system development because it studies users, such as managerial staff, in their work setting, reveals their unique behavioral traits, and enables design refinement; without it, designers may create invalid designs and give essential user activities equal importance to unnecessary features, compromising usability.

35/S5/F1.text: User activities observed in contextual inquiry must be supported as features in the system design; in the calendar app for managerial staff, the observed activities are setting meeting dates and reminders, so the app must support them to be usable for that user group.

36/S0/F0.text: Contextual inquiry is a usability requirement-gathering method that observes targeted or specified groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

36/S0/F1.text: Contextual inquiry can be performed in two broad modes: active mode, where the observer is physically present in the environment where the users are doing their tasks, and passive mode, where no observer is present, user activities are recorded or videotaped and later observed by the observer, and issues are clarified through interaction with the users.

36/S0/F2.text: In genuine contextual inquiry, the observer must act as an apprentice or learner and treat users as masters or teachers, the master-apprentice model, learning how users behave instead of advising or teaching them how to behave; such advice is prohibited.

36/S1/F0.text: The five stages of contextual inquiry are plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect, in that order, and they provide a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process.

36/S1/F1.text: The plan stage of contextual inquiry involves identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, planning arrangements for recording observations, identifying the users and the date, time, and place of the observation, and, as a helpful practice, scripting and rehearsing the procedure.

36/S1/F2.text: The initiate stage of contextual inquiry involves obtaining all necessary permissions from relevant authorities before observing employees in their workplace and opening communication with end users to remove anxieties that the observation may lead to something bad for them, so that they behave naturally.

36/S1/F3.text: The execute stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the actual inquiry takes place, through performing observations and recording data.

36/S1/F4.text: The close stage of contextual inquiry ideally involves formally closing by sending thank-you notes or a message of gratitude to the users and possibly the authorities, because such users may be useful for future activities such as usability testing.

36/S1/F5.text: The reflect stage of contextual inquiry is the stage in which the observer or experimental team analyzes the data collected during the execute stage and identifies the design goals.

36/S1/F6.text: The affinity diagram method is a technique used in the reflect stage of contextual inquiry to arrange the collected data so that patterns can be found more easily, leading to the design specification of the design goals.

36/S2/F0.text: The affinity diagram method is a method for analyzing data collected through contextual inquiry, and it consists of five steps: generate ideas, display ideas, sort ideas into groups, create a header or name for each group, and draw the finished diagram.

36/S2/F1.text: In the affinity diagram method, the generated ideas are the observers' final notes from contextual inquiry, possibly refined in later processing, and displaying the ideas means putting those notes together in a place such as a wall or a board.

36/S2/F2.text: Sorting ideas into groups in the affinity diagram method is done to find patterns among ideas that may look random, by moving similar ideas into the same group so that meaningful conclusions can be drawn.

36/S2/F3.text: In the affinity diagram method, a group header is a name or identifier assigned to a group after the ideas have been sorted, and it refers to the pattern that binds the ideas within that group; the header is not present in the initial ideas.

36/S2/F4.text: In the class note-taking application example, the 19 affinity-diagram ideas are organized into six groups with the headers navigation in notebook, media content, navigation in notes, note organization, text formatting, and storage and privacy, containing 3, 5, 2, 2, 4, and 3 ideas respectively.

36/S2/F5.text: After the finished affinity diagram is drawn, reflection means deciding what to do with the data and formulating a set of design recommendations based on the data.

36/S2/F6.text: Design recommendations or guidelines derived from contextual inquiry are informed design choices because they are produced by analyzing the collected inquiry data, whereas guidelines created without contextual inquiry are uninformed design choices that do not ensure that users' needs and expectations are taken into account.

36/S2/F7.text: A design recommendation such as providing an erase-content facility in the class note-taking application for correcting mistakes is a requirement, not a prescription for implementation; it states what must be done to make the system usable, and it does not specify how to implement it.

36/S3/F0.text: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the observations that all users set reminders and that three out of five users used a mobile app to check the day and date and set a reminder for assignment submission are grouped under the header reminder setting.

36/S3/F1.text: In the calendar app affinity diagram example, the five contextual inquiry (CI) observations that do not relate to reminder setting, namely checking upcoming deadlines, checking the date and then the timetable, checking meeting dates, checking meeting schedules on a particular day, and checking lecture schedules on a particular day, were first grouped under the header work scheduling and then refined into the headers overall scheduling and day-wise scheduling, giving a finished diagram with three groups: reminder setting, overall scheduling, and day-wise scheduling.

36/S3/F2.text: In an affinity diagram, there is no unique way to group the observations; different groupings are possible.

37/S0/F0.text: The outcome of contextual inquiry, a usability requirement gathering method, can be utilized as design guidelines, design recommendations, or design principles, and also as functional requirements.

37/S0/F1.text: Functional requirements are requirements specified in terms of functions that have a well-defined input and a well-defined output, and this functional specification makes them easy to convert to code so that the transition to code design becomes easier.

37/S1/F0.text: In the note-taking application example, guidelines framed from observations are generic and specify what the application should or should not do, not how to do it.

37/S1/F1.text: Some of the guidelines that can be framed from the observations in the note-taking application example state that the application should support viewing of upcoming deadlines for assignment submission for the current day and the next seven days, viewing of scheduled meetings for the current date, viewing of the timetable on any given day, and viewing of lecture schedules on any given day.

37/S1/F2.text: In the note-taking application example, guidelines based on behaviors observed in the context of use are used to include those behaviors in the overall system, thereby ensuring that the user is involved in the design based on observations and feedback.

37/S2/F0.text: A functional requirement (FR) is a formally specifiable requirement that is easy to convert into code because it specifies a system feature as a black-box function with a well-defined input, a well-defined output, and an optional description of its purpose.

37/S2/F1.text: Usability requirements, which are non-functional requirements (NFRs), can be converted into functional requirements (FRs) and added to the already obtained set of functional requirements, so that usability requirements are directly incorporated into the system through code and support code design.

37/S2/F2.text: A software requirements specification (SRS) is the textual document that specifies all requirements of a system, both functional and non-functional, and it includes the formal specification of the functional requirements.

37/S2/F3.text: In a software requirements specification (SRS), requirements are generally organized in a hierarchy with identifiers such as R1 for a top-level requirement and R1.1 for a sub-requirement, and each requirement identifier represents a function with a clearly defined input, a clearly defined output, and an optional description of what it does.

37/S2/F4.text: The output of contextual inquiry is a group-wise organization of the notes taken during observation, and it can be used as design guidelines to ensure usability that cannot be immediately converted to code or, for some of them if not all, converted into functional requirements (FRs) that can be directly implemented as code.

37/S2/F5.text: In the calendar app for college students example, the functional requirement R1 views takes a date as input and generates a specific view such as timetable, submission deadlines, or meeting list, with subrequirements R1.1 timetable view (date input, day timetable output), R1.2 deadline view (date input, submission deadlines output), and R1.3 meeting schedule (date input, list of meetings scheduled on the day output).

37/S3/F0.text: Usability requirements for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour were gathered by making field trips to Majuli, interviewing people, observing people in their natural work settings, and collecting data in the form of notes.

37/S3/F1.text: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour is intended for people who do not reside on Majuli rather than residents, because residents are least likely to use it since they are already on the island.

37/S3/F2.text: Three potential user groups in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study were identified through field trips, interviews, observations, and local people's experience of typical visitors and their activities: students or learners interested in knowing about the island, tourists interested in exploring tourist spots or other interesting places on the island, and pilgrims interested in religious places and practices.

37/S3/F3.text: The usability of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour is claimed only for the three identified user groups—students or learners, tourists, and pilgrims—and it is not claimed to be usable for any person in any work context or task.

37/S3/F4.text: Contextual inquiry (CI) in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was conducted after the user groups were identified, on samples from those user groups, to learn their needs and expectations, identify the system features to be supported for each group, and identify specific issues for those groups related to broad design challenges.

37/S3/F5.text: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide a comprehensive view of a large geographical area with large multimodal data while avoiding cyber sickness, because exploring the entire island with all collected data is time consuming and may cause cyber sickness.

37/S3/F6.text: The large geographical area and cyber sickness challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was addressed by allowing each user group to access only a subset of the collected data, with each subset identified through contextual inquiry (CI) based on what that group typically does.

37/S3/F7.text: The data-subset restriction in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study reduced the expanse of information and the need to explore everything in detail, reduced the possibility of cyber sickness, and increased interest for each group, whereas making the entire data set accessible to all users could confuse users, reduce their interest, and lead to cyber sickness.

37/S3/F8.text: Accurate location information in any virtual reality (VR) tour is crucial, especially for large geographies, because it prevents disorientation and gives users more confidence and purpose by telling them where they are in the geographical space.

37/S3/F9.text: Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.

37/S3/F10.text: A key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was to provide both tangible and intangible heritage experiences and to combine them for a seamless user experience.

37/S3/F11.text: Another key design challenge in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was interaction aid for enhanced user experience, which includes navigation support to cover a large geography, user-friendly interfaces, and increased presence through natural interactions.

37/S4/F0.text: Contextual inquiry is one of many methods available for usability requirement gathering.

38/S0/F0.text: The interactive system development lifecycle has two design stages: the design stage in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and code design.

38/S0/F1.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle, code design is the same as code design in any other non-interactive software development.

38/S1/F0.text: Designing an immersive experience involves the design-prototype-evaluation cycle in order to incorporate user requirements.

38/S1/F1.text: Interface and interaction design involves two issues: where or how to start the design process and how to express a design so that it can be brainstormed and refined, which means having a design language.

38/S1/F2.text: Interface and interaction design requires creativity and imagination, and the design process can be started from creativity aided by intuition, expertise, experience, or domain knowledge, and/or from guidelines, often called checklists, heuristics, or thumb rules.

38/S1/F3.text: Some design guidelines are generic, small in number, and cover broad high-level aspects of interactive systems; examples are Shneiderman's eight golden rules and Donald Norman's seven principles, both primarily intended for graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but applicable to other domains, with Norman's seven principles developed in the 1980s.

38/S1/F4.text: Other design guidelines are more detailed and specific, generally large in number, and cover the micro details of a particular system or product; for example, Apple's human interface guidelines were originally developed for Apple's user interfaces.

38/S1/F5.text: A design language is a specification of design, and there can be different languages for specifying a design; the language used to specify interface design is generally different from the language used to specify code design.

38/S1/F6.text: A prototype can be considered a language for expressing interface and interaction design ideas.

38/S2/F0.text: The virtual reality (VR)-specific guidelines for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness are specific design guidelines that are typically applicable to virtual reality or immersive systems where immersion is very important, but may not be specifically applicable to augmented reality (AR) systems because augmented reality immersion differs from virtual reality immersion.

38/S2/F1.text: Generic design guidelines are guidelines applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality (XR) systems, although they are mostly, not fully, applicable to extended reality systems.

38/S2/F2.text: Ben Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules are a set of eight generic design rules originally developed in 1986 primarily for graphical user interfaces (GUIs), and can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces, including extended reality (XR) systems.

38/S3/F0.text: Shneiderman's first golden rule of system and interface design is to strive for consistency.

38/S3/F1.text: The consistency required by Shneiderman's first golden rule has two types: internal consistency and external or environmental consistency.

38/S3/F2.text: Internal consistency in system design means using the same elements and interactions for the same task across different parts of a design and different usage instances, rather than using separate objects, elements, or interactions.

38/S3/F3.text: External or environmental consistency in system design means that the elements and interactions in a virtual world should closely match the user's real-world experience and knowledge, so that real-world knowledge transfers to the virtual world as closely as possible.

38/S3/F4.text: Shneiderman's second golden rule is to design for universal usability, meaning a system should provide facilities for all user categories and support different user categories rather than only specific user categories.

38/S3/F5.text: Menu-based options can be preferable to hotkey options for users who may not remember hotkey combinations because menu options rely on recognition rather than recall, and recall is a skilled task, whereas hotkeys such as Control plus S (Ctrl+S) are faster for users who do not want to use slower menu-based options.

38/S4/F0.text: The third rule of usable design is to provide informative feedback to users for whatever action the user performs.

38/S4/F1.text: A progress bar is informative feedback that sometimes appears during a task, shows the percentage of the task completed, and gives the user a sense of how much longer to wait; without it, the user cannot tell what the system is doing or how much of the task is completed.

38/S4/F2.text: A color change on a save icon after a save operation is informative feedback that indicates the save operation is done successfully; without it, the user cannot tell whether the save operation worked.

38/S4/F3.text: The fourth rule is to design dialogues to yield closure by organizing task execution into beginning, middle, and end parts and providing feedback at the end of each group, so the user feels the task is started, executed, and completed.

38/S5/F0.text: The fifth rule in system design is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.

38/S5/F1.text: In system design, user errors cannot be completely eliminated, so a design should aim to keep error rates low; for example, close and start options for the same interface should not be placed side by side because a user may accidentally choose the wrong action.

38/S5/F2.text: In system design, when an error occurs, error handling should give simple, easy-to-understand information rather than complicated error messages, because complicated messages can confuse and scare the user.

38/S5/F3.text: The sixth rule in system design is to permit easy reversal of actions, ideally by keeping a reversal option available so users can return from an erroneous situation.

38/S5/F4.text: Undo and redo facilities are primarily meant to permit easy reversal of actions.

38/S6/F0.text: The seventh usability rule, keeping users in control, requires that lay users feel in control of the system, perceive that their interaction changes the system state, and receive feedback on their actions and results, because lack of this feeling makes them feel at a loss and reduces usability.

38/S6/F1.text: In a broad sense, human memory comprises short-term and long-term memory, where short-term memory is a note-like non-permanent store used to bring information from long-term memory to aid day-to-day activities.

38/S6/F2.text: George Miller's 1956 psychological finding, the seven plus or minus two rule, gives the short-term memory limit as five to nine chunks of information at a time, so holding fewer underutilizes short-term memory and holding more overutilizes it and is harmful.

38/S6/F3.text: The last usability rule, reducing short-term memory load, requires keeping the information needed to operate an interface or perform an interaction between five and nine chunks for the user's optimum outcome, and not forcing users to remember more than nine chunks.

38/S6/F4.text: A chunk of information is a unit of information that can be one letter, one word, a whole sentence, or a whole concept, depending on the application.

38/S6/F5.text: The eight generic usability rules are not specific to a particular product or system, and they can be analyzed for applicability to a broad class of interactive systems, including extended reality systems.

38/S7/F0.text: Interaction in non-immersive settings, such as augmented reality (AR), is similar to familiar interactions such as touch and gesture.

38/S7/F1.text: For immersive virtual reality (VR) or mixed reality (MR) experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and suitable interaction techniques should be known and used to design the experience properly and enhance presence.

38/S7/F2.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

39/S0/F0.text: In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.

39/S1/F0.text: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.

39/S1/F1.text: For a given virtual experience, the kind of object selection technique that is suitable is determined by some of the most important parameters or variables that influence user performance while accomplishing the selection task, including the distance of the object to be selected from the current viewpoint or camera position, the direction of the object to be selected, the size of the object to be selected, the density of objects around the target object, and the number of targets to be selected, so that selection performance is maximized.

39/S1/F2.text: Target occlusion can also be an important factor in selection performance: if a target is partly occluded by other surrounding objects, locating and selecting it is challenging and specialized techniques may be required, while fully occluded objects may also be selected, but the user must first be made aware of their presence, and specialized selection of fully occluded objects is a special case, with the majority of cases involving partially occluded or partially visible objects.

39/S1/F3.text: Object selection techniques in a virtual world include selection with the hand, pointing-based selection, image plane selection, volume-based selection, and bimanual selection.

39/S2/F0.text: A hand selection technique selects virtual objects in a virtual world with the user's hand by having the user directly reach out to virtually touch the object and trigger a grab; conventionally, selection with hand involves one hand, using a single finger or multiple fingers of one hand.

39/S2/F1.text: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

39/S2/F2.text: The virtual hand technique is the simplest and most intuitive hand selection technique, in which a visible virtual hand acts as an avatar of the user's physical hand and is tied to it through a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand's motion and orientation, typically implemented with three-dimensional (3D) tracked controllers, allowing natural hand movements.

39/S2/F3.text: The virtual hand technique has a problem for selecting distant objects because moving the physical hand to reach them can require a long duration of physical hand movement, which can be tiring and annoying.

39/S2/F4.text: The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.

39/S2/F5.text: The go-go technique has a low-precision problem for selecting distant small objects because the virtual hand moves faster when the object is farther away, so a small physical hand movement can miss, bypass, or cross the target and is difficult to control.

39/S2/F6.text: The prism technique is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's physical hand moves below a specified speed, and if the hand velocity is slower than a specified minimum velocity, the virtual hand remains still.

39/S2/F7.text: For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go.

39/S2/F8.text: Prism can result in a mismatch between the real and virtual hand positions because it does not use a one-to-one mapping, which may be counterintuitive.

39/S2/F9.text: Intent-driven selection is a hand selection technique in which the user moves the virtual hand toward an object and positions virtual fingers, or uses the posture of virtual fingers, around the object to indicate the user's level of confidence in selecting that object.

39/S2/F10.text: Intent-driven selection techniques typically use proximity spheres that encompass multiple objects at a larger distance and progressively reduce in size, depending on hand or finger postures, as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection to a specific object.

39/S2/F11.text: In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

39/S3/F0.text: Pointing-based selection is a selection technique in which the user operates a controller to extend a ray into the distance in the virtual world, sees the ray, and can select the first object intersected by the ray through a user-controlled trigger on the controller.

39/S3/F1.text: Pointing for pointing-based selection can be done by hand pointing with a hand or handheld input device, by head pointing, in which a head-mounted display extends the ray from the head position and moves it with head movement without using the hand, or by eye-gaze pointing with an eye tracker.

39/S3/F2.text: A virtual ray in pointing-based selection is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye, with head position or eye gaze used when hand tracking is unavailable.

39/S3/F3.text: Some pointing-based selection methods combine gaze pointing to estimate the target and hand pointing to trigger selection.

39/S3/F4.text: Ray casting is the most basic way to extend a ray in pointing-based selection, in which the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

39/S3/F5.text: In ray casting, selecting small distant objects is difficult and can require practice because the ray must be pointed precisely, and the difficulty increases when the small object is surrounded by other objects of similar, smaller, or larger size.

39/S3/F6.text: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting in which the system bends the ray toward the closest selectable object, detected by calculating the point-line distance from each selectable object, so the user need not point precisely, and a circular arc can provide visual feedback for the bending.

39/S3/F7.text: Bend cast works best when only a few objects are near the ray's path, because with many nearby objects and similar distances the intended object may not be the closest, reintroducing the precision problem.

39/S3/F8.text: Depth ray is an improvement over basic ray casting in which a user-controlled depth marker, positioned by moving the hand forward or backward, disambiguates multiple intersected objects and selects the object intersected by the pointing vector and closest to the marker.

39/S4/F0.text: The third category of object selection techniques is image plane or volumetric selection.

39/S4/F1.text: Image plane selection, also known as occlusion and framing, is a two-dimensional (2D) selection technique in which the user selects on a view plane that contains the object as viewed from a distance.

39/S4/F2.text: In image plane selection, the user holds one or two hands or fingers between the eye and the desired object and provides a signal, such as a gesture or hand movement, to select the object when it lines up with the hand and the eye.

39/S4/F3.text: The image plane selection techniques include the head crusher technique, the sticky finger technique, the lifting palm technique, and the framing hands technique, with framing hands being more common and the other techniques less common.

39/S4/F4.text: In the head crusher technique, the user positions the thumb and forefinger so that they surround or enclose the desired object in the two-dimensional (2D) image plane.

39/S4/F5.text: In the sticky finger technique, the object underneath the user's finger is selected.

39/S4/F6.text: In the lifting palm technique, the user selects an object by flattening the outstretched hand and positioning the palm below the desired object as if trying to lift the object with the palm.

39/S4/F7.text: In the framing hands technique, the user positions hands to form the two corners of a frame in the two-dimensional (2D) image surrounding an object, as typically seen while capturing movies or such visual media.

39/S4/F8.text: Volumetric selection extends image plane selection by enabling the user to select a three-dimensional (3D) region in virtual space, with the objects within that region selected, where the region can be a box or cube, a sphere, or a cone.

39/S4/F9.text: The cone casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique that extends ray casting by casting a cone instead of a ray to a distance and selecting the objects within the cone.

39/S4/F10.text: The cone casting flashlight technique can select multiple objects because the cone is volumetric, so selecting smaller or tightly grouped objects may be difficult.

39/S4/F11.text: The sphere casting flashlight technique is a volumetric selection technique in which a sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface and the objects found within the sphere are selected.

39/S4/F12.text: The two-handed box selection technique is a bimanual volumetric selection technique in which the user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, usually a cube but possibly a rectangular parallelepiped, and progressively reduces it to select a specified region of three-dimensional (3D) space.

39/S4/F13.text: Volumetric selection techniques are most useful for selecting small or well-defined isolated objects in a less complex virtual environment, and selecting smaller objects becomes problematic with any volumetric selection technique when the virtual environment is complex with many objects.

39/S5/F0.text: Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.

39/S5/F1.text: Manipulation techniques include hand manipulation, indirect manipulation, bimanual manipulation, and integrated hybrid manipulation.

39/S5/F2.text: Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea and uses a virtual hand to manipulate objects.

39/S5/F3.text: Hand manipulation follows hand selection and is implemented using smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction, and it is the most intuitive way of manipulating objects.

39/S5/F4.text: Hand manipulation requires somewhat more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly.

39/S6/F0.text: Indirect manipulation is a method sometimes used to manipulate virtual objects in which the user does not directly manipulate the virtual object using the physical hand, but instead manipulates other objects mapped to the virtual object, and those other objects in turn manipulate the virtual object.

39/S6/F1.text: Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.

39/S6/F2.text: Each three-dimensional (3D) widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of a given object; instead, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using the individual widgets.

39/S6/F3.text: Indirect proxies are an indirect manipulation technique that provides a more natural grasping method by letting the user manipulate a local proxy, such as a physical proxy prop linked to a neurological data set, so that moving the proxy moves the linked virtual object in the virtual world.

39/S6/F4.text: World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

39/S6/F5.text: World in miniature (WIM) allows manipulation of virtual objects both within and outside the user's reach; for a distant object, the user does not need to select it, but can manipulate its representation in the miniature model, which then manipulates the distant object.

39/S6/F6.text: Implementing world in miniature (WIM) for large and complex virtual environments is not very practical because creating the miniature model for such environments is very difficult.

39/S7/F0.text: A bimanual manipulation technique manipulates objects with both hands, and its hand movement can be synchronous, in which both hands move together, or asynchronous, in which the hands do not need to move simultaneously.

39/S7/F1.text: The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous bimanual manipulation technique that uses two handheld controllers with six degrees of freedom, placed symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis and moved simultaneously, to define a virtual spindle.

39/S7/F2.text: In the spindle technique, moving both hands in unison can move a virtual world object, and the technique can also be used to rotate the object simultaneously.

39/S7/F3.text: The spindle technique is not easy to use because it requires synchronous hand movement while interacting in a virtual world, which is not necessarily easy for everybody and requires a lot of practice to use efficiently.

39/S7/F4.text: Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric but synchronous technique and an extension of the spindle technique, in which both hands need to be moved together but need not be symmetrically placed around the sides of an imaginary axis.

39/S8/F0.text: Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques are techniques that switch automatically from selection to manipulation after selection, without any explicit signal from the user, and switch back to selection mode after manipulation.

39/S8/F1.text: Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER) is an integrated hybrid manipulation technique that mixes ray casting, a pointing-based selection method, with hand manipulation, so selection and manipulation are integrated and the user does not need to perform them separately.

39/S8/F2.text: In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), the user selects an object using a ray casting technique, and when the ray intersects the desired object, the user's virtual hand moves automatically to the object and attaches to it, rather than the ray being attached to the object.

39/S8/F3.text: In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), after the user's virtual hand attaches to the object, the technique switches to manipulation mode, allowing the user to change the object's position and orientation through hand manipulation.

39/S8/F4.text: In Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting (HOMER), manipulation ends when the user indicates to the system that the manipulation job is done through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.

39/S9/F0.text: Augmented reality systems allow regular interaction techniques to be used to interact with the virtual augmentation of the real world because the user's senses are not blocked.

39/S9/F1.text: Immersive environments block the user's senses and cut the user off from the real world in the ideal case, so improved interaction techniques are needed to provide a better immersive experience.

39/S9/F2.text: Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

39/S9/F3.text: Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.

39/S9/F4.text: System control interaction is a third category of interaction that primarily relies on regular interaction techniques that are familiar when dealing with any computer system.

40/S0/F0.text: The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.

40/S0/F1.text: The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.

40/S1/F0.text: The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is the motor component of navigation and refers to the actual movement between two locations.

40/S1/F1.text: Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.

40/S1/F2.text: Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

40/S1/F3.text: Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

40/S1/F4.text: In the four broad locomotion technique types, object manipulation may not be involved in walking-based, steering-based, or selection-based locomotion; manipulation-based locomotion involves navigating by manipulating certain things, and navigation mostly involves no object manipulation while manipulation is not entirely avoided when implementing travel techniques in an immersive setting.

40/S2/F0.text: Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual environment in which physical walking or movement in the physical world is mapped to corresponding movement in the virtual environment.

40/S2/F1.text: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

40/S2/F2.text: In full gait techniques, the user actually walks in the real world and that walk is translated to virtual movement in a virtual environment, which is the most natural way to travel.

40/S2/F3.text: In full gait techniques, completely free walking is not practical or possible for virtual navigation, so walking is restricted within a specified limit in the physical space and translated to any amount of movement in a potentially infinite virtual space, creating a mismatch between physical and virtual movement.

40/S2/F4.text: In a partial gait technique, the user walks in place, so the user does not change position and is not actually moving forward, backward, left, or right.

40/S2/F5.text: Partial gait techniques require specialized devices in addition to other immersive hardware to provide input, may involve active walking interfaces such as pressure mats, pressure sensors, or interfaces with pressure sensors, and map the user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

40/S2/F6.text: Gait negation techniques require a specialized setup that cancels the user's lateral movements and keeps the user's physical position fixed, because natural walking involves lateral movement that may be difficult to map to a focused virtual movement, and the setup detects and eliminates the lateral movement before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation, making it easier for the system to understand the user's intention.

40/S2/F7.text: Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.

40/S3/F0.text: Steering-based navigation is a navigation category in which direction and speed are continuously controlled while the user moves from one point to another, and continuous control of direction and speed essentially indicates that a system has implemented steering-based navigation.

40/S3/F1.text: Steering-based navigation has two types: spatial steering-based navigation, which is controlled using the user's body parts, and physical steering-based navigation, which is controlled using vehicular props or additional hardware.

40/S3/F2.text: Spatial steering-based navigation can be gaze-directed, where looking at a target location moves the user continuously in the direction of looking; hand-directed, where hand gestures determine the direction of travel; or body-leaning directed, where leaning the body toward a movement direction is mapped to corresponding travel.

40/S3/F3.text: Physical steering-based navigation involves physical setups or separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms and virtual reality (VR) simulators for aircraft, merchant ships, cars, boats and spaceships, in which physically moving the steering controls travel in the virtual world.

40/S4/F0.text: Selection-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user selects where to go rather than continuously specifying how to move there by steering or looking.

40/S4/F1.text: Selection-based locomotion has two types: target selection-based locomotion and route planning-based locomotion.

40/S4/F2.text: In target selection-based locomotion, the user selects a destination or target, and the virtual viewpoint changes so that the user feels moved to the target.

40/S4/F3.text: Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

40/S4/F4.text: Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

40/S4/F5.text: Manipulation-based locomotion is a category of locomotion technique in which the user's position, orientation, or scale is manipulated using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

40/S4/F6.text: Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.

40/S4/F7.text: In a world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects causes a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, as if the user moves from one place to another.

40/S5/F0.text: Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

40/S5/F1.text: Wayfinding refers to location awareness, ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination, and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

40/S5/F2.text: Wayfinding is essentially a mental model, and the goal of wayfinding is to build a mental model or cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment so that it is easier to locate oneself and identify a suitable path.

40/S5/F3.text: The objective of environment design is to make it easier for the user to build a mental map; if the design does not support creation of this mental map, many problems may occur and the overall user experience deteriorates.

40/S5/F4.text: The spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model consists of landmark knowledge of the surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment, together forming the essential knowledge base of the mental model.

40/S5/F5.text: A mental model can be created by aiding the user to get, understand, or infer knowledge through the traditional methods of systematic study of a map of a place, exploration of real space, exploration of a copy of the real space or a model of the real space, or any combination of these methods.

40/S5/F6.text: For a good immersive user experience in a complex virtual environment with many objects and different ways to reach targets, wayfinding support is essential; locomotion or travel support alone is not sufficient, and regardless of how many or how sophisticated the travel techniques are, without suitable wayfinding support the user cannot use them efficiently or effectively.

40/S5/F7.text: Landmark support for wayfinding uses obvious distinct non-mobile objects positioned in a given place, and a good landmark should be clearly visible from several different locations or viewpoints.

40/S5/F8.text: Map support for wayfinding can provide maps of the space or place, such as a copy of the virtual world map, where the term world means the virtual world rather than the real world, or a world in miniature display that can show the entire virtual world with objects at different points, the current position of the user, and different routes to different points.

40/S5/F9.text: Path following support for wayfinding can denote multiple paths through a single space by colors, so the user knows that there are different paths to reach a destination.

40/S5/F10.text: Breadcrumb support for wayfinding leaves a trail of markers along the path followed by predecessors, so users can recognize that a path has already been explored, avoid getting lost, and choose another path or destination to save time.

40/S5/F11.text: A compass or another direction indicator can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space, and a compass can be designed and placed in the environment.

40/S6/F0.text: Interaction for system control is an interaction technique whose goal is to issue commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file, and these commands are most of the regular operations associated with using any software.

40/S6/F1.text: Interactive methods for system control include physical controllers such as buttons and switches; graphical menus, adapted two-dimensional (2D) menus suitable for three-dimensional (3D) massive environments, one degree of freedom menus, and three-dimensional widgets; voice commands; gesture commands such as mimic gestures, symbolic gestures, sweeping gestures, sign language, speech-corrected hand gestures, and whole-body interactions; tools such as physical tools, virtual tools, and tangible interfaces; and multimodal interaction techniques that combine multiple techniques, for example voice with gestures or other interactions.

41/S0/F0.text: The design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was framed by its broader objectives of capturing tangible and intangible heritage, enhancing user presence, and minimizing cyber sickness, with corresponding design considerations of user experience design, exploration of the island, and handling cyber sickness.

41/S0/F1.text: A large, content-rich geographic spread in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour can lead to cyber sickness if the tour is not carefully designed, because exploring that spread requires time.

41/S0/F2.text: The final design of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour was developed using the interactive system development lifecycle (ISDL) model, an iterative design-prototype-evaluate cycle that started with a design based on design guidelines and continuously refined design ideas from feedback and observations obtained by involving end users passively or actively.

41/S0/F3.text: Initial prototypes for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour were influenced by observations of the behaviors and preferences of the island's visitors, who were the potential users, and those observations informed design choices about which locations to cover, how to categorize and identify user groups, and how to integrate cultural videos and navigation features suitable for those user groups.

41/S0/F4.text: User feedback and interaction with users for the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour led to incorporated design elements such as a minimap, a notification system, and user controls.

41/S1/F0.text: In user experience design, the first stage is to identify the users, so that the experience can be designed accordingly.
