41/S1/F1.text: The three distinct user categories identified for the virtual tour of the island are pilgrims, students and tourists, each with its own preferences for visiting or exploring the island, and the virtual tour's content and features were tailored to those preferences, which were collected through contextual inquiry methods.

41/S1/F2.text: The information points on the island were identified based on, among other things, interaction with users, field trips, user feedback, and the need to cover the entire island.

41/S1/F3.text: The 24 information points on the island are 9 prominent satras, 6 villages, and 9 towns and other places of importance.

41/S1/F4.text: The virtual tour of the island was designed to cover all 24 information points on the island so that it could comprehensively capture the tangible and intangible heritage aspects of the entire island.

41/S2/F0.text: The starting point of the virtual tour uses a curved screen in an immersive setting to show an introductory video about Majuli island and a tutorial video that acquaints users with how to use the system.

41/S2/F1.text: A boat ride experience at the very start of the virtual tour uses a 360-degree boat ride video to give the user the feeling of being transported by boat from one bank of a river to the other bank, that is, from the mainland to the island or from the island to the mainland.

41/S2/F2.text: Before the actual virtual tour experience begins, the user chooses a user group, indicated by icons for the user categories pilgrims, students, or tourists.

41/S3/F0.text: Preprocessing of the collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and the user's quality of experience involved using high-resolution content and removing unwanted elements, such as the tripod of a 360-degree camera or its shadow.

41/S3/F1.text: The images and videos, mostly the images, were edited with image editing tools for uniform illumination because the 360-degree images captured at different times have different illumination and changing illumination while the user moves from one image to another will make the user feel that something is odd.

41/S3/F2.text: Ambient sounds such as temple bells, birds chirping, and bike horns were added and played depending on the place being visited to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience, with temple bells played for a satra or a religious site.

41/S4/F0.text: The virtual tablet interface provided to users acts as the main interface and provides navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

41/S4/F1.text: The navigation tools of the virtual tablet interface include a left-side island map presented as a world in miniature and buttons for opening the mini map.

41/S4/F2.text: The video player in the virtual tablet interface has a volume controller and other controls and is used to view cultural videos or top-view drone videos of a place.

41/S4/F3.text: The virtual tablet interface provides access to information content through info elements.

41/S4/F4.text: The design of the virtual tablet interface is inspired by real-world tablet use so that it is familiar and easy for users to use.

41/S5/F0.text: A minimap is a world-in-miniature map for a specific place on the island, such as a village or town; it differs in appearance from the global island map and is provided at each of the island's 24 information points to give the user a sense of belonging or local orientation to that place.

41/S5/F1.text: Each place on the island, such as a village, town, or satra, is modeled using captured 360-degree images, with the number of images per place varying, for example more than five or six, 10, or 50.

41/S5/F2.text: On the minimap, white dots represent the arrangement of the 360-degree images; the user navigates by moving from one image to another along the dots, and the arrangement provides direction and orientation; the user's current image is highlighted green.

41/S5/F3.text: An arrow shown to the user indicates a direction, and selecting the arrow moves the user in that direction along the arrangement of the 360-degree images.

41/S5/F4.text: At each place, notifications alert users to available cultural videos; when there is something to see at a spot, the information icon becomes active, and selecting it shows whether a cultural video is available at that spot, which can be played on the tablet interface.

41/S5/F5.text: For location awareness, the system uses dual maps: a global map, which is a world-in-miniature map of the entire island, on the tablet interface and a local minimap on the local interface, to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

41/S5/F6.text: The global map and the local minimap support wayfinding and orientation awareness by showing the entire world in miniature; the minimap provides dynamic spatial orientation awareness about which direction to move, helping users create a mental map and wayfind.

41/S6/F0.text: In the island tour, each place is designed using a series of 360-degree images, so moving from one point to another is moving from one image to another.

41/S6/F1.text: View interpolation ensures a smooth visual transition between two 360-degree images by blurring their boundaries, preventing the sudden movement or jerks that an unhandled image transition would cause and that reduce the user experience.

41/S6/F2.text: Navigation arrows guide the user from one image to another, prevent random movement, and create a seamless exploration experience while supporting smooth travel.

41/S6/F3.text: A virtual vehicle metaphor is a three-dimensional (3D) model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.

41/S6/F4.text: Walking-based navigation is used for a single spot, but exploring the entire island by walking-based navigation would take a lot of time and may lead to cybersickness, so a different travel technique was required.

41/S6/F5.text: The virtual vehicle travel technique gives the user a seated viewpoint inside the vehicle when it is selected, changes the surrounding scenes as the vehicle moves to create the feeling of motion, and lets the user operate the vehicle through ray casting interactions to provide a direction of movement and select a destination, to which the vehicle moves.

41/S6/F6.text: The virtual vehicle travel technique is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the route is pre-planned and the user selects a destination to select a route; it is route selection, not target selection or instantaneous movement.

41/S7/F0.text: In the virtual tour system, the tablet interface includes a video player that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the user's current location in the virtual world; the videos can be 360-degree videos, drone videos, or regular two-dimensional (2D) videos.

41/S7/F1.text: The virtual tour system's tablet interface shows a list of videos available for a given spot, and when the user is at a spot the corresponding material for that spot is added to the interface so the user can choose it, giving access to the most relevant information for that spot, and that relevant information is also determined by the user type.

41/S7/F2.text: The virtual tour system provides textual descriptions of a place as informative notifications and descriptions that provide additional context about locations and significant spots.

41/S7/F3.text: In the virtual tour system, point-of-interest awareness is supported by directional arrows that indicate which way to move and guide users toward points of interest, and by information icons that, when selected, provide further details about the place, mostly as textual information, so users do not overlook important elements in the environment.

41/S8/F0.text: The system design implemented a controlled navigation technique to minimize cybersickness, in which users navigate or teleport using a joystick, so that controlled movement does not support abrupt movements that can cause discomfort and reduces the chances of discomfort.

41/S8/F1.text: In vehicular movement, the speed of change of viewpoint may cause cybersickness if it is not chosen carefully.

41/S8/F2.text: Consistent visual cues and smooth transitions in the system design help maintain spatial orientation, give the user a better feeling and awareness of the place, reduce anxiety and sensory conflicts, and in the long term help avoid severe cybersickness effects.

41/S9/F0.text: In the design of immersive experiences, the term design refers to interface and interaction design rather than code design.

42/S0/F0.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle, empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

42/S0/F1.text: The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality (XR) systems.

42/S0/F2.text: The interactive system development lifecycle consists of a feasibility study stage, a requirement gathering, analysis and specification stage, a cycle of design, prototyping, and quick evaluation, then code design, coding and implementation, and code testing, and finally an empirical study or usability evaluation stage after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

42/S0/F3.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle, the design, prototype, and quick evaluation stages form a cycle in which the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

42/S0/F4.text: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation in interactive system development are standard software development lifecycle (SDLC) stages with nothing special or distinct for virtual reality or augmented reality system design or implementation.

42/S0/F5.text: Besides the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the interactive system development lifecycle can have cycles between code design, coding and implementation, and code testing; after empirical usability evaluation, back to the design-prototype-evaluate cycle or interface design; and between the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and requirement gathering.

42/S0/F6.text: In the interactive system development lifecycle, cycles should generally be kept infrequent because frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, although the design-prototype-evaluate cycle may be frequent.

42/S1/F0.text: The design-prototype-evaluate cycle in experience design consists of designing, quickly prototyping the design, evaluating it, finding problems, refining the design, and repeating this with new prototypes and evaluations, which may require many cycles before the design is stabilized.

42/S1/F1.text: In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, the term design refers only to interface and interaction design, not code design.

42/S1/F2.text: A quick usability evaluation technique is required in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle so that the many possible cycles can be accommodated within a reasonable timeframe without cost overrun and so that design ideas, once implemented, lead to a usable system; if usability evaluation is not done quickly, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun.

42/S1/F3.text: Quick evaluation of design ideas in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle requires both a prototype that models or demonstrates the design idea and can be built quickly, and a quick evaluation method for testing the prototype; both requirements are equally important for a quick execution of the cycle.

42/S2/F0.text: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation of a prototype, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

42/S2/F1.text: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested to determine whether it will work.

42/S2/F2.text: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, that is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice, so one does not always need to fully implement the idea first.

42/S2/F3.text: A full implementation of a software idea involves highly skilled manpower, specifically programmers, and many cost components, including setting up or procuring resources and engaging the manpower, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted.

42/S2/F4.text: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or, in the best case, it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

42/S3/F0.text: Prototypes can be broadly considered in two categories, horizontal prototypes and vertical prototypes.

42/S3/F1.text: A horizontal prototype is a prototype that depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing how the interface appears to the user in terms of look, feel, and appearance, without any functionality or interaction, so no real work can be done with it.

42/S3/F2.text: Horizontal prototypes are suitable for discussing, brainstorming, and eliciting user feedback about the look, feel, and appearance of an interface, including whether its appearance is understandable, intuitive, and usable.

42/S3/F3.text: A vertical prototype primarily represents interactions or functionalities by implementing a few selected features likely to be most commonly used in practice, in depth from the first screen to the last screen after the last action is performed, not all functionalities, because that would amount to having the full system.

42/S3/F4.text: Vertical prototypes are suitable for analysis of interactions and features because they implement interactions.

42/S3/F5.text: In the description of a vertical prototype, the term implemented and the term screen are generic, so implemented does not necessarily mean writing code, and screen can refer to a two-dimensional (2D) computer screen or a scene in a virtual or immersive environment.

42/S4/F0.text: A low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood, and paper mockups of the look, feel, and functionality of an interface are a popular example.

42/S4/F1.text: Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes compared with approaches that require coding and computers, and it is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.

42/S4/F2.text: Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.

42/S4/F3.text: An interface sketch is a simple drawing that can be made on paper and depicts the major components of an interface, including the screen elements the user sees, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout, so that an interface idea can be expressed to others or users for comments and feedback and its appearance can be envisioned.

42/S4/F4.text: A single interface sketch is primarily used to represent a horizontal prototype and is not sufficient to prototype interactions because it does not show the sequence of user actions and the corresponding interface changes needed to execute a task.

42/S4/F5.text: To represent interaction, a low-fidelity prototype needs a series of interface sketches rather than a single sketch, a practice often called storyboarding; a single sketch gives a horizontal prototype, whereas a series of sketches can give a vertical prototype depicting interaction.

42/S4/F6.text: In a storyboard, each sketch is a keyframe, which is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time; the keyframes visualize the interaction for a specific task and its corresponding scenes, and the storyboard captures the sequence of user actions and the screen appearances the user sees from the beginning of the task to its end.

42/S4/F7.text: The overall purpose of a prototype is to convert an idea into a prototype, evaluate it, and revise the idea and prototype if evaluation finds issues; consequently, an interface sketch need not be replicated exactly in the final design, and feedback can change interface elements, their appearance, position, or layout.

42/S5/F0.text: A medium-fidelity prototyping approach uses a computer to create simple prototypes without involving coding, whereas a low-fidelity prototyping approach does not rely on computers or digital media.

42/S5/F1.text: A high-fidelity prototyping approach uses computer programs or programming to create a prototype, so it is effectively actual software development, maybe on a reduced scale.

42/S5/F2.text: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

42/S5/F3.text: In medium-fidelity prototyping, a computer used only to create static interface sketches produces a horizontal prototype because no real functionality is present, while an Adobe Flash animation video or a Microsoft PowerPoint (PPT) slideshow with simple key presses or timers can simulate interaction and create a vertical prototype.

42/S5/F4.text: Low-fidelity prototypes are primarily meant for horizontal prototypes, medium-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for both horizontal and vertical prototypes, and high-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, so making horizontal prototypes using a high-fidelity approach may not make much sense.

42/S6/F0.text: The Wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique in which a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen human operator, called the wizard, operates the computer and returns the requested response or result to the subject.

42/S6/F1.text: International Business Machines (IBM) used the Wizard of Oz approach in its 1984 listening typewriter experiment to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system idea before committing resources to build a speech recognizer, because speech recognizer technology was not yet available.

42/S6/F2.text: The 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup consisted of a human user speaking into a microphone while facing a computer that the user believed was a real computer, a hidden wizard separated from the user by a wall, and two computers connected through an intermediary.

42/S6/F3.text: The hidden wizard in the 1984 International Business Machines (IBM) listening typewriter Wizard of Oz setup heard the user's speech through the microphone that was also connected to a computer speaker, typed the corresponding characters, and the characters were transmitted to the user's screen, making the user believe that the speech had been automatically converted, although no automatic technology existed at that time to convert the speech into the displayed text.

43/S0/F0.text: Prototypes can be used in different ways: as throwaway prototypes, incremental prototypes, and evolutionary prototypes.

43/S0/F1.text: Throwaway prototypes are prototypes that are used for quick evaluation and then discarded.

43/S0/F2.text: Low-fidelity cardboard mockups and paper sketches are mainly suitable for throwaway prototypes because they are less costly and discarding them does not incur significant cost, and throwaway prototypes should be easy and fast to create, otherwise working with them becomes expensive.

43/S0/F3.text: Incremental prototypes are created when the system design divides the system into units or modules, each module is separately prototyped and tested, and the modules are then integrated into the overall system.

43/S0/F4.text: Evolutionary prototypes are created by prototyping and testing the whole system from the beginning, starting with a simpler version, refining it, adding more functionalities, and altering it based on testing results until it becomes the final product, rather than prototyping separate modules and combining them.

43/S1/F0.text: Quick evaluation of prototypes, also known as expert evaluation, is a technique for quickly and cheaply evaluating a prototype at an early stage of design, unlike a robust evaluation technique, which typically involves suitably skilled evaluators, resources, and an evaluation setup.

43/S1/F1.text: The prerequisites for performing quick or expert evaluation are at least a low-fidelity prototype, with higher-quality prototypes being better, and a team of evaluators.

43/S1/F2.text: Quick evaluation is a usability test, but although the primary condition of usability testing is to involve users, the evaluation team for quick or expert evaluation is primarily the design team itself or skilled designers with knowledge and skill in the problem domain, and may optionally include a few end users.

43/S1/F3.text: Quick or expert evaluation can rely on design-team members or domain experts rather than end users because they are assumed to have user-like experience, their feedback likely reflects users, and engaging them is less complicated, quicker, and cheaper than engaging a full evaluation team with end users.

43/S1/F4.text: The evaluation team for expert evaluation should have at least three to five members; more members are welcome, but three to five is sufficient.

43/S1/F5.text: In expert evaluation, each evaluator is presented with the prototype, evaluates it independently, and produces a report containing the usability issues perceived by that evaluator; the design team or team lead then combines these reports into a final list of usability issues.

43/S2/F0.text: Cognitive walkthrough is a quick expert evaluation technique and usability inspection method in which usability problems are identified by inspecting a prototype.

43/S2/F1.text: A cognitive walkthrough requires at least a low-fidelity vertical prototype, a prototype that supports several tasks and may be low- or medium-fidelity, and an evaluation team of three to five members; a high-fidelity prototype is more welcome but involves more time and cost.

43/S2/F2.text: A low-fidelity prototype for a cognitive walkthrough can be made as simple paper prototypes using the storyboarding approach, in which each prototype is a series of sketches depicting screen changes after each interaction, that is, a storyboard.

43/S2/F3.text: In a cognitive walkthrough, a scenario or task description is created for the evaluators, and the task described in the scenario is converted into interface-level tasks, which are the actions that must be performed in the prototype to accomplish that task; the evaluators then perform those actions with the prototype.

43/S2/F4.text: Usability questions are framed before a cognitive walkthrough to reflect usability issues, and evaluators use them as guidelines to identify problems users are likely to face while performing the tasks.

43/S2/F5.text: For each usability question, evaluators must give a detailed report rather than a simple yes or no answer, explaining where they felt difficulty in the interface or interaction and why.

43/S2/F6.text: The evaluators' reports are collected, combined, and analyzed at the end of the evaluation session to identify broader usability issues.

43/S3/F0.text: Heuristic evaluation is an evaluation technique in which evaluators assess a presented prototype by ticking items on a checklist of heuristics, without a task scenario or task performance, to perform a comprehensive evaluation of the whole system rather than a task-specific evaluation.

43/S3/F1.text: Available checklists for evaluating interfaces include detailed system-specific checklists and checklists focused on broader usability principles, and the broader checklists contain fewer heuristics because they are broader in nature and not specific to any particular interface.

43/S3/F2.text: Nielsen's 10 heuristics is a general set of heuristics proposed in 1994 that is primarily related to graphical user interfaces (GUIs) but equally applicable to most interactive systems.

43/S3/F3.text: Nielsen's 10 heuristics consist of: 1) visibility of system status, in which the status of the system should be visible to the user; 2) match between system and the real world, in which what the user does on the system should closely match the user's real-world experience; 3) user control and freedom, concerning whether the user is given freedom and what kind of controls are provided; 4) consistency and standards, in which elements and layout should be consistent across different screens and standards should be followed; 5) error prevention, in which the design should help the user prevent errors; 6) recognition rather than recall, in which the user should not have to remember what to do but should be able to recognize from elements what to do because recollection is more difficult than recognition; 7) flexibility and efficiency of use; 8) aesthetic and minimalist design, in which the design should have a minimum number of elements and should be aesthetically pleasing; 9) help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; and 10) help and documentation, in which the system should provide help and documentation support.

43/S3/F4.text: Nielsen's 10 heuristics can be used to identify usability problems at an early stage of design on the basis of simple low-fidelity prototypes, primarily horizontal prototypes, with vertical prototypes optional in heuristic evaluation, unlike the cognitive walkthrough method, where a vertical prototype is mandatory.

43/S3/F5.text: Heuristic evaluation requires a team of at least three to five evaluators, who can be members of design teams or other skilled or expert designers not necessarily involved in the design team.

43/S3/F6.text: In heuristic evaluation, each evaluator is given the prototype and the checklist of heuristics, evaluates the prototype against each heuristic, reports whether each heuristic is followed or violated and, if violated, gives reasons, and the evaluators' reports are combined and compiled to identify the violated heuristics and major issues.

44/S0/F0.text: User evaluation is a quick evaluation technique that obtains feedback by asking users directly, and it requires user involvement, unlike expert evaluation techniques in which user involvement was optional.

44/S0/F1.text: User evaluation is often called evaluation with self-reports, and user feedback is collected with rating scales, with the data sometimes called subjective or preference data.

44/S0/F2.text: In user evaluation, collecting user feedback with rating scales is easy compared with more rigorous evaluation techniques.

44/S0/F3.text: In user evaluation, the items provided to users to rate are questions or statements, and these items are commonly called questionnaires although they need not contain questions.

44/S0/F4.text: One major concern in user evaluation is that identifying suitable questionnaires is challenging.

44/S0/F5.text: In user evaluation, data can be collected after every task and at the end of the session, collecting data at both points is desirable if feasible, otherwise one of the two points must be chosen, and suitable questionnaires must be created for the point at which data are collected, so the questionnaires used after every task need not be the same as those used after the whole session.

44/S0/F6.text: Well-known questionnaires available for post-task data collection include the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), designed by Lewis in 1991, and the Expectation Measure (EM), designed by Albert and Dixon in 2003.

44/S0/F7.text: Well-known questionnaires available for post-session data collection include the System Usability Scale (SUS), designed by Brooke in 1996; the Computer System Usability Questionnaire (CSUQ), designed by Lewis in 1995; the Questionnaire for User Interface Satisfaction (QUIS), designed by Chin et al. in 1988; and the Usefulness Satisfaction and Ease of Use questionnaire (USE), proposed by Lund in 2001.

44/S1/F0.text: The After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) is a post-task questionnaire consisting of three statements: 'I am satisfied with the ease of completing the tasks in this scenario'; 'I am satisfied with the amount of time it took to complete the tasks in this scenario'; and 'I am satisfied with the support information that is comprised of online help, messages, documentation when completing the tasks'.

44/S1/F1.text: In the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ), users rate each statement on a seven-point rating scale in which rating 1 means strongly disagree with the statement and rating 7 means strongly agree with the statement.

44/S1/F2.text: The three statements of the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be roughly mapped to the three usability measures in the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) definition: ease of completing the tasks relates to effectiveness, the amount of time taken to complete the tasks relates to efficiency, and the three statements together represent satisfaction.

44/S1/F3.text: Feedback from the After Scenario Questionnaire (ASQ) can be summarised by taking either the average rating for each statement across all users who participated in the evaluation or the average rating for all statements taken together.

44/S2/F0.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) is a post-session questionnaire, containing statements rather than questions, that is administered at the end of a session after users have completed all the tasks.

44/S2/F1.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) consists of 10 numbered statements: 1, 'I think that I would like to use this system frequently' (positive); 2, 'I found the system unnecessarily complex' (negative); 3, 'I thought the system was easy to use' (positive); 4, 'I think I would need the support of a technical person to be able to use the system' (negative); 5, 'I found the various functions in this system were well integrated' (positive); 6, 'I thought the system was too inconsistent' (negative); 7, 'I would imagine that most people would learn to use the system very quickly' (positive); 8, 'I found the system very cumbersome to use' (negative); 9, 'I felt very confident using the system' (positive); and 10, 'I needed to learn a lot of things before I could get going with this system' (negative); each even-numbered statement is the negatively worded counterpart of the preceding odd-numbered statement.

44/S2/F2.text: Each System Usability Scale (SUS) statement is rated by the user on a 5-point agreement scale, where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree.

44/S2/F3.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) score S is calculated from all 10 statement ratings r_i, with i from 1 to 10, as S = 2.5 × (Σ_{i∈{1,3,5,7,9}}(r_i − 1) + Σ_{i∈{2,4,6,8,10}}(5 − r_i)), where r_i is the user's rating for statement i.

44/S2/F4.text: The System Usability Scale (SUS) score is interpreted directly as a percentage, and a score of 70% or higher is typically considered desirable, indicating that the interface is usable or has only minimal problems, while a score below 70% may indicate usability problems that may require a design review.

44/S2/F5.text: Unlike expert evaluation techniques, which give designers more detailed reports from each evaluator, the System Usability Scale (SUS) gives a quick general indication from user ratings of whether usability problems exist but does not explain the reasons, so designers must identify the specific problems through further brainstorming or by examining the scores of individual statements.

44/S3/F0.text: The questionnaires identified as ASQ and SUS are generic questionnaires applicable to any interactive system, not specifically meant for extended reality (XR) systems.

44/S3/F1.text: The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) is the most extensively used of the questionnaires specifically designed for cyber sickness in extended reality (XR).

44/S3/F2.text: The virtual reality sickness questionnaire (VRSQ) and the cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) are questionnaires relevant to cyber sickness in extended reality (XR).

44/S3/F3.text: The cyber sickness questionnaire (CSQ) is good for evaluating virtual reality (VR) experiences with head-mounted displays (HMDs).

44/S3/F4.text: Shorter, more precise, and more concise questionnaires for extended reality (XR) that assess specific conditions include the misery scale (MIS) and the fast motion sickness scale (FMS).

44/S3/F5.text: Susceptibility to cyber sickness (CS) in extended reality (XR) can be measured using the Motion History Questionnaire (MHQ), the Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (MSSQ), and the Visually Induced Motion Sickness Susceptibility Questionnaire (VIMSSQ).

44/S3/F6.text: Questionnaires commonly used to assess overall discomfort in immersive extended reality (XR) experiences include the nausea scale and the motion sickness assessment questionnaire (MSAQ).

44/S4/F0.text: The Majuli VR Tour was developed with Unity engine version 2021.3.22f1 for the Oculus Quest 2 platform and Android smartphones, with Android 6.0 as the operating-system requirement for both versions.

44/S4/F1.text: The Majuli VR Tour used the Extended Reality (XR) toolkit for its Oculus Quest version and the Google Virtual Reality (VR) software development kit (SDK) for its Google Cardboard version.

44/S4/F2.text: Autodesk Maya software was used to create the three-dimensional (3D) models for the Majuli VR Tour immersive experience, using real images as references and as textures on the modeled objects.

44/S4/F3.text: The initial Majuli VR Tour application size was 9.85 gigabytes (GB) because its content was heavy to cover the entire geographic spread.

44/S4/F4.text: To reduce the space requirements of the Majuli VR Tour, all videos were stored in cloud services and loaded from the cloud when a user clicked a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest video player, so the videos were not always stored on the client device, reducing the application size to 5.1 gigabytes (GB).

44/S4/F5.text: Because the Majuli VR Tour application was 5.1 gigabytes (GB) and not suitable for mobile deployment, a mobile version for Google Cardboard was made by compressing high-resolution 360-degree and two-dimensional (2D) images and removing most video playback support, reducing the application size to 0.7 gigabytes (GB).

44/S4/F6.text: The Oculus Quest version of the Majuli VR Tour used 597 images, 11 cultural videos, 8 drone videos, and 5 360-degree videos, while the Google Cardboard mobile version used all 597 images in compressed form, no cultural videos, no drone videos, and 1 360-degree video for the initial experience.

44/S5/F0.text: The Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour has three implementations: a 360-degree-image tour for the Oculus Quest headset, a three-dimensional (3D) model tour for the Oculus Quest headset, and a mobile-device tour using Google Cardboard.

44/S5/F1.text: The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses 360-degree images, cultural videos, 360-degree videos, and ambient sound.

44/S5/F2.text: In the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the start screen uses a ray-casting-based selection method and plays introductory videos about Majuli and a tutorial that explains how to control and use the system.

44/S5/F3.text: After user group selection in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user experiences a boat ride from the mainland to Majuli island, using a 360-degree video captured during field trips.

44/S5/F4.text: When the user reaches the riverbank in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, a tablet interface appears that lets the user select a location on a map and move to that particular location.

44/S5/F5.text: Inside a location in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, the user can move forward and backward using arrow keys and can see icons intended to provide information.

44/S5/F6.text: At different points in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, cultural videos and activities are available, and a notification for cultural videos is played on the tablet interface.

44/S5/F7.text: The 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation supports movement from one point to another using an overall island minimap on the tablet interface, in which each white dot represents a 360-degree image and the user's current location is marked in green.

44/S5/F8.text: Travel from one point to another in the 360-degree-image Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation uses teleportation together with a vehicle-metaphor route-planning method, in which the road route is fixed and the user experiences motion as if riding a vehicle along the road.

44/S5/F9.text: The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for the Oculus Quest headset and uses three-dimensional (3D) models to create the experience instead of 360-degree images and videos.

44/S5/F10.text: The three-dimensional (3D) model Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation includes models of the entrance to Kamalabadi Satra, the entire campus with roads, and the villages and dwelling units.

44/S5/F11.text: The three-dimensional (3D) models in the model-based Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation use textures from real images to create a realistic-looking appearance.

44/S5/F12.text: The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is for Google Cardboard, in which the user's smartphone is inserted into the Google Cardboard device to provide a 360-degree experience.

44/S5/F13.text: The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation is a reduced form of the full Oculus Quest experience, with simpler controls and fewer features, but its navigation, selection, and manipulation modes are more or less the same.

44/S5/F14.text: To optimize size in the mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation, most videos and cultural videos are omitted, and only some prominent videos are used.

44/S5/F15.text: The mobile-device Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour implementation retains the boat-ride experience and a tablet interface in a different form, with a minimap available at each place.

45/S0/F0.text: Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, usability study, or empirical research, is a stage in interactive system development in which the usability of a developed system is evaluated with end users.

45/S0/F1.text: In interactive system development, empirical evaluation follows the code testing stage, which produces an executable system but does not establish that the system is usable.

45/S1/F0.text: Quick prototype evaluations are limited-scale early evaluations that use a limited number of evaluators and evaluate prototypes, so they can quickly identify some major usability issues but cannot give a conclusive result about the overall usability of the end system.

45/S1/F1.text: A conclusive usability assessment of the overall system requires evaluating the whole fully implemented system rather than a prototype, preferably with a larger number of users, through a controlled experiment that collects and analyzes user behavioral data.

45/S1/F2.text: A controlled experiment used for usability evaluation is generally referred to as empirical research, an empirical study, or a user study, and in the context of usability evaluation it can also be called a usability study.

45/S2/F0.text: An empirical study broadly has four stages: formulating the research questions, determining the variables after the research questions (without which a controlled experiment cannot be designed and executed), designing and executing the experiment to collect data, and properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the data to reach a reliable conclusion about the system's overall usability aspects.

45/S3/F0.text: An empirical study, after a system has been fully implemented, is the process of setting up an experiment, executing the experiment, and collecting empirical data for analysis to measure the usability of the implemented interface.

45/S3/F1.text: The first stage in an empirical study is formulating a research question, and the experiment is conducted to find the answer to that question, with observations or empirical data collection and data analysis performed based on the question.

45/S3/F2.text: The research question 'Is the new text entry graphical user interface (GUI) good?' is problematic because asking several users, for example five users, to judge its quality can produce divided judgments, such as two good, two poor or very bad, and one in between, neither good nor bad, so no answer to the question is likely and no conclusion can be drawn.

45/S4/F0.text: Research question 2 (RQ2), asking whether a proposed text input interface is better than Microsoft Word (MS Word), elicits somewhat more concrete feedback than standalone evaluation, but it does not give a definitive quality conclusion because 'better' means more or fewer features to different users.

45/S4/F1.text: Research question 3 (RQ3), asking whether the new interface lets a user enter text faster than Microsoft Word (MS Word), is less prone to subjective interpretation than a vague quality question because it asks users to complete a text input task and compare the two interfaces on speed.

45/S4/F2.text: Dependence on subjective feedback is problematic and may not support a definitive conclusion, even for a clear question about which text entry interface is faster, because responses can split.

45/S4/F3.text: An experiment collects objective data for a text entry speed question by having all users input the same text, logging their speed as characters per minute (CPM), and comparing CPM values to objectively determine which interface is faster.

45/S5/F0.text: A testable research question, also called a hypothesis, is a question for which a study can be conducted to collect objective data, such as text entry speed, and draw objective conclusions independently of users' subjective interpretation.

45/S5/F1.text: A non-testable research question, also called an untestable question, is a question that cannot be directly tested objectively because it depends on users' subjective interpretation and feedback, so a controlled experiment cannot be set up to collect objective data and, generally, a reliable scientific conclusion cannot be drawn.

45/S5/F2.text: Research questions should not be framed from generalized concepts such as whether something is good, because such concepts are ambiguous and can lead to untestable questions.

45/S5/F3.text: Testable research questions should be used instead of untestable questions, because user feedback on untestable questions is subjectively interpreted and generally cannot support a reliable, definite scientific conclusion, whereas testable questions allow reliable, definite conclusions.

45/S5/F4.text: A more specific testable research question, such as whether one interface is faster than another, may answer a specific aspect but may not answer the broader generalized question of whether one interface is better, because faster and better are different concepts.

45/S5/F5.text: To balance the trade-off between testability and generalization, stage 1 of an empirical study frames multiple testable research questions covering different aspects of a system and combines their conclusions to reach a definitive conclusion about a broader untestable generalized question, such as the overall goodness of an interface.

45/S6/F0.text: A variable whose values are assigned and controlled is called an independent variable, also called a factor.

45/S6/F1.text: The values assigned to an independent variable or factor are called the levels of that independent variable or factor.

45/S6/F2.text: Factors combined with their levels give the test conditions for an experiment and are used to design the experiment; in the text-entry example, the interface factor has two levels, the course's design and MS Word, and these two levels give two test conditions in which text entry speed is observed with each.

45/S6/F3.text: A dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on an independent variable or factor, specifically on its levels; in research question 3 (RQ3), the text entry rate (TER) is the dependent variable because its value depends on the interface, specifically the interface levels.

45/S7/F0.text: Empirical evaluation, also called empirical study, empirical research, or usability research, means observation in the real world of real users.

45/S7/F1.text: Empirical evaluation is carried out at the end, when the system is fully implemented, to obtain an idea of the overall usability of the system.

45/S7/F2.text: The empirical research process has four stages, the first stage being research question framing and the second stage being variables.

45/S7/F3.text: In empirical research, research question framing addresses broader generalizable questions that are untestable by framing multiple testable research questions, collecting objective data for each, reaching a definite conclusion for each, and combining those conclusions to draw a conclusion about the untestable questions.

45/S7/F4.text: In the variables stage of empirical research, the variables in the testable questions are identified to design an experiment; the two most important variable types are independent variables, or factors, which can take levels or values, and dependent variables, which depend on the factors and levels.

46/S0/F0.text: In experiment design, the selected participants form a sample or subset of all potential users, and the subset must be chosen carefully to be representative of the whole user group; otherwise the conclusions drawn from the subset are not valid or reliable.

46/S0/F1.text: A homogeneous user group is a user group whose members have similarities such as the same age group and similar educational, socio-economic, and/or cultural backgrounds; using a homogeneous subset is acceptable when the system is for such a homogeneous group, but it is not reliable for drawing conclusions for a heterogeneous user group.

46/S0/F2.text: In experiment design, a user profile is a set of well-defined user profile characteristics or entries; the user is first defined by such a user profile, and experiment participants are selected only on the basis of that profile.

46/S0/F3.text: Older people may have different typing behavior from teenagers, and regular computer users are likely to have different typing speeds from infrequent users of computers, so such user characteristics must be considered when choosing experiment participants based on user profiles.

46/S1/F0.text: For a controlled empirical experiment, the number of participants is generally assumed to be between 12 and 25 to draw reliable conclusions, more than 25 can be used, and below 12 the conclusions may not be reliable and may change if the number is increased.

46/S1/F1.text: In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, users perform tasks, and the task performance data collected from them are mostly objective data that are analyzed to draw conclusions about the interface.

46/S1/F2.text: In a controlled experiment evaluating an interface, only a small subset of all tasks supported by the system can be used because of less time or practicality, and that subset must be chosen carefully, otherwise the observed data may not be useful for drawing a reliable conclusion about the overall usability of the interface.

46/S1/F3.text: For an interface, a representative task set is a small, well-defined subset of tasks that are used by everybody most of the time, namely the tasks that potential users most frequently or commonly use when the interface is deployed in practice, and in an empirical study one or more tasks from this set should ideally be chosen so that the collected data and drawn conclusions are reliable.

46/S1/F4.text: For a typing task used to compare typing interfaces, a random piece of text is not a representative task, whereas representative tasks are text strings chosen based on certain metrics and measures that indirectly encompass activities spanning the entire interface and the users' typing skills.

46/S2/F0.text: In an experimental study, tasks can be assigned using a within-subject (repeated measures) design, in which every participant performs the tasks corresponding to all test conditions, or a between-subjects design, in which the tasks for all test conditions are divided and distributed among subsets of participants.

46/S2/F1.text: Within-subject designs are easier to manage than between-subject designs, but choosing between them depends on circumstances, such as the availability of participants and resources, which may force a between-subject design.

46/S2/F2.text: In a within-subject design, the practice effect is an improvement in task performance from repeated practice; it is also called a confounding variable and confounds the analysis by adding noise to the data, because performance gains may be due to practice rather than to the interface.

46/S2/F3.text: To reduce the practice effect in a within-subject design, the task sequence can be randomized or systematically varied; statistically, these random or systematic variations are supposed to nullify the practice effect.

46/S2/F4.text: A Latin square design systematically varies the task sequence allocated to each participant, for example by shifting a numbered task sequence one position for each successive participant.

46/S3/F0.text: In the system implementation process, stage 4, data analysis, is the stage in which empirical data from an experiment are processed and tested for statistical significance before drawing conclusions about the efficacy of a design, such as its text-entry speed.

46/S3/F1.text: In empirical interface studies, the data are obtained from a sample of users rather than the actual population, while the conclusions of interest are about the larger population, such as any user and any text-entry interface.

46/S3/F2.text: A straightforward conclusion from experimental data can be misleading because an observed result may be due to chance, and if it is due to chance, changing the participants or conditions may produce different data and a different conclusion.

46/S3/F3.text: A statistical significance test indicates whether an observed data difference is reliable by showing whether the difference is due to chance or to the tested conditions; a statistically significant difference is not due to chance, and a non-significant difference is due to chance.

46/S3/F4.text: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, the analysis uses the mean text-entry speed of each group and concerns the relative difference between the means rather than the absolute values.

46/S3/F5.text: In comparing two text-entry interfaces, a higher mean text-entry speed alone may be due to chance, so a statistically significant difference between the means is required to conclude that one design is better in speed or efficiency.

46/S4/F0.text: The method for performing a statistical significance test depends on the design of the experiment and the nature of the input data.

46/S4/F1.text: The result of a statistical significance test can include the absolute difference in group means, the two-tailed p-value, the T value, the degrees of freedom, and whether the difference is statistically significant, and such results are typically reported, for example, as t = 1.70, p < 0.05, statistically significant, which is the standard way of representing any statistical significance test.

46/S4/F2.text: In a statistical significance test, such as a paired sample t-test, the p-value is the probability of obtaining the data by chance, and a lower p-value means the result is less likely to have been obtained by chance.

46/S4/F3.text: There are many statistical significance tests, which fall into two groups, parametric tests and non-parametric tests.

46/S4/F4.text: For an experimental design with a nominal or categorical scale of measurement and one factor having two levels, the non-parametric chi-square test is used for a between-subject design, and the non-parametric McNemar's test is used for a within-subject design.

46/S4/F5.text: For an experimental design with one factor having two levels and no other condition mentioned, a between-subject design can use the parametric independent samples t-test or the non-parametric Mann-Whitney U test, and a within-subject design can use the parametric paired sample t-test or the non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

46/S4/F6.text: For between-subject designs, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for one factor with more than two levels and factorial analysis of variance (ANOVA) is used for two or more factors each having two or more levels, and these two tests are parametric tests; the Kruskal-Wallis test can also be used for a between-subject design with one factor having more than two levels.

46/S4/F7.text: For a within-subject design with one factor having three or more levels, or for a within-subject design with two or more factors each having two or more levels, the parametric repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Friedman test can be used.

47/S0/F0.text: The objective of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour case study is to capture tangible and intangible ecological and cultural heritage aspects of the Majuli river island and to digitally preserve that heritage information by providing users an immersive experience, because the island is disappearing.

47/S0/F1.text: The evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour aims to measure usability aspects of the system, specifically user engagement, presence, and comfort in the virtual environment, and to identify potential areas for improvement by analyzing participants' responses and symptoms of cyber sickness.

47/S0/F2.text: The evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour collected data from end users through a controlled experiment and a structured questionnaire, and participant responses were collected subjectively, objectively, or both.

47/S0/F3.text: The structured questionnaire used in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation was related to the evaluation research question and could be used to measure objective data or behavioral data, or sometimes to collect data through a rating scale.

47/S1/F0.text: The empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour used 27 volunteer participants, comprising 17 males and 10 females, who were divided into three groups of nine corresponding to the tour system's supported user categories of pilgrims, students, and tourists, with participants selected to have the characteristics of those categories.

47/S1/F1.text: The participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour had ages between 23 and 40 years, with a mean age of 25.1 years and a standard deviation of 3.03 years.

47/S1/F2.text: Among the 27 participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, 21 had prior virtual reality experience, which may bias the evaluation output.

47/S1/F3.text: All participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour were familiar with the joystick-based controller and with controller-based interaction, having used that type of controller in a virtual reality or non-virtual reality context.

47/S1/F4.text: All participants in the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.

47/S1/F5.text: In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the system was developed for the Meta Quest 2 head-mounted display (HMD), with a display resolution of 1920 by 1832 pixels per eye, and the HMD was connected to a personal computer (PC) via an enabled Oculus Link, the standard setup.

47/S1/F6.text: In the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, the stimuli were rendered on a 64-bit computer running Windows 11 Professional operating system (OS), equipped with a 3.6 GHz quad-core processor and a 4GB GeForce GTX 1080 graphics processing unit (GPU).

47/S1/F7.text: During the empirical evaluation study of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour, participants were seated on a swivel chair while performing the tasks.

47/S2/F0.text: Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.

47/S2/F1.text: The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

47/S2/F2.text: The QEP questionnaire includes 19 core items and 3 optional items related to sound.

47/S2/F3.text: Responses to the QEP questionnaire were recorded on a Likert scale ranging from 1 to 7.

47/S2/F4.text: For the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour assessment, the QEP questionnaire was tailored with two subjective items asking whether the user had previously visited the island in person and, if so, whether the virtual tour corresponded with the experience gained during the real visit.

47/S2/F5.text: The simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) was used to measure cyber sickness, and it is a standard questionnaire that is popular for measuring cyber sickness in immersive experiences although it was not originally developed for cyber sickness.

47/S2/F6.text: Participants rated their cyber sickness symptoms on the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) using a scale from 0 to 3, where 0 means no symptoms and 3 means the most severe symptoms.

47/S2/F7.text: The scores considered from the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) were nausea, disorientation, oculomotor discomfort, and total sickness.

47/S2/F8.text: The participants' simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) scores were computed before and after exposure and compared to get an idea of the effect of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) tour assessment design on those scores.

47/S3/F0.text: In a virtual reality (VR) experiment, unfamiliar users may produce results much different from familiar users, so a brief pre-experiment training session that demonstrates the system's features and how to use them can bring participants to the same level and reduce or nullify familiarity or prior-experience bias, which otherwise may lead to incorrect conclusions.

47/S3/F1.text: In the virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation, participants completed the simulator sickness questionnaire (SSQ) before exploration as a pre-exposure assessment, meaning before exposure to the system, completed the SSQ again after the experimental session as a post-exposure cybersickness measure, and completed the presence questionnaire (QEP) after exploration.

47/S3/F2.text: In the virtual reality (VR) tour evaluation, each participant individually explored the entire tour in a controlled setting within 45 to 50 minutes.

47/S3/F3.text: The 45 to 50 minute exploration time was estimated from pilot studies, trials, and literature to give users sufficient time to explore the large island and obtain heritage information while minimizing the possibility of cybersickness, which depends on exposure.

47/S3/F4.text: In a standard controlled experiment, the important stages are to define the users and carefully identify the participants, to prepare the setup including hardware, software, questionnaires, and logistical support, and to define a procedure that eliminates possibilities of biases.

47/S4/F0.text: The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

47/S4/F1.text: The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

47/S4/F2.text: The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

47/S4/F3.text: The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

47/S4/F4.text: Previous visitors to Majuli Island's more favorable opinions for all factors, despite their higher expectations, indicated that they felt more comfortable with the digital exploration of the island and that the system reasonably well mimicked the physical island environment in its design elements, interaction, and overall implementation, and that the digital avatar was close to reality.

47/S4/F5.text: A statistically significant difference between users with prior exposure to digital or virtual tours and users without such exposure was revealed by a Welch t-test, supporting the conclusion that prior exposure to such systems always helps users gain a better experience.

47/S5/F0.text: The cyber sickness evaluation of the Majuli virtual tour used the SSQ questionnaire and collected pre-exposure and post-exposure data for nausea, disorientation, oculomotor effects, and total severity.

47/S5/F1.text: The box plots of average pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour showed little difference for nausea and disorientation, indicating that the Majuli virtual tour system did not generally induce cyber sickness, although total severity and oculomotor severity showed some difference.

47/S5/F2.text: The statistical significance test performed on the pre- and post-exposure SSQ data for the Majuli virtual tour was a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and it revealed a statistically significant difference between pre- and post-exposure outcomes for the oculomotor item and the total sickness item.

47/S5/F3.text: The statistically significant pre- to post-exposure change in total sickness in the Majuli virtual tour indicates that the Majuli virtual tour design had some effect on total sickness.

47/S6/F0.text: In the evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour, the presence measure gave mostly good results, and prior experience may lead to even better results, with people with prior experience possibly finding the VR Tour more acceptable than people without prior experience.

47/S6/F1.text: In the evaluation of the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour, certain cybersickness items were not found to affect severity, but the oculomotor component may be affected, which may lead to some effect on total sickness.

48/S0/F0.text: In the requirement gathering stage of interactive system development, functional and non-functional requirements, including usability requirements, are collected from end users and clients, who may be the same but are usually different; usability requirements primarily come from end users, other non-functional requirements may come from clients, and functional requirements may come from both clients and end users.

48/S0/F1.text: The interface design part of interactive system development uses a design-prototype-evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping, and quick evaluation of the prototype; design may be based on intuition, design guidelines, or team brainstorming, quick evaluation may use methods such as cognitive walkthrough or heuristic evaluation, and the cycle is repeated until a stable interface design is reached, meaning further evaluation is unlikely to produce many new issues.

48/S0/F2.text: Code design in interactive system development requires producing a code design through iterations and brainstorming, using design languages or notations such as data flow diagram (DFD), entity relationship (ER), object-oriented approaches, and unified modeling language (UML).

48/S0/F3.text: Implementation in interactive system development involves coding followed by code testing; primary-level testing may be review-based, secondary-level testing may be more systematic or structured, such as black box or white box testing, and testing can be performed at unit levels, then integration, and then system-level testing.

48/S0/F4.text: Code testing shows that a system is executable, but it does not show whether the system is usable; usability testing or an empirical study is therefore needed to estimate usability, although usability was expected because the design-prototype-evaluate cycle was followed.

48/S0/F5.text: An empirical study in interactive system development requires identifying participants, setting up the study, and obtaining participants' time.

48/S0/F6.text: In the traditional interactive system development lifecycle, the requirement gathering stage may span months; the design-prototype-evaluate stage can take months, although each cycle may take one or two days and, considering repeated cycles and other activities, may take from a couple of weeks to a month; code design may take months or at least a couple of weeks; code testing may take weeks; and an empirical study may take weeks.

48/S0/F7.text: The traditional interactive system development lifecycle is rigid in requiring all activities and requirements in a stage to be completed before the next stage starts and before deployment; for example, all requirements must be identified before the requirement gathering stage is complete and all units must be coded before the coding stage is sent to testing; this strict stage completion can lead to time and cost overruns and even non-acceptance by the client.

48/S0/F8.text: In the traditional interactive system development lifecycle, deployment is reached only after all requirements are identified, coding is done, code is tested, and usability is tested; because each stage can take a long time, deployment may take a very long time.

48/S0/F9.text: In the standard interactive system development lifecycle, each stage requires a long time not only because of executing the stage but also because documentation for the stage must be prepared.

48/S0/F10.text: In the standard interactive system development lifecycle, the five documents required before deployment are a feasibility study report, a software requirement specification (SRS) for the requirement gathering, analysis, and specification stage, design documents for interface and interaction design and for code, a code testing document, and a usability study report.

48/S1/F0.text: Agile development is a development framework or approach that encourages fast development in practice, starts small by not trying to do everything from the beginning, does not collect all requirements or develop and test the entire system from the beginning, eliminates unnecessary elements and documentation, and ensures quick turnaround of projects that are more acceptable to clients.

48/S1/F1.text: Agile development keeps delivering by adding features over successive deliveries, unlike the standard Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) method, where the system is first completed and then delivered.

48/S1/F2.text: The agile development process flow consists of conceptualization, inception (creation of the team and arranging funds and resources), iteration or sprint (the development cycle, which includes all the other stages of the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC)), release (testing, training, and documentation, and deployment), production (ongoing support and maintenance), and retirement (end-of-life activities); conceptualization and inception together roughly refer to physical feasibility study and requirement gathering.

48/S1/F3.text: An agile iteration or sprint typically requires four to six weeks, whereas the whole Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) may take six to nine months, because the sprint does not try to do everything.

48/S1/F4.text: An agile sprint includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery: requirements are based on the product sprint backlog and customer and stakeholder feedback, then development occurs, then testing including training and documentation, then delivery to production.

48/S1/F5.text: To deliver within an agile sprint, the development team holds daily meetings or brainstorming, provides a live demonstration after each iteration, and regularly collects quick feedback from stakeholders and customers, which is shared with the team before the next sprint so that it can be addressed; this keeps the team agile by making changes based on feedback as quickly as possible.

48/S1/F6.text: Popular agile methods or frameworks include Scrum (SCRUM), Extreme Programming, Disciplined Agile Delivery (DAD), and Dynamic System Development Method (DSDM).

48/S1/F7.text: Agile methods provide a better way to develop acceptable products for practical purposes, whereas the Interactive System Development Life Cycle (ISDLC) is primarily meant for understanding the overall flow and for pedagogical purposes rather than for building practical systems within a reasonable time frame.

48/S2/F0.text: The book Human-Computer Interaction, User-Centric Computing for Design and the NPTEL course on the design and implementation of human-computer interfaces, specifically weeks 4, 5, and 10 to 12, are recommended for further study of concepts such as prototype building, prototype evaluation, empirical study, and agile methods.

49/S0/F0.text: Optimization in virtual reality (VR) can be considered from two perspectives: optimized experience, that is, psychophysiological experience optimization, and optimized resource utilization or resource requirement, that is, technological optimization; these requirements are present in any extended reality (XR) system, but they gain more prominence in an immersive experience.

49/S0/F1.text: In virtual reality (VR), experience optimization can roughly be taken to mean designing the experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction.

49/S0/F2.text: Extended reality (XR) systems, and virtual reality (VR) systems in particular, are generally resource-hungry; if their resource requirements are too high, the systems will not be affordable and it will be difficult to make products for the masses, where affordability is a major concern.

49/S0/F3.text: In virtual reality (VR), effective resource optimization means minimizing resource requirements while maximizing the immersive experience, without compromising it and, to the extent possible, without reducing its quality; this requires balancing the trade-offs between resource requirements and experience.

49/S1/F0.text: Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

49/S1/F1.text: The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

49/S1/F2.text: Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

49/S1/F3.text: Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

49/S1/F4.text: The challenge in developing cybersickness mitigation strategies is to avoid compromising presence, which is indirectly related to user experience.

49/S2/F0.text: Cybersickness is minimized by reducing either the duration of exposure to the virtual world or the distance covered during navigation in the virtual environment, while presence is preserved or maximized.

49/S2/F1.text: Virtual locomotion techniques (VLTs), used to navigate or perform a virtual reality (VR) tour by moving from one point to another, are broadly categorized into walking-based techniques (full gait, partial gait, and gait negation techniques, involving physical walking), steering-based techniques, selection-based techniques, and manipulation-based techniques.

49/S2/F2.text: Virtual reality (VR) tours are categorized into user-controlled tours, in which the user controls how and where to navigate using controllers or other input modalities, and system-controlled tours, in which the system or application controls the user's movement, often following a predetermined path or sequence of movements.

49/S2/F3.text: System-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours are often an effortless experience with reduced cognitive demands because the system decides how and where the user moves, allowing the user to concentrate more on the experience itself.

49/S2/F4.text: Lack of user involvement in system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tours makes them less realistic and defeats the purpose of presence because the user is unable to control the movement.

49/S3/F0.text: In a virtual reality (VR) tour, a system-controlled tour is a navigation mode in which the system forces the user to move from one place to another.

49/S3/F1.text: A realistic walking experience in a system-controlled tour is important because it helps the user feel present rather than controlled by the system and reduces awareness of the difference between realistic and unrealistic elements.

49/S3/F2.text: System-controlled tours, also described as system-automated tours, typically do not allow continuous user input, making it difficult to align user input with walking speed or to judge whether the speed provided by the system is natural.

49/S3/F3.text: Optic flow is the speed at which the visual scene changes, and movement is perceived through this change in the view of the surroundings; in a virtual reality (VR) tour, user movement appears as a constantly changing scene.

49/S3/F4.text: When the navigation in a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is assumed to be walking, the scene-change speed (optic flow) should match the user's actual, or typical, real-world walking speed rather than VR walking speed; otherwise the movement looks unrealistic because it may be too fast or too slow.

49/S3/F5.text: A more realistic system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour requires matching its optic flow to the user's instantaneous walking speed using a model of the user's typical walking behavior, because a constant optic flow is not very realistic as people rarely walk at constant speed.

50/S0/F0.text: A model of natural walking behavior can be used as a realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation to address the need for a realistic walking experience.

50/S0/F1.text: The development of the realistic walking behavior model for system-controlled virtual reality (VR) navigation is carried out in four steps: empirical research to collect empirical data used to build the model, analysis of the data, creation of the model, and validation of the model.

50/S1/F0.text: The empirical study was conducted to collect real-life data of a user moving from one point to another and to propose a speed estimation model.

50/S1/F1.text: The empirical study involved 40 participants, comprising 26 male and 14 female participants, aged 19 to 42 years.

50/S1/F2.text: In the empirical study, participant heights were recorded because earlier studies indicate that height affects walking behavior, and the participants' heights ranged from 150 to 184 centimeters.

50/S1/F3.text: The corridor experiment used a corridor in a physical building in which seven paintings representing images of the seven wonders of the world were placed at distances of 20, 20, 13, 16, 6.4, 19, and 4 meters from the start.

50/S1/F4.text: The seven paintings simulated points of interest in a system-controlled virtual tour, where a user may need to stop, pause, and then move.

50/S1/F5.text: Participants were instructed to start walking from the starting place and stop at each painting to click a photograph, a task assigned to ensure that the user stopped after walking a predefined distance.

50/S1/F6.text: Video recordings of the user's footsteps were made with a Samsung M30 smartphone camera fixed on the user's back and focused on the user's legs; the recording started just before the user started walking and was captured at 30 frames per second.

50/S2/F0.text: In the data-analysis stage, participants' instantaneous step frequency (number of steps per second) was computed by manually playing the videos: a step was one foot strike to the next foot strike on the ground, foot-strike timestamps and distances between paintings were noted, and step frequencies at each step were calculated from the timestamps.

50/S2/F1.text: When step frequency was plotted against distance, a pattern more or less followed by all participants was seen: step frequency started low, increased to a maximum, plateaued, and then decreased to zero at the target painting where the user stopped to click a photo; this pattern is called the slow-in-slow-out pattern.

50/S2/F2.text: The velocity just before the target painting slowed because the user knew they had to stop there to click a photo.

50/S3/F0.text: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern observed in the study is similar to the Fourier-series approximation of a square pulse wave, which starts, remains approximately constant, and then returns to zero.

50/S3/F1.text: A Fourier series with appropriate weights can approximate any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision, and a practical approximation can be obtained by taking the first few terms of the corresponding Fourier expansion.

50/S3/F2.text: The slow-in-slow-out walking pattern is modeled by a Fourier-series expansion of harmonically related sinusoids, and the weights of those sinusoids are calculated from empirical data.
