50/S3/F3.text: In virtual walking, the user's actual movement speed and perceived movement speed need not be the same, and generally an individual perceives visual or optic flow more slowly than the actual movement.

50/S3/F4.text: A virtual tour should not change the scene at the user's actual walking velocity; instead it should make the perceived scene-change speed differ from the actual movement speed so that the user perceives natural walking behavior.

50/S3/F5.text: The desired perceived scene-change speed, denoted v_visual or v_perceived, is computed by multiplying the visual gain g by the actual instantaneous walking speed v_actual, so v_visual = g × v_actual, where v_actual is the user's movement speed and is related to the instantaneous step frequency.

50/S3/F6.text: The visual gain g is typically set to 2.10 because prior studies have identified that value as providing a good visual gain for natural walking behavior.

50/S3/F7.text: In the model, the actual walking speed V_actual is calculated as V_actual = f(x) × 0.157 × (h × 1.72)^2, where f(x) is the instantaneous step frequency as a function of distance x and h is the user's height.

50/S3/F8.text: The instantaneous step frequency f(x) is computed from the Fourier-series expression f(x) = (4/π) × 1.8 × Σ_{k=0}^{d/2−1} [1/(2k+1) × sin((2k+1)ωx)], where ω = 2πf0, f0 is the initial frequency and equals 1/(2d), and d is the distance between the source and destination.

50/S4/F0.text: The natural walking speed model was formed by multiplying computed natural walking behavior by a visual gain factor to let the user perceive natural walking.

50/S4/F1.text: The empirical study was carried out to confirm whether the natural walking speed model, described as instantaneous speed, enhances perceived realism compared with a constant average speed.

50/S4/F2.text: The empirical study was conducted with 34 participants: 20 male and 14 female, aged 15 to 47 years with a mean age of 29.3 years, and with heights of 159 to 170 centimeters with a mean height of 167.97 centimeters.

50/S4/F3.text: The empirical study used a virtual art exhibition environment experienced with an Oculus Rift, in which system-controlled navigation moved the user at constant speed or instantaneous natural walking speed through pictures, with a forced 10-second stop at each picture.

50/S4/F4.text: Each participant experienced both constant speed and instantaneous speed conditions in a randomized order, with breaks between the conditions, to avoid practice effect and bias in the subsequent data collection.

50/S4/F5.text: The study used two 1-to-10 rating scales, with 1 representing worst and 10 representing the best value, to rate level of realism and user preference, and speed with levels constant and instantaneous was the independent variable, with realism and preference as the dependent variables.

50/S4/F6.text: Box plots of the realism and preference ratings showed that instantaneous speed produced higher realism ratings and higher user preference than constant speed, and paired sample t-tests with a p-value of 0.05 showed these differences were statistically significant.

50/S4/F7.text: The instantaneous natural walking speed model is suitable for a realistic walking experience in controlled virtual reality (VR) tools and is likely to increase presence.

50/S4/F8.text: The instantaneous natural walking speed model alone does not address cyber sickness, and the question of how to minimize cyber sickness with only that model cannot be answered, so additional measures are required.

51/S0/F0.text: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour is intended to provide a realistic walking experience by displaying a visual speed, or optic flow (the rate at which scenes change in the virtual world), that matches the user's perceived instantaneous walking speed, producing the perception of movement.

51/S0/F1.text: The natural walking model for a system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour does not provide anything related to experience optimization; it can only be used to enhance presence in the virtual world.

51/S0/F2.text: The approach to optimizing virtual reality (VR) navigation experience that uses the natural walking model addresses cyber sickness by controlling the duration of exposure in the virtual world.

51/S0/F3.text: In a virtual reality (VR) environment, cyber sickness is correlated with exposure duration, with the degree of the symptoms rising proportionally as the VR session duration increases, so if possible, shorter exposure duration can help eliminate or at least minimize the onset of cyber sickness.

51/S1/F0.text: The duration of virtual reality (VR) exposure depends on the size of the virtual world, the travelling speed, the travelling time, and the interaction time spent inspecting, selecting, or manipulating virtual objects.

51/S1/F1.text: A larger virtual reality (VR) environment leads to a longer duration of VR exposure because the user needs to cover a larger geographical area.

51/S1/F2.text: Increasing the virtual travel or navigation speed reduces the duration of exposure to a virtual world because a higher speed lowers the time needed to travel and explore the entire geographical area.

51/S1/F3.text: To provide a realistic walking experience in a virtual world, virtual travel speed cannot be modified arbitrarily; an arbitrary speed imposed on the user while navigating may not be a good idea.

51/S1/F4.text: Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

51/S1/F5.text: Manipulating the virtual terrain or adjusting the distances between points of interest (POIs) can reduce travel time and therefore exposure time, but arbitrary terrain changes prevent users from perceiving the true size and feel of the real space and can hamper their mental map and wayfinding in the virtual world.

51/S1/F6.text: In a purely system-automated or system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tool, users do not interact with virtual objects, so the interaction time required to interact with virtual objects can be ignored.

51/S1/F7.text: A semi-interactive tour in virtual reality (VR) is a system-controlled navigation scenario in which travel is automatic, users may interact with objects after a navigation task is complete, and interaction is limited to a small set of objects at points of interest (POIs), while users cannot interact with other objects in the virtual environment.

51/S2/F0.text: In a semi-interactive virtual tour, interaction time at each point of interest (POI) can be limited to an estimate in advance of the maximum time an average user needs to interact with that POI, after which the system automatically forces the user to move to another POI.

51/S2/F1.text: In a semi-interactive virtual reality (VR) tour, the duration of exposure can be optimized, under a limit on interaction time, by finding an optimum path that either minimizes the total navigation and interaction time required to experience all points of interest (POIs) or maximizes the number of POIs experienced within a fixed time limit for navigation and interaction.

51/S2/F2.text: Optimizing the duration of exposure in a virtual reality (VR) tour is expected to optimize the prevalence and onset of cyber sickness, because exposure duration and cyber sickness are directly related.

51/S3/F0.text: The virtual world part of a virtual experience is represented as a weighted graph G = (V, E), where V is the vertex set of all points of interest (POIs) and E is the set of weighted edges between POIs, representing a top view of the virtual world.

51/S3/F1.text: The graph G used to represent the virtual world need not be complete, because in a realistic environment there may not always be a direct path from one place to another.

51/S3/F2.text: For every pair of vertices v1 and v2 in the vertex set V, the assigned edge weight is the Euclidean distance between v1 and v2 if they are directly connected, and a very large number represented by the infinity symbol if they are not directly connected.

51/S3/F3.text: In the mapping of the virtual world to the graph, each point of interest (POI) is a node, while a single object or structure is not necessarily a single node because it may contain multiple points of interest.

51/S3/F4.text: The optimum travel path problem covering all points of interest (POIs) is to find a path P in the given graph G that covers all vertices in V, which are the POIs, and finishes in the least possible time while maintaining a realistic speed throughout, so that the user gets a realistic feeling.

51/S4/F0.text: The first stage of the travel-time algorithm is to compute the time to travel between two directly connected nodes using the natural walking-speed model.

51/S4/F1.text: In the natural walking-speed model, perceived instantaneous walking speed is the visual gain of 2.1 multiplied by the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act).

51/S4/F2.text: Because speed is dx/dt, the instantaneous time dt for a distance element dx is dx divided by 2.1 times the actual instantaneous realistic walking speed (V act), and the total travel time over a distance D between directly connected nodes is the integral from 0 to D of dx/(2.1 V act).

51/S4/F3.text: In the natural walking-speed model, f is the instantaneous step frequency and h is the height of the user.

51/S4/F4.text: After solving the integral with simplifications, rearrangements, and Fourier-series expansion up to n0, the travel-time estimate tau D for a directly connected vertex pair under the natural walking model is D/V naught times (3 - (16/pi^2) * sum_{k=1}^{n0} 1/(2k-1)^2).

51/S4/F5.text: V naught is a constant for a given height h, equal to 2.1 h^2 divided by (0.157 * 1.72^2 * 1.8^2), where h is the user's height.

51/S5/F0.text: For a path P in a graph that contains n vertices, the total travel time for P is the sum over i = 1 to n - 1 of the edge weight epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) between consecutive vertices, and epsilon(v_i, v_{i+1}) is the Euclidean distance between that pair of vertices.

51/S5/F1.text: In the travel-time minimisation problem for a graph, the objective is to find a path P that contains all vertices of the graph with the minimum total travel time, and this problem is a variation of the travelling salesman problem (TSP).

51/S5/F2.text: The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks, given a complete graph, for the shortest possible path that visits each node exactly once and returns to the starting node, where the shortest path is defined by the total weight of the edges in the path.

51/S5/F3.text: The graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is not assumed to be a complete graph, so there may be no Hamiltonian path in that graph, where a Hamiltonian path is a path that covers all nodes and visits each node exactly once.

51/S5/F4.text: For any two vertices in the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem that are not directly connected, a hypothetical edge is introduced for computation, and the modified edge weight epsilon dash(v1, v2) is d(v1, v2), the Euclidean distance, if v1 and v2 are directly connected, or the shortest path length between v1 and v2 if they are not directly connected, where that shortest path length is the sum of the edge weights in the shortest path.

51/S5/F5.text: The shortest path lengths used for the hypothetical edges are well-defined because the graph used for the travel-time minimisation problem is connected.

51/S6/F0.text: The algorithm takes the original graph G, with vertex set V and edge set epsilon, as input and produces the optimal time T and the path P of the minimum-time path that covers all vertices in G.

51/S6/F1.text: The algorithm first converts the original graph G into a complete graph G' by keeping every directly connected edge unchanged and, for each pair of vertices that is not directly connected, adding a hypothetical edge whose length is the shortest path between those vertices in G.

51/S6/F2.text: After the graph is complete, the algorithm replaces the Euclidean-distance edge weights with the travel time between each pair of vertices, producing a complete time-weighted graph G'' whose edge weights are travel times rather than Euclidean distances.

51/S6/F3.text: The complete time-weighted graph G'' can be solved with a standard travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, without needing a new algorithm, and the solver returns the optimal time tau_opt and the optimal path p_opt for that modified graph.

51/S6/F4.text: Because the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver's optimal path p_opt may contain hypothetical edges that are not in the original graph G, the algorithm post-processes p_opt into p_dash_opt by checking each path edge and replacing each edge whose endpoints were not directly connected in G with the shortest path between those endpoints in G.

51/S6/F5.text: The minimum travel time to cover all vertices, as computed by the algorithm that maps the original graph to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) instance, may still exceed the cybersickness time threshold when the terrain or virtual environment is large, so its purpose may be defeated in such cases.

51/S7/F0.text: There are two approaches to minimizing the possibility of cybersickness in a virtual world: finding a path that covers all points of interest in minimum time, and finding a path that covers the maximum possible points of interest within a given time limit.

51/S7/F1.text: In the minimum-time approach, the virtual world is represented as a graph whose nodes are points of interest, whose directly connected edges are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest, and whose graph need not be complete.

51/S7/F2.text: The problem of finding the minimum-duration travel that covers all points of interest in the virtual-world graph is mapped to the travelling salesman problem (TSP), a standard classical problem.

51/S7/F3.text: In the minimum-time approach, travel times between pairs of vertices are computed using the natural walking speed model, so if the vertices are directly connected the model gives the travel time between them, and if they are not directly connected a hypothetical edge representing the shortest path between them is introduced and the travel time along that shortest path is computed using the model.

51/S7/F4.text: In the minimum-time approach, the computed travel times become the weights of a complete graph formed by adding hypothetical edges, and this complete graph is given as input to a travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver, which outputs the optimum time and optimal path.

51/S7/F5.text: The optimal path produced by the travelling salesman problem (TSP) solver may contain hypothetical edges, which must be removed before the final solution path is produced.

51/S7/F6.text: The minimum-time approach that covers all points of interest may still produce a travel time beyond the threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur, motivating the use of a time limit in the alternative path optimization approach.

52/S0/F0.text: A time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks an optimal path that covers the maximum number of points of interest (POIs) while completing within the time threshold (TTH).

52/S0/F1.text: The time threshold (TTH) for cybersickness (CS) is the maximum duration of a virtual reality (VR) tour, meaning the user's movement time, experience time, or VR exposure time should be kept within it, because crossing it may cause cybersickness.

52/S0/F2.text: A virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of a virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce cybersickness (CS) if its traversal time exceeds the threshold above which cybersickness occurs.

52/S0/F3.text: There is no easy way to determine the time threshold (TTH); recommended thresholds may depend on content and movement speed, and a threshold can be obtained from an empirical study with a limited number of users or from pre-existing study results.

52/S1/F0.text: When planning a tour to be completed within a given time threshold, visiting every node or vertex representing a point of interest is neither mandatory nor always possible.

52/S1/F1.text: The importance of a node is assigned by an importance function that maps every node, vertex, or point of interest to a positive real number, with a larger number indicating higher importance.

52/S1/F2.text: The importance of the nodes is needed to determine which nodes to cover within a given time threshold.

52/S1/F3.text: The total importance of a path P containing nodes V1 through Vn is the sum of the individual importance f(Vi) for i = 1 to n, where n is the number of nodes in the path.

52/S1/F4.text: The objective is to identify a path that takes time less than or equal to the time threshold and that has the maximum total importance among all such paths.

52/S2/F0.text: In the virtual reality path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.

52/S2/F1.text: In the virtual reality path optimization formulation, the waiting time at a node, which is a point of interest, is the maximum time a user requires to inspect or interact with the object at that node, and it is represented by a waiting-time function W that maps each node v in V to a positive real number.

52/S2/F2.text: For a path P with vertices v1 to vn, the total waiting time W(P) is the sum of the individual waiting times W(v_i) for i = 1 to n.

52/S2/F3.text: The revised virtual reality path optimization problem maximizes the total importance F(P) of a path P subject to the constraint that the path's total completion time, T(P) + W(P), is less than or equal to the time threshold T_H.

52/S3/F0.text: Vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP), an operations research problem, in which not all nodes must be visited and the route maximizes profit within a time constraint, and in this formulation profit is the importance of the nodes.

52/S3/F1.text: Existing vehicle routing problem with profit (VRPP) solvers can be used to find the optimal path that maximizes total importance of the nodes within the given time threshold.

52/S3/F2.text: The optimized path must keep the user's exposure below a time threshold beyond which cybersickness may occur and, within that time, let the user visit as many of the most important points of interest (POIs) as possible.

52/S4/F0.text: The input to the optimal-path algorithm for a virtual environment is the original graph G, which is a fully connected graph but not necessarily a complete graph, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.

52/S4/F1.text: The desired output of the algorithm is the optimal path P that maximizes the importance value F, covers the maximum number of most important points of interest (POIs), and keeps the total exposure time, i.e. the traveling time plus the waiting time, less than the time threshold.

52/S4/F2.text: The first stage of the algorithm is to compute the complete graph G dash by replacing every pair of vertices that is not directly connected with the shortest path between those vertices.

52/S4/F3.text: The algorithm then replaces the edge weights in the complete graph, which are originally the Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using the natural walking model, producing the final graph G double dash, whose edges are weighted by travel duration to give a realistic experience.

52/S4/F4.text: The final graph G double dash, together with the importance f and waiting time w of each node, is given as input to a virtual reality path planning (VRPP) solver, and the solver returns the optimal path P_opt.

52/S4/F5.text: The optimal path returned by the solver is modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices V_i and V_j with the shortest path between those vertices in the original graph, and the algorithm returns this modified optimal path.

53/S0/F0.text: The optimal path approach in virtual reality (VR) navigation optimization identifies a path that lets a user explore all points of interest in minimum time, but in a very large virtual world such as the Majuli River Island virtual tour, that minimum time may still be very large compared with the expected user exposure duration, so the approach may still lead to cybersickness.

53/S0/F1.text: In a walking-based virtual reality (VR) exploration, the optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, called the time threshold, for the user's exposure to the virtual tour, and within that duration it identifies a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, where covering includes interacting with or inspecting those points and navigating from one to another.

53/S0/F2.text: Majuli is a river island on the Brahmaputra River in the state of Assam, surrounded on all sides by the Brahmaputra River and its tributaries.

53/S0/F3.text: Satras on Majuli are monasteries of the Vaisnavite faith that contain tangible and intangible cultural aspects, and there are 22 Satras in total.

53/S0/F4.text: Auniati Satra is one of the largest, most prominent, and most visited Satras on Majuli, with a campus covering approximately 1200 square meters and at least 25 points of interest.

53/S0/F5.text: Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking may take up to a day, including stoppage at the points of interest, and a full-day exposure to a virtual reality (VR) tour is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness.

53/S0/F6.text: The system-controlled virtual reality (VR) tour of Auniati Satra uses walking-based exploration with the natural walking speed model to provide a realistic experience.

53/S0/F7.text: For the exploration of Auniati Satra in virtual reality (VR), an optimized navigation path can be proposed using either the optimal path approach or the optimal path under a time constraint approach to maximize the user experience.

53/S1/F0.text: The Satra campus is modeled as a graph in which the points of interest (POI) are the nodes, the graph has at least 25 nodes, and the edges connecting pairs of nodes are weighted by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

53/S1/F1.text: Converting the Satra site into a graph representation is an iterative process that requires detailed field study and revision of an initial graph.

53/S1/F2.text: A team collected the Satra graph data through a field study, described as a kind of contextual inquiry, during the Kati Bihu festival, by observing people's travel and stopping behavior throughout the day, manually recording that behavior, and interviewing campus residents and Satra committee members about the places people typically visit and the places interviewees recommended to tourists.

53/S1/F3.text: A point of interest (POI) in the Satra graph does not have to refer to an actual physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.

53/S1/F4.text: When the first navigation optimization approach gives a minimum time above the time threshold, the second approach requires each point of interest (POI) node to be assigned a relative importance from discussions with people and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior.

53/S1/F5.text: The maximum wait time at a point of interest (POI) is the time a user needs to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

53/S1/F6.text: Once the graph is obtained, a traveling salesman problem (TSP) solver can be used to find a minimum-time path covering all 25 nodes, or a vehicle routing problem with profits (VRPP) solver can be used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for the maximum wait time at each point of interest.

54/S0/F0.text: Extended reality (XR), in particular virtual reality (VR), is resource hungry, meaning that XR and VR require a lot of resources.

54/S0/F1.text: The objectives of virtual reality (VR) resource optimization are to minimize resource requirements without compromising the VR experience, that is, to maximize the VR experience.

54/S0/F2.text: In extended reality (XR) and particularly in virtual reality (VR), resources can include any or all of hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure; in VR these include hardware such as input devices, processing devices, and output devices; software such as development tools, software development kits, software packages, or application packages; manpower such as staff for development, deployment, maintenance, and marketing; and supporting infrastructure such as rooms to store the hardware setup, electricity supply, furniture, and network infrastructure such as network gear, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

54/S0/F3.text: Each resource type in extended reality (XR) can be optimized separately, but such optimization is not easy because the considerations vary widely and include money such as availability of funds and how resources are managed, availability of the resources before use, policy issues, and geopolitical issues.

54/S0/F4.text: Virtual reality (VR) resource optimization generally does not try to optimize every resource, assumes some resources are given, and instead focuses on hardware requirements at the client end (the user end), because focusing on client-end hardware is the most straightforward way to optimize resources without being entangled in many issues; the objective is for the end user to have a good experience with affordable hardware resources.

54/S1/F0.text: For a good virtual reality (VR) immersive experience, client-end hardware is needed to support requirements arising from rendering or computer graphics and to manage rendering or computer graphics related issues, and the complexity required to render a scene corresponds to the need for high-end hardware support.

54/S1/F1.text: The image displayed on a computer screen is the whole interface, that is the content seen on the screen, not only the main object, and it comprises geometric shapes or objects, including interface objects such as menus and icons, with colors assigned to them.

54/S1/F2.text: In computer graphics, interaction is the manipulation of an image or parts of it by a user using input devices, such as a joystick or devices associated with virtual reality (VR) input, which changes the object's appearance and the screen.

54/S1/F3.text: Computers understand only binary representation, that is zeros and ones, whereas humans perceive realistic representation, not strings of zeros and ones.

54/S1/F4.text: The fundamental problem of computer graphics is to create or represent objects, synthesize objects into a scene, and render the scene on a computer display so that humans can perceive it.

54/S1/F5.text: The fundamental problem of computer graphics gives rise to four basic issues: representing objects or parts of an image; synthesizing parts to form complete realistic imagery; allowing users to manipulate images on a screen, which is related to interactive systems; and creating the perception of motion, which is related to animation.

54/S2/F0.text: A generic graphics system has a host computer and a display, with three major components in between: a display controller, video memory, and a video controller.

54/S2/F1.text: In a generic graphics system, the host computer, or its central processing unit (CPU), has two-way communication with the display controller, in which the CPU sends display commands and may receive interaction data.

54/S2/F2.text: The display controller is responsible for image generation, meaning it creates a representation of a scene as a two-dimensional image that can be displayed on a two-dimensional screen.

54/S2/F3.text: Image generation is a multi-stage computational process, and if all rendering-related computations were carried out by the central processing unit (CPU), the CPU's time would be consumed by rendering, leaving it with very little time for other tasks and the system could do little except rendering; to avoid this and increase efficiency, rendering is usually carried out by a dedicated component.

54/S2/F4.text: The dedicated rendering component is typically the graphics card, which usually contains its own graphics processing unit (GPU); in a generic graphics system this component is called the display controller, and the central processing unit (CPU) passes graphics rendering tasks to it so the computation takes place in the GPU rather than in the CPU.

54/S2/F5.text: The display controller generates the image in a digital format, as strings of zeros and ones, and sends that image representation to video memory for storage.

54/S2/F6.text: Video memory is the dedicated part of the overall memory hierarchy of the computer where the digital image is stored, typically as part of a separate graphics unit, and in modern graphics cards it is sometimes called video random-access memory (VRAM).

54/S2/F7.text: A graphic display screen generally has a grid of picture elements, or pixels; when these pixels are activated, or excited, by an electrical or electromechanical means, they emit light with specific intensities that the viewer perceives as a colored image on the screen.

54/S2/F8.text: The video controller uses the data stored in video memory to render an image on the screen, converting the digital image into some analog voltages required to activate the pixels, and it controls the pixel excitation mechanism using the video memory content.

54/S3/F0.text: Graphic devices are broadly of two types, determined by the method used for excitation of pixels: vector scan devices and raster scan devices.

54/S3/F1.text: Vector scan devices, also called random scan, stroke writing, or calligraphic devices, view an image as composed of continuous geometric primitives such as lines and curves and render the image by exciting only selected pixels that represent the primitives, on the assumption that rendering the primitives will make the whole image be perceived.

54/S3/F2.text: Vector scan devices require high precision to target and excite specific pixels, which makes vector scan devices costly and typically unaffordable for mass production or mass consumption; vector scan devices are therefore typically used in specialized settings where limited quantities are required.

54/S3/F3.text: A raster scan device views an image as represented by the whole pixel grid, activates all pixels in sequence, typically left to right and top to bottom, with appropriate inputs that make the pixels emit light at appropriate intensities, and the sequential activation of all pixels is called scanning or raster scanning.

54/S3/F4.text: Raster scan rendering requires less precision and is much cheaper than vector scan rendering.

54/S3/F5.text: Commercial products such as smartphones, televisions, and any device with a computer and display typically comprise raster scan displays.

54/S4/F0.text: In a raster scan system, the frame buffer is the video memory component that stores the intensity values for all pixels in the grid, and it contains one memory location for each pixel that stores the intensity as a bit string of 0s and 1s.

54/S4/F1.text: The size of a frame buffer is the size of the screen and is equal to the screen resolution of a raster scan device.

54/S4/F2.text: In a raster scan device, the light emitted from excited pixel elements decays over time, causing the rendered scene to fade even when the image is not changing.

54/S4/F3.text: In raster scan rendering, pixels are excited in a left-to-right, top-to-bottom order, so the top-left pixel is excited much earlier than the bottom-right pixel; because the emitted light decays, pixels may fade out of sync and the displayed image may appear non-uniform or distorted.

54/S4/F4.text: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels on a raster scan device, done to avoid fading and distortion and to keep the rendered image uniform even when the image is not changing.

54/S4/F5.text: The refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on a screen, is represented in hertz, and a good refresh rate for most devices is 60 hertz.

54/S4/F6.text: A higher refresh rate is always preferable for a virtual reality (VR) experience because the VR screen is much closer to the eyes than in typical computer usage, where the screen and the eyes are at a reasonable distance.

54/S4/F7.text: In a color display, each pixel contains multiple light-emitting elements, typically three although sometimes four can be used for different purposes; the typical three elements emit red, green, and blue primary colors at different intensities.

54/S4/F8.text: Color is perceived when the red, green, and blue light emitted by the pixel elements of a color display is mixed in the eye, so the observed color is a combination of different amounts of red, green, and blue.

54/S5/F0.text: The three-dimensional (3D) computer graphics pipeline (3D graphics pipeline) is a stage-wise process of computation starting from object representation to rendering on the pixel grid.

55/S0/F0.text: The color values stored in the frame buffer are computed by the display processor, which is part of the display controller, in distinct stages.

55/S0/F1.text: The graphics pipeline is the set of the distinct stages in which the color values stored in the frame buffer are computed.

55/S1/F0.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller.

55/S1/F1.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline contains five stages: first object representation, second modeling transformation, third lighting, fourth the viewing pipeline, and fifth scan conversion.

55/S1/F2.text: The first stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, object representation, defines the objects that together form the rendered image in each object's own local coordinate system.

55/S1/F3.text: The second stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, modeling transformation, transforms objects from their local coordinate systems to the common world coordinate system to construct the scene.

55/S1/F4.text: The third stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, lighting or illumination, assigns color to the constructed scene in the world coordinate system, making the scene's three-dimensional nature more perceptible.

55/S1/F5.text: The device coordinate system is equivalent to the screen, but it is not the same as the screen.

55/S1/F6.text: The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is a viewing pipeline that comprises viewing transformation, clipping, hidden surface removal, projection transformation, and window-to-viewport transformation.

55/S1/F7.text: Within the viewing pipeline, viewing transformation maps the scene from the world coordinate system to the view coordinate system, clipping and hidden surface removal operate in the view coordinate system, projection transformation maps the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation maps the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; together, these sub-stages transform a scene from the world coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

55/S1/F8.text: The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, scan conversion, transforms the continuous device coordinate system description, whose points can take real-number coordinates, into the discrete pixel-grid or screen coordinate system, where each pixel coordinate is an integer.

55/S1/F9.text: Transforming an object definition to a pixel-level scene description in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline uses six coordinate systems: the local coordinate system, the world coordinate system, the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, the device coordinate system, and the pixel-grid or screen coordinate system.

55/S2/F0.text: The fundamental objective of three-dimensional (3D) object representation is to balance the requirement to represent objects of different shapes and sizes with their intricate details so that they render realistically in a synthesized environment, rather than as simplistic geometric approximations that lose realism, and the requirement to make the operations of the subsequent stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline efficient in space and time.

55/S2/F1.text: In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, the computation of pixel intensities depends on the object representation, and more complex representations lead to more complex calculations, so realistic rendering can suffer lags or require expensive hardware if the computation is not efficient.

55/S2/F2.text: A single three-dimensional (3D) object representation technique is not sufficient because different object representation techniques are available, and the appropriate technique must be chosen for a particular problem.

55/S2/F3.text: The broad categories of three-dimensional (3D) object representation techniques are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning based representation, with boundary representation comprising mesh representation, parametric representation, and implicit representation, and space partitioning based representation comprising the octree method, binary space partitioning (BSP) method, and constructive solid geometry (CSG) method.

55/S3/F0.text: The broad representation categories are point sample rendering, boundary representation, and space partitioning-based representation.

55/S3/F1.text: Point sample rendering is the simplest broad representation category, in which the captured scene information is represented as a set of raw data points on the scene, with each point carrying that information as attributes.

55/S3/F2.text: In point sample rendering, the scene information is captured from the real world in the form of points using input sensors such as three-dimensional (3D) range scanners, range finders, or computer vision techniques.

55/S3/F3.text: In point sample rendering, the captured points are processed or mapped to pixels to generate a synthetic image, relying on real-world information rather than synthetically defining objects.

55/S3/F4.text: Boundary representation is a broad representation category in which objects are represented by the surfaces that define the object's boundary, and those surfaces can be polygonal or curved.

55/S3/F5.text: Mesh representation is a popular boundary representation technique in which object surfaces are assumed to be polygons, the connected polygons form a mesh that represents the whole object, and a vertex or edge list stores all vertices or edges and their connections, allowing the object to be reconstructed.

55/S3/F6.text: Objects with non-polygonal surfaces can be represented using mesh representation by approximating the surfaces with polygonal meshes, typically triangles, although other simple convex polygons may also be used.

55/S3/F7.text: In mesh representation, a greater number of polygons gives a better approximation of the surfaces but makes the vertex list more complex and harder to construct, so a trade-off must be maintained.

55/S3/F8.text: Mesh representation is the most basic form of representation for any object in a rendered scene used in computer graphics, and all other representations are converted to a mesh representation at the end of the pipeline before the objects are rendered.

55/S4/F0.text: Spline representation is a higher-level boundary representation for curved surfaces or curves that falls under parametric representation.

55/S4/F1.text: Spline representation is typically preferred by developers or designers of scenes who want to create an artificial environment, and it is used to construct quality scenes for rendering and to represent complex surfaces with complex properties that cannot be represented by simple polygons or simple polynomial equations.

55/S4/F2.text: In polynomial representation of a curve, a more complex curve is represented by a polynomial of higher degree, and computing points on a higher-degree polynomial becomes more time-consuming.

55/S4/F3.text: In spline representation, a complete curve consists of several lower-degree polynomial pieces instead of a single higher-degree complex polynomial, and each piece is called a blending function or basis function so that simpler polynomials can compute points on the curve segment represented by that piece.

55/S4/F4.text: Third-order polynomials are the most common form of polynomial used to construct spline curves.

55/S4/F5.text: In spline representation, the polynomial pieces that make up the complete curve must join smoothly, and certain geometric and other properties need to be satisfied by each piece.

55/S4/F6.text: In boundary representation, mesh is the most basic form, and higher-level boundary representations use implicit or parametric forms.

55/S5/F0.text: Space partitioning representation is a broad category of object representation in which the three-dimensional (3D) space occupied by an object is divided into several disjoint, non-overlapping regions, so that any point inside the object lies in exactly one region and the object can be represented by representing the occupied regions.

55/S5/F1.text: A space partitioning tree is a hierarchical, tree-like structure that represents the space occupied by an object and is used to create a space partitioning representation.

55/S5/F2.text: Space partitioning representations include the octree method, binary space partitioning, and constructive solid geometric methods.

55/S5/F3.text: Specialized sophisticated representation techniques are often required for application-specific or very complex photorealistic objects rather than the broader boundary or space partitioning categories.

55/S5/F4.text: Fractal representation is a specialized representation method for self-repeating structures, such as a leaf whose individual parts repeat in the larger part.

55/S5/F5.text: Particle system representation is a specialized representation method for objects such as a waterfall that relies on the simulation of physical properties.

55/S5/F6.text: A skeletal model is a specialized representation method for complex characters such as a cat that captures the character's overall appearance and motion behavior, and such models are typically used in animation or computer animation to represent objects or complex characters.

55/S6/F0.text: In an implementation of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, all pipeline stages are present, the stages are more important than their sequence, and the order of the stages and sub-stages may differ from the stage-wise sequence used to show how the computations occur.

56/S0/F0.text: Rendering, the key component of any immersive experience in which the scene is rendered in front of the user's eyes on the display device, is covered by computer graphics, so some knowledge of computer graphics is needed to understand the complexities involved in rendering.

56/S0/F1.text: Object representation in the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is called the first stage for simplicity, although there is no computation as such related to intensity calculation or determination of the pixel intensities.

56/S1/F0.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline consists of five stages in order: object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling transformation, which transforms a local coordinate description to a world coordinate description; lighting, which takes place in the world coordinate reference frame; the viewing pipeline, which contains viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to a three-dimensional view coordinate system, clipping in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional view coordinate system to the device coordinate system; and scan conversion, which transforms the device coordinate scene description to a screen coordinate or pixel grid description.

56/S2/F0.text: Modeling transformation, also called geometric transformation and referred to as stage 2, applies operations to an object's local or object coordinate system description to place the object in a common scene or world coordinate system so that multiple objects can be assembled into a scene.

56/S2/F1.text: An object's local or object coordinate system description is an individual definition of the object in which its position and dimension are defined in its own coordinate reference frame.

56/S2/F2.text: The basic transformations in modeling transformation are translation, rotation by an angle clockwise or anticlockwise around an axis, scaling by increasing or reducing an object's size, and shearing by changing an object's shape; combinations of these four can create any transformation required to construct a scene.

56/S3/F0.text: Each transformation is typically represented by a matrix in a homogeneous coordinate system, where one extra dimension is added, so a two-dimensional (2D) transformation can be represented by a 3 by 3 matrix and a three-dimensional (3D) transformation can be represented by a 4 by 4 matrix.

56/S3/F1.text: Two-dimensional (2D) translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing in the homogeneous coordinate system can be represented by 3 by 3 matrices, using translation amounts Tx and Ty along the x and y directions, the rotation angle phi, scaling factors Sx and Sy along the x and y directions, and shearing factors Sx, Shx, and Shy along the x and y directions.

56/S3/F2.text: A point (x, y) in an object's local coordinate system can be transformed to the world coordinate system by representing the point as the column vector P, multiplying it by the transformation matrix S to obtain the new point P dash, and thereby performing a matrix multiplication of points on the object's surface into new points that ideally should be in the world coordinate system.

56/S4/F0.text: A composite transformation matrix is used when constructing a world coordinate scene requires multiple basic geometric or modeling transformations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, or shearing.

56/S4/F1.text: In the worked example, transforming rectangle ABCD from its local coordinate system to the chimney-like shape A′, B′, C′, D′ in the world coordinate scene cannot be done with one basic transformation and requires two basic transformations, scaling and translation.

56/S4/F2.text: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and the transformed chimney shape A′, B′, C′, D′, the scaling matrix has Sx (the scaling factor along the x direction) equal to 0.5 and Sy (the scaling factor along the y direction) equal to 1 because the object is halved in length while its height remains unchanged, and the translation matrix has Tx (translation along the x-axis) equal to 5 and Ty (translation along the y-axis) equal to 5 because vertex D at (0, 0) moves to D′ at (5, 5).

56/S4/F3.text: A composite transformation matrix is formed by arranging the individual transformation matrices from right to left according to the order of application: the first transformation applied is placed rightmost, each subsequent transformation is placed to its left, and the matrices are multiplied.

56/S4/F4.text: In the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, scaling is applied first and translation is applied second, so the translation matrix is placed to the left of the scaling matrix and the two matrices are multiplied to obtain the composite transformation matrix.

56/S4/F5.text: To obtain transformed vertices in the world coordinate scene, each current vertex is multiplied by the transformation matrix; in the worked example involving rectangle ABCD and A′, B′, C′, D′, A′ = M A, B′ = M B, C′ = M C, and D′ = M D, where M is the composite transformation matrix.

56/S4/F6.text: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so the right-to-left sequence of transformations must be set correctly; an incorrect sequence may produce an incorrect transformed result.

56/S5/F0.text: In the computer graphics pipeline, the third stage is color computation, which uses lighting or shading models to assign colors to objects in the scene; if a color is not assigned, depth cannot be perceived and the quality of experience is reduced, whereas properly assigning colors can give a more realistic perception.

56/S5/F1.text: In computer graphics, lighting models and shading models are distinct, although they may physically represent more or less similar things, and they are differentiated by the computation involved: lighting models involve more computation than shading models, and shading models are used to reduce computation without compromising the quality of experience.

56/S5/F2.text: Shading models are approximations of the color-assignment methods used by lighting models, and they rely on lighting models.

56/S5/F3.text: Lighting models compute colors in terms of continuous intensity values, which are essentially real numbers, typically within the range 0 to 1 and typically normalized, and these values are mapped to computer-supported discrete values.

56/S6/F0.text: A light source emits light that falls on a surface point directly, or in some cases after being reflected from surrounding surfaces, and the light incident at that point reflects to the viewer's eye; the intensity of the reflected light reaching the viewer's eye determines the color perceived.

56/S6/F1.text: In computer graphics, a lighting model is used to simulate the reflection of incident light from a surface point to the viewer's eye, in order to compute the intensity of that reflected light, which is essentially the color of the surface point.

56/S6/F2.text: In the simple lighting model, the light intensity reaching the viewer from a surface point is modeled as the sum of three intensities: ambient light intensity (I amb), diffuse reflection intensity of direct light (I diff), and specular reflection intensity of direct light (I spec).

56/S6/F3.text: In the simple lighting model, the ambient light component is light that falls on a surface after being reflected from surrounding surfaces.

56/S6/F4.text: In the simple lighting model, the diffuse light component is light that comes directly from a light source and is reflected in a diffuse manner from the surface.

56/S6/F5.text: In the simple lighting model, the specular reflection component is light that comes from a light source and is reflected with a specular effect, producing a shiny bright spot.

56/S7/F0.text: The intensity of light reflected from a surface and reaching the viewer's eye is a fraction of the incident light intensity, and this fraction is determined by the surface property known as the reflection coefficient or reflectivity.

56/S7/F1.text: The simple lighting model defines three reflection coefficients: Ka for ambient light, Kd for diffuse reflection of direct light, and Ks for specular reflection of direct light.

56/S7/F2.text: Each of the three reflection coefficients of the simple lighting model has a value from 0.0 to 1.0, where a value close to 0 represents a dull surface with no reflection because most of the light is absorbed, a value close to 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface where all light gets reflected, and varying the coefficients generates different effects between dull and shiny surfaces.

56/S7/F3.text: The ambient component of the reflected light intensity is computed by multiplying the ambient light intensity falling on a surface point by the reflection coefficient for ambient light Ka.

56/S7/F4.text: The diffuse reflection component is computed by multiplying the diffuse reflection coefficient for direct light Kd, the source light intensity Is, and the dot product of the surface normal vector N at the surface point from which light is reflected and the light source direction vector L, using that product only when N dot L is greater than 0 and otherwise setting it to 0, which means no diffuse reflection.

56/S7/F5.text: The specular component is computed using an approximate model named after its inventor, Phong.

56/S7/F6.text: The angle phi in the specular calculation is the angle between the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, which is the direction a mirror would reflect the light, and cos phi is the dot product V dot r.

56/S7/F7.text: The specular component is computed as the specular reflection coefficient for direct light Ks times the source light intensity Is times the dot product of the viewer direction vector V and the ideal specular reflection direction vector r, raised to the power Ns, and it is 0 when V dot r is not greater than 0.

56/S7/F8.text: The ideal specular reflection direction vector r is represented by r equal to twice the dot product of the light source direction vector L and the surface normal vector N, multiplied by the surface normal vector N, minus the light source direction vector L.

56/S8/F0.text: In lighting, the intensity of light from a source typically diminishes with the distance from the source to a surface point, so an intensity attenuation factor over distance is needed.

56/S8/F1.text: The radial intensity attenuation factor accounts for the diminishing of light intensity with distance and is typically computed as an inverse quadratic function of the distance d between the light source and the surface point, using coefficients a0, a1, and a2 that can be varied for a more realistic effect.

56/S8/F2.text: Angular intensity attenuation is considered primarily for generating spotlight effects, in which elements inside the spotlight region are visible or brightly visible and elements outside the spotlight zone are darker.

56/S8/F3.text: A commonly used angular intensity attenuation factor is 0 when the surface point is outside the angular limit theta, the range of the spotlight cone, and when the surface point is within that angular limit it varies as the cosine of phi raised to the power A1, where A1 is a positive angular attenuation exponent that can be varied to achieve different effects.

56/S8/F4.text: In the simple lighting model modified for radial and angular intensity attenuation, the I_M intensity component is left unchanged, while the sum of the diffuse reflection component I_D and the specular reflection component I_SPEC is multiplied by the radial and angular attenuation factors; if those factors are 1, the model reduces to I_M + I_D + I_SPEC.

56/S9/F0.text: In a colored light source model, emitted light intensity has three components corresponding to the primary colors red, green, and blue, rather than a single component, and the source intensity is the three-element vector Is = (Isr, Isg, Isb).

56/S9/F1.text: In a colored light source model, the red, green, and blue components of the source intensity are computed individually, and their combination gives the perception of any color.

56/S9/F2.text: In a colored light source model, the reflection coefficients named k, kd, and ks are specified as three-element vectors, each having the value one in the red, green, and blue components.

56/S9/F3.text: For n light sources, the single-light-source lighting model is revised to I_P = I_ambient plus the summation from i = 1 to n of the contribution from each light source, with each contribution calculated separately and added together, and for colored light sources each contribution is computed separately for the red, green, and blue components.

56/S10/F0.text: In intensity mapping, a lighting model computes a pixel intensity that can be any value in an infinite range between 0 and 1, whereas a display supports only a finite set of intensity values, such as 256 values per pixel on an 8-bit display.

56/S10/F1.text: The determination of device-supported intensity values uses the number n of levels, the minimum device-supported intensity value I0 measured with a photometer, and the known maximum intensity value 1.

56/S10/F2.text: The successive device-supported intensity values are represented by I1 = r I0, I2 = r^2 I0, I3 = r^3 I0, and so on up to In = r^n I0, where the factor r is computed using the relation In = r^n I0.

56/S10/F3.text: The use of a multiplicative factor r in the successive device-supported intensity levels is based on the psychophysiological property that humans perceive relative changes between two intensity values rather than absolute changes in intensity values.

56/S10/F4.text: A table stores the calculated device-supported intensity values and their assigned bit patterns, and a lighting-model pixel intensity is mapped to the nearest table intensity so that the corresponding bit pattern is stored in the frame buffer at the pixel location.

57/S0/F0.text: Realistic scene generation in virtual reality (VR) is more important than in augmented reality (AR) and requires more resources in virtual reality than in augmented reality.

57/S0/F1.text: The fourth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is view transformation, which is also called the viewing pipeline.

57/S0/F2.text: The basic idea of view transformation, which is the viewing pipeline, is that an image on a screen or head-mounted display (HMD) is produced by selecting a portion of a three-dimensional (3D) scene and projecting the portion onto a two-dimensional (2D) display or view plane.

57/S0/F3.text: The viewing pipeline consists of a viewing transformation that defines a view coordinate system and transforms a scene from a three-dimensional (3D) world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, a projection transformation that projects the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate scene to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane or two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, a window-to-viewport transformation that maps the projected scene to a two-dimensional (2D) device coordinate space, and the operations clipping and hidden surface removal, which in the described pipeline take place in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

57/S0/F4.text: The sequence of stages or sub-stages in the viewing pipeline is not fixed, because different implementations can alter the sequence.

57/S1/F0.text: The world coordinate system is the reference frame in which all scene points are defined.

57/S1/F1.text: The three-dimensional (3D) viewing transformation transforms a 3D world coordinate description of a scene to a 3D view coordinate description to simulate looking at the scene with the camera viewing mechanism, and it is performed after defining a view coordinate system from the camera parameters.

57/S1/F2.text: The camera parameters used to set up the view coordinate system are the camera position, represented as an origin vector in the world coordinate system; the view-up point, represented as a vector; and the center of interest, also called the look-at point.

57/S1/F3.text: The view coordinate system is defined by three mutually orthogonal unit basis vectors N, V, and U, where N is the unit basis vector opposite the looking direction, obtained from the camera origin vector and the look-at point; V is the unit basis vector along the view-up direction, obtained from the vector from the origin point to the view-up point; and U is the cross product of V and N.

57/S1/F4.text: Once the view coordinate system is defined, the three-dimensional (3D) transformation from world coordinates to view coordinates is performed by translation and rotation, using a composite transformation matrix that is the product of the rotation and translation transformation matrices; a point in view coordinates is obtained by multiplying the corresponding world-coordinate point vector by this matrix, and the matrices are formed from the view-coordinate axis vectors and their scalar components.

57/S2/F0.text: Projection transformation maps objects described in a three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to a two-dimensional (2D) view plane.

57/S2/F1.text: The view plane used in projection is usually a rectangular area, also called a clipping window.

57/S2/F2.text: A view volume is a three-dimensional (3D) region in the scene that defines the portion of the scene that is projected onto the view plane, so objects inside the view volume are projected and objects outside it are discarded.

57/S2/F3.text: Clipping is the process of discarding objects that are part of the scene but outside the view volume, and it takes place before projection.

57/S2/F4.text: Perspective projection is a projection type in which the projectors from an object in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the view plane are not parallel and converge at a center of projection, also called a point of projection; it produces realistic rendering and is used when a realistic scene is to be generated.

57/S2/F5.text: Parallel projection is a projection type in which the projectors from the object to the view plane are parallel to each other, so their center of projection or point of projection is at infinity and they never meet.

57/S2/F6.text: For parallel projection, the view volume is a rectangular parallelepiped-shaped region, and for perspective projection, the view volume is a frustum, with one face or side of the view volume serving as the clipping window on which objects inside the view volume are projected.

57/S2/F7.text: The naive clipping method computes the intersection of view volume boundaries with object boundaries, and this calculation is computationally intensive for arbitrarily shaped view volumes such as frustums.

57/S2/F8.text: A canonical view volume is a normalized unit cube into which any arbitrarily defined view volume for parallel or perspective projection is converted in order to simplify pipeline computations.

57/S2/F9.text: For parallel projection, a canonical view volume is obtained by scaling an arbitrarily defined view volume into a unit cube.

57/S2/F10.text: For perspective projection, a canonical view volume is obtained by converting the frustum into a normalized unit cube, which requires scaling and shearing operations to change its size and shape and involves more computation than the parallel case.

57/S2/F11.text: A parallel projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a four-by-four parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance of the clipping window from the origin of the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, and then dividing the obtained homogeneous coordinate values by the homogeneous factor w, which is typically not equal to 1, to obtain the Cartesian x, y, and z values.

57/S2/F12.text: A perspective projection is computed by multiplying a point vector in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system by a perspective projection matrix that is more complex than the parallel projection matrix, in which D is the distance from the clipping window to the center of projection, which is typically assumed to be at the origin but not always; the obtained homogeneous coordinate values are then divided by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

57/S2/F13.text: To project a point P from the world coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view plane, P is first transformed to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, then the view volume containing P is transformed to a canonical view volume before clipping, and finally the point in the canonical view volume is projected onto the view plane; the final point P' is obtained by multiplying P by the world coordinate system to three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system transformation matrix, the canonical view volume transformation matrix, and the projection transformation matrix.

57/S3/F0.text: A window is the same as a normalized clipping window, is another term for the view plane, and is an abstract intermediate representation that has nothing to do with the display.

57/S3/F1.text: A viewport is not defined on the view plane but in device space as a portion of the final screen where the scene will be rendered, and it is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and the screen or display dimensions.

57/S3/F2.text: The window-to-viewport transformation maps a point from the abstract window representation to a device-specific viewport representation, specifically from a window point (Wx, Wy) to a viewport point (Vx, Vy).

57/S3/F3.text: In the window-to-viewport transformation, the transformation matrix is a three by three matrix whose Sx is defined in terms of the viewport and window dimensions along the x-axis, whose Sy is similarly defined with respect to the viewport and window dimensions along the y-axis, and whose Tx and Ty are computed in terms of Sx and Sy and the corresponding x-axis or y-axis window and viewport dimensions.

57/S3/F4.text: To obtain the transformed viewport point, the window point vector is multiplied by the window-to-viewport transformation matrix, and because the resulting point is in homogeneous coordinate representation, the Cartesian point is obtained by dividing the result by the homogeneous factor W.

57/S4/F0.text: Clipping defines a view volume, discards objects or portions of objects outside that view volume, and is performed before projection so that projection is applied to fewer vertices and computational complexity is reduced.

57/S4/F1.text: Hidden surface removal identifies and removes objects, surfaces, or surface points inside the view volume that are not visible from a particular viewer position because they are occluded, before the scene is rendered, to reduce computational complexity and support realistic image generation.

57/S5/F0.text: The fifth stage of the graphics pipeline is scan conversion.

58/S0/F0.text: Rendering is the most challenging part of immersive experience generation from the point of view of the system.

58/S0/F1.text: The three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline has five stages, and the first four stages are object representation in the local coordinate system; modeling or geometric transformation from the local coordinate system to the world coordinate system; lighting in the world coordinate system; and viewing transformation from the world coordinate system to the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system.

58/S0/F2.text: In the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline, after the viewing transformation, the view pipeline includes clipping in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, hidden surface removal in the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system, projection transformation from the three-dimensional (3D) view coordinate system to the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system, and window-to-viewport transformation from the two-dimensional (2D) view coordinate system to the device coordinate system.

58/S0/F3.text: The fifth stage of the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline is the scan conversion stage, also called the rendering stage, which transforms a device coordinate description into a screen coordinate description on the pixel grid.

58/S1/F0.text: The device coordinate system used to define the two-dimensional (2D) viewport is a continuous coordinate system, so its coordinate values can be any real number.

58/S1/F1.text: A display device uses a pixel grid to render an image, and points on that pixel grid can only have integer coordinates.

58/S1/F2.text: Scan conversion, also called rendering or rasterization, is, after the earlier four stages, the fifth stage in which mapping algorithms transform continuous two-dimensional (2D) viewport coordinates into a discrete pixel-grid coordinate system by choosing the nearest integer-coordinate pixels, so a line is rendered by coloring specific pixels.

58/S2/F0.text: In point rendering, a point represented by real-number coordinates is mapped to the nearest integer coordinate values, which maps from device space to discrete space; this rounding method is suitable for points but not for other geometric shapes such as lines and circles.

58/S2/F1.text: A naive line-rendering method requires many floating-point operations, and because floating-point operations slow down a computer, the objective of efficient line-rendering algorithms is to avoid floating-point operations.

58/S2/F2.text: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is a popular line-rendering algorithm that identifies the pixels that approximately represent a line without using floating-point operations.

58/S2/F3.text: The Bresenham line-drawing algorithm is described for line slopes between -1 and +1, with minor modification needed for other slopes; its input is the two line endpoints and its output is the set of pixels that approximate the line segment.

58/S2/F4.text: In Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm for line slopes between -1 and +1, the algorithm first computes delta x, the difference between the two endpoints' x coordinates, delta y, the difference between their y coordinates, and the decision parameter p, defined as twice delta y minus delta x; it initializes x and y to the first endpoint's x and y coordinates and adds that pixel to the output pixel set; then, in a loop until the other endpoint is reached, if p is less than 0 it increments x by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y, otherwise increments x and y by 1 and resets p to the older p plus twice delta y minus twice delta x, adding each computed coordinate to the output pixel set.

58/S2/F5.text: Bresenham's line-drawing algorithm is efficient and speeds up line rendering because it uses integer arithmetic, such as addition and multiplication, and avoids floating-point operations such as rounding, division, and sometimes floating-point multiplication.

58/S2/F6.text: Speeding up line rendering makes the system more efficient because at any instant a system may need to render a large number of line segments, and in interactive graphics such as virtual reality each user input can change the scene and require redrawing hundreds of thousands of lines.

58/S2/F7.text: Similar efficient rendering algorithms exist for other geometric shapes, such as circles, ellipses, filled areas, and polygons, and they are more complex than line rendering.

58/S2/F8.text: The basic idea for rendering a shape on a screen is to map the original shape to the set of pixels that represent it as fast as possible by reducing floating-point operations.

58/S2/F9.text: For lines, floating-point operations can be completely eliminated, whereas for other shapes they may not be completely eliminated but can be minimized.

58/S3/F0.text: Aliasing is distortion that may occur in an original shape after scan conversion because scan conversion renders pixels that are close to points on the original shape rather than exactly rendering the points, so an approximated line may not exactly match the original line.

58/S3/F1.text: If aliasing is left unaddressed, it may lead to distortion that is visible with a change in resolution and that will reduce the quality of experience.

58/S3/F2.text: Anti-aliasing operations are additional operations, using complex algorithms, that remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing so that the end effect is better.

58/S3/F3.text: Anti-aliasing is essential and adds further computation to the overall computation of pixel intensities along with the other rendering stages.

58/S3/F4.text: In virtual reality (VR), a realistic experience with rich realistic content, a dynamic scene that changes with user input, a high degree of interaction, motion achieved through animation or video, and the fact that a simple lighting model may not be a good option increase the computational complexity of rendering manifold.

58/S3/F5.text: The challenge in virtual reality (VR) rendering is to handle a computationally complex rendering process without the user perceiving lag or distortion.

58/S4/F0.text: A computer graphics (CG) programmer does not always need to implement the stages of a graphics pipeline from scratch; instead, the programmer can import graphics libraries and use the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by those libraries to deal with the lower-level tasks, choosing a library whose APIs suit the requirements.

58/S4/F1.text: Examples of graphics libraries include OpenGL, which stands for Open Graphics Library, Vulkan, and Direct3D.

58/S4/F2.text: The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries are predefined sets of functions that, when invoked with appropriate arguments or parameters, perform specific tasks.

58/S4/F3.text: The application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by graphics libraries eliminate the need for a programmer to know every detail of the underlying system or platform, such as processor details, memory details, and operating system details, in order to build a graphics application.

58/S5/F0.text: A layered virtual reality (VR) software architecture consists, from top to bottom, of the VR application layer, the software development kit (SDK) layer, the VR engine or game engine layer, the native rendering library layer with libraries such as OpenGL, Vulkan and Direct3D, the operating system layer, and the hardware layer including the graphics processing unit (GPU); the application layer calls the SDK layer, the SDK layer calls the VR engine layer, the VR engine calls the application programming interfaces (APIs) of the native rendering libraries to perform rendering, the native rendering libraries sit on top of the operating system layer, and the operating system layer sits on top of the hardware layer.

58/S5/F1.text: In a layered virtual reality (VR) system, a developer can rely on the software development kit (SDK) layer to access the VR engine; the developer has to install the VR engine and import the SDK within the engine, and the VR engine's job is to let the developer deal with graphics through the application programming interfaces (APIs) provided by the native rendering libraries without directly accessing those native rendering libraries.

58/S6/F0.text: A graphics processing unit (GPU) is the processing unit of a separate graphics card, with its own memory elements, that is used in computer graphics and virtual reality to exploit the inherent parallelism of graphics operations, which are highly parallel, whereas central processing units (CPUs) are generally not designed for large-scale parallel activities, although modern CPUs have some parallel features.

58/S6/F1.text: A GPU is typically a multicore system in which many cores, each capable only of simple integer and floating-point arithmetic, work simultaneously on one single instruction and produce data simultaneously, and groups of cores form streaming multiprocessor units, each containing several cores.

58/S6/F2.text: A GPU is broadly organized with a host, input assemblers and a thread execution manager, where the manager allocates work to many streaming multiprocessors, each of which has a parallel data cache, and a texture storage stores predefined surface colors, with the elements exchanging data with global memory through load and store information.

58/S6/F3.text: The GPU performs modeling transformation by applying transformations such as rotation, multiplying the same transformation matrix with each vertex vector simultaneously for all vertices, producing a stream of transformed triangles from local coordinates to world coordinates, which gives a significant performance gain in real-time rendering because millions of vertices need to be processed per second and even more for a realistic immersive experience.

58/S6/F4.text: Most graphics systems assume that a scene to be rendered is made of triangles, so surfaces are converted into triangular meshes regardless of how a developer defines an object, and the GPU assumes such a mesh as input.

58/S6/F5.text: Graphics libraries provide application programming interfaces (APIs) through which triangles in a mesh are sent to the GPU one vertex at a time, and the GPU assembles the vertices into triangles.

58/S6/F6.text: The GPU computes vertex color by performing vector dot products, as in the simple lighting model, simultaneously for multiple vertices.

58/S6/F7.text: The GPU projection stage combines viewing transformation, projection transformation and viewport transformation in a composite matrix multiplied with vertices, producing a stream of triangles in screen or device coordinates, a continuous coordinate space, ready to be converted to pixels.

58/S6/F8.text: In rasterization, the pixels overlapped by device-space triangles are determined, and algorithms exploit the fact that each pixel can be treated independently from all other pixels so that the colors of all pixels can be determined simultaneously in parallel.

58/S6/F9.text: In the GPU pixel processing stage, the two activities that take place are surface texturing and hidden surface removal.

58/S6/F10.text: In the pixel processing stage, the simplest surface texturing method applies stored texture images to the geometry being rendered by replacing the computed pixel color with the texture color at the corresponding texture point; GPUs store textures in high-speed texture storage on the graphics card, which each pixel calculation must access, and because nearby pixels tend to access nearby texture image locations, specialized memory caches reduce access time.

58/S6/F11.text: In the pixel processing stage, hidden surface removal uses a depth buffer algorithm in which a dedicated depth buffer stores the depth information for points in a three-dimensional (3D) scene before projection onto a two-dimensional (2D) plane, where depth is the viewer's distance with respect to each pixel.

59/S0/F0.text: Majuli is the world's largest inhabited river island, located in eastern India on the river Brahmaputra and surrounded by the Brahmaputra and its tributary.

59/S0/F1.text: The objective of the Majuli case study is an immersive, interactive virtual reality tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage, and each information point reveals related information for interactive exploration.

59/S0/F2.text: The Majuli virtual tour contains a large number of geographically spread information points, including satras (Vaishnavite monasteries), villages, tribal villages, towns, and other places of interest, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.
