59/S0/F3.text: The Majuli virtual tour uses a combination of navigation techniques, with walking within each information point and teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between points, because the island's large geographical spread means a single technique such as walking or teleportation alone may not be good.

59/S0/F4.text: The Majuli multimodal archive consists of regular images, 360-degree images, and videos for the indigenous architectural heritage of satras (Vaishnavite monasteries) and village life, 3D models for landscape and architecture, 2D drone shots for landscape, flora, and fauna, 2D videos for intangible cultural heritage, and textual descriptions.

59/S0/F5.text: The Majuli virtual tour application is almost 10 gigabytes in size because the collected multimodal information is vast.

59/S0/F6.text: Rendering the Majuli application's rich multimodal content, which can be interactively changed and includes videos and animations, involves a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a simple static image and requires fast storage and retrieval support for real-time realistic interactive rendering.

59/S0/F7.text: Regular systems cannot support the Majuli application, so resource optimization was needed.

59/S1/F0.text: The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device comprising a headset and handheld controllers, with its own processor and memory, and does not need to be tethered to a fixed computer.

59/S1/F1.text: Compared with a high-end graphics workstation, the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage, so the Oculus Quest 2 application required optimization to reduce its size and associated computations, including memory access, because reducing the size reduces rendering requirements and the associated memory access.

59/S1/F2.text: The Oculus Quest 2 application used a cloud computing-based optimization in which all videos, not images, were stored in the cloud because videos take up more space; when a user selected a video thumbnail from the Oculus Quest 2 video player, the video was loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally, reducing storage and data-access requirements.

59/S1/F3.text: Because the videos were stored in the cloud, the application deployed on the Oculus Quest 2 client device was reduced to 5.1 gigabytes (GB), and a corresponding computational reduction occurred.

59/S1/F4.text: The cloud-based video-loading optimization for the Oculus Quest 2 application relied on a cloud server, so it required high bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time; if these network connectivity issues were not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.

59/S2/F0.text: A cardboard virtual reality headset is a cardboard housing in which a smartphone is placed, and when the smartphone displays stereoscopic views and the housing is worn as a headset, it provides an immersive environment without an expensive headset, and cardboards cost about 500 to 1000 Indian rupees, making deployment on widely owned smartphones a low-cost option.

59/S2/F1.text: Deploying the Majuli virtual reality system on a smartphone placed in a cardboard required an optimization strategy because the full system's size and the associated computation exceed what average smartphones typically support.

59/S2/F2.text: The optimization strategy for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli virtual reality system was to compress the images to reduce storage requirements and to remove video playback support, because most videos could not be utilized.

59/S2/F3.text: Compressing the images and removing video playback support made the Majuli virtual reality system experience less realistic than the full version implementation.

59/S2/F4.text: Compressing the images and removing video playback support reduced the overall size of the Majuli virtual reality system from roughly 10 gigabytes (GB) to 0.7 gigabytes.

59/S2/F5.text: Approaches to address computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences include cloud-based services, which could allow video playback to be retained, and compression techniques, while in extreme cases some features may have to be removed.

59/S2/F6.text: Deploying the whole immersive virtual reality system on a platform is not possible when rendering cannot be performed on the device.

59/S3/F0.text: The book Computer Graphics published by Oxford University Press is the source from which the topics covered in the lecture were taken, and it can be used to study those topics in more detail.

59/S3/F1.text: A National Programme on Technology Enhanced Learning (NPTEL) massive open online course (MOOC) on computer graphics offered by the lecturer covers all the topics mentioned in the lecture and can be used to learn more details about the stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline.

60/S1/F0.text: Unity is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems.

60/S1/F1.text: The Unity platform comprises the Unity three-dimensional (3D) game engine and a developer's interface that a developer can use to implement ideas.

60/S1/F2.text: The Unity platform is intended to provide implementation support for the computer graphics pipeline, including object definition, scene construction, lighting effects, view transformation, and scan conversion or rendering, so that a developer can focus on building the immersive experience rather than mastering and implementing the pipeline.

60/S1/F3.text: Unity is a cross-platform game engine that Unity Technologies initially released in 2005.

60/S1/F4.text: Unity supports both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) games or interactive content, and it supports over 20 different platforms, including personal computer (PC), mobile, Android-based mobile, and Apple's iOS mobile platform.

60/S2/F0.text: Unity Hub is a standalone application that is the primary way to install the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine; installing Unity Hub gives the Unity Editor interface and the Unity Game Engine and streamlines finding, downloading, and managing Unity projects and installations.

60/S2/F1.text: The Unity Game Engine is a middleware and interface that allows developers to build extended reality experiences or extended reality systems and deploy them on a specific platform.

60/S2/F2.text: The Unity Editor interface is essentially an integrated development environment (IDE) whose menu options provide developers the features required to build and deploy a system, and it allows developers to build and deploy realistic immersive environments without having to master and implement the computer graphics (CG) pipeline.

60/S2/F3.text: The main advantage of Unity Hub is that it supports multiple versions of Unity and lets the developer manage multiple versions of Unity together in one place.

60/S2/F4.text: Unity Hub installation is not mandatory; the Unity Editor and the Unity Game Engine can be installed separately, and in that case the developer can deal with only one version of Unity.

60/S2/F5.text: Unity Hub can manually add versions of Unity that are already installed on a system, if any, to the Hub.

60/S3/F0.text: In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

60/S3/F1.text: The Unity editor interface includes the scene view, game view, hierarchy window, inspector window, toolbar, status bar, project window, and console window.

60/S3/F2.text: The Unity scene view is the developer's interactive view of the scene being created, and it shows the scene while it is being built and lets the developer select, manipulate, and modify the game objects, which are the fundamental concepts in Unity, that together comprise the scene.

60/S3/F3.text: The Unity game view is the final view used to preview a developed scene, and it renders the scene from the camera set by the developer to represent the final published or deployed application.

60/S4/F0.text: A Unity asset is any item used in a Unity project to create an application, can represent visual or audio elements such as three-dimensional (3D) models or textures, and examples of Unity assets are scenes, animations, materials, scripts, and prefabs.

60/S4/F1.text: A Unity asset can be imported from outside Unity as a file, such as a three-dimensional (3D) model, an audio file, or an image, or it can be created inside the Unity environment.

60/S4/F2.text: A Unity scene is a specific type of Unity asset that contains all or part of a game or application, and a scene can comprise components, each of which can be a different asset.

60/S4/F3.text: A Unity project can contain any number of Unity scenes, depending on how many levels or layers it has, and Unity provides a scene interface to create, edit, or modify a scene.

60/S4/F4.text: A Unity game object is a fundamental object that represents characters, props, or a scenario and acts as a container for components that implement the object's functionality, so its properties are given by adding components to it.

60/S4/F5.text: Built-in component types can be assigned to Unity game objects through the Unity editor interface, and custom components and game objects can be created using scripting application programming interfaces (APIs).

60/S4/F6.text: Cube, sphere, capsule, cylinder, and plane are primitive object types that can be created directly within Unity as Unity game objects.

60/S4/F7.text: A Unity prefab is a template created by configuring and storing a Unity game object, and it allows the user to make instances of that game object in a Unity scene.

61/S0/F0.text: The Unity developer environment is an implementation platform with an editor interface through which a developer can create, build, and deploy a system, and it provides support for building an XR experience.

61/S0/F1.text: Render pipeline support is an important graphics support offered by Unity, providing support to implement the entire render pipeline—camera and view transform, lighting, meshes, materials, textures, shaders, and environment creation (world scene or world-coordinate-system scene creation, special environments such as skies, and different visual effects)—and also letting the user have customized control over individual pipeline stages.

61/S0/F2.text: Unity provides three pre-built render pipelines, the built-in render pipeline, the Universal Render Pipeline (URP), and the High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP), and a developer can also create a custom render pipeline using Unity's scriptable render pipeline application programming interfaces (APIs).

61/S0/F3.text: The built-in render pipeline in Unity has limited options for customization, so a developer has to work with the options that are already provided.

61/S0/F4.text: The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) in Unity is a quick and easy way to customize graphics and create optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms.

61/S0/F5.text: The Universal Render Pipeline (URP) in Unity has many pipeline stages optimized by the pipeline implementation itself, and it takes care of pipeline-implementation optimization to some extent, so a developer need not manage those aspects and resource requirements are minimized.

61/S0/F6.text: The High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) in Unity is a customizable pipeline specifically meant for creating cutting-edge, high-fidelity, photorealistic graphics.

61/S0/F7.text: The High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP) in Unity requires a good amount of resources and is typically meant for high-end platforms, such as high-end graphics workstations with good graphics processing unit (GPU) support.

61/S1/F0.text: Unity's built-in render pipeline supports object definition by providing models, which are files containing data on the shape and appearance of three-dimensional (3D) objects and are essentially the object representation.

61/S1/F1.text: A Unity model file can contain mesh, material, and texture data, and, if the object represents an animated character, it can also contain animation-related data.

61/S1/F2.text: Unity supports more than 10 standard and proprietary model file formats, including the .fbx format, the .dae format, the .dxf format, and the .obj format, so models created in different formats can be imported into Unity and made to work.

61/S1/F3.text: In Unity, three-dimensional (3D) meshes are the main graphics primitives, and Unity supports triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal meshes, meaning meshes whose polygons are triangles or quadrangles.

61/S1/F4.text: In Unity's mesh rendering workflow, the mesh renderer takes geometry from the mesh filter and renders it at the position defined by the game object's transform component.

61/S1/F5.text: In a Unity model file, materials describe the appearance of an object's surface by specifying how the surface should be rendered, including references to textures used, tiling information, color tints, and other information, whereas meshes describe the object's shape.

61/S1/F6.text: In Unity, textures are bitmap images applied over a mesh surface as a way to assign colors to the surface, and they can represent many other aspects of a material's surface in addition to basic color, such as reflectivity and roughness.

61/S2/F0.text: The Unity editor supports scene creation by transferring objects from local coordinates to world coordinates and by providing tools to create and modify environmental features such as landforms, vegetation, and the landscape.

61/S2/F1.text: The Terrain Tools Preview package provides additional functionality on top of the built-in terrain features in the Unity editor.

61/S2/F2.text: The Tree Editor is a Unity editor tool that lets developers design trees directly in the editor; the latest Unity version supports the SpeedTree toolkit instead of the Tree Editor, while earlier versions still provide the Tree Editor.

61/S2/F3.text: A skybox in Unity is a sky background that a camera draws before it renders a frame; it is a cube with different textures on its faces to create the feel of a 360-degree environment, and Unity always renders the skybox at the back.

61/S2/F4.text: Unity provides support for realistic lighting on game objects, allowing developers to specify the intensity, direction, and color of the light and to render real-time shadows using shadow mapping.

61/S2/F5.text: In the Unity developer environment, visual effects can be applied to the camera, game objects, light sources, and other elements of the game.

61/S2/F6.text: The halo effect is a visual effect that creates light areas around light sources, typically to give the impression of small dust particles in the air.

61/S2/F7.text: The lens flare effect is a visual effect that simulates the effect of lights refracting inside a camera lens.

61/S2/F8.text: The line renderer effect is a visual effect that takes an array of two or more points in 3D space and draws a straight line between those points, enabling anything from a simple straight line to a complex spiral to be drawn.

61/S2/F9.text: View transformation, also called the viewing pipeline, is an important stage in the 3D graphics pipeline.

61/S2/F10.text: Unity supports view transformation through its camera concept; after a developer sets up a camera, Unity performs the other calculations automatically.

61/S2/F11.text: In Unity, a camera is created by adding a camera component to a game object.

61/S3/F0.text: Unity does not implement the graphics pipeline itself but uses functions of native rendering libraries to implement the graphics pipeline, and Unity takes care of implementation concerns, so a developer does not need to manage the graphics pipeline implementation.

61/S3/F1.text: The major native graphics libraries supported by Unity are DirectX, which is primarily in the Windows environment, Metal for Apple systems, Open Graphics Library (OpenGL), and Vulkan, and many other native graphics libraries are also supported.

61/S3/F2.text: Depending on the availability of an application programming interface (API) on a particular platform, Unity can support the corresponding native graphics library.

61/S3/F3.text: Unity's default graphics application programming interfaces (APIs) access native graphics library application programming interfaces (APIs).

61/S3/F4.text: To use Unity's default graphics application programming interfaces (APIs), a developer opens the Player Settings editor interface using Edit Project Settings, selects the Player category, navigates to Other Settings, and checks the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) option.

61/S3/F5.text: When the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) option for a platform is checked, the Unity player build includes a set of built-in graphics application programming interfaces and uses the appropriate one at runtime to produce the best-case scenario, so a developer does not need to decide which one to use or what is supported for a given platform.

61/S3/F6.text: When the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) option is not checked, Unity's editor uses the first graphics application programming interface (API) in the list, and if that one is not supported by the specific platform, Unity uses the next one in the AutoGraphics application programming interface (API) list until it finds an appropriate match.

61/S4/F0.text: Unity's physics engine simulates physical laws in a project so that objects correctly accelerate and respond to collisions.

61/S4/F1.text: The Unity physics engine includes rigid bodies, colliders, joints, physics articulation, and character controllers as components essential to give a realistic feeling.

61/S4/F2.text: A rigid body in Unity is a concept and a property that, when attached to a game object, allows the game object to respond to gravity, so falling or bouncing from a surface appears realistic in accordance with everyday experience.

61/S4/F3.text: The isKinematic property, used with a Unity rigid body, can remove the object from physics engine control and allow it to be moved kinematically from a script, so it does not automatically follow gravity, and the developer can choose whether the object follows gravity.

61/S4/F4.text: A collider in Unity defines the shape of a game object for physical collisions, allows the developer to deal with the object's shape after it collides with another object, and includes types that are primitive colliders such as box collider, sphere collider, and capsule collider, or mesh collider, which is more processor-intensive but accurate.

61/S4/F5.text: In Unity, static colliders can be added to a game object without a rigid body component to create floors, walls, and other motionless elements of a scene.

61/S4/F6.text: In Unity, physics materials are used to configure the friction and bounce of a surface.

61/S4/F7.text: A collider in Unity configured as a trigger using the isTrigger property does not behave as a solid object and simply allows other colliders to pass through.

61/S4/F8.text: In Unity, a joint connects a rigid body to another rigid body or to a fixed point in space, can apply forces that move the rigid bodies, has limits that restrict that movement, and can be used to model the realistic movement of specific objects or characters such as a ball and socket joint like a hip or shoulder, any skeletal joint, doors, finger joints, or a piece of elastic.

61/S4/F9.text: Physics articulation (articulation) in Unity is the overall movement of a structure or object comprising joints, and it provides realistic physics behavior that involves joints.

61/S4/F10.text: In Unity, articulations can be configured via the articulation body class or the corresponding articulation body component, which provides inbuilt support that automatically implements joint constraints, so a developer does not need to control each individual joint to make a complex figure move realistically.

61/S4/F11.text: The articulation body class in Unity represents articulation bodies as a logical tree in which each node is a joint and each parent-child relationship reflects mutually constrained relative motion, so the relations and relative movements of the joints define the overall articulation.

61/S5/F0.text: Unity provides an animation system that supports importing animation clips and animations created within Unity, humanoid animation retargeting, a simplified workflow for aligning animation clips, convenient preview of animation clips, transitions and interactions between animation clips, management of complex interactions between animations with a visual programming tool, and animating different body parts with different logics.

61/S5/F1.text: Humanoid animation retargeting in Unity is the ability to apply animations from one character model onto another.

61/S5/F2.text: Although animation processing in Unity involves stages similar to the three-dimensional (3D) graphics pipeline stages, Unity lets a developer work directly with animations without implementing those pipeline stages or their computations.

61/S5/F3.text: Unity provides support for the audio sense in immersive experiences through dedicated components for audio perception and playback: audio source, audio listener, and audio filters.

61/S5/F4.text: The Unity audio source is the primary component attached to a game object to make it play a sound, and it allows an audio clip, which can be any standard audio file such as MP3 or WAV, to be played back when triggered through a mixer, code, or by default.

61/S5/F5.text: The Unity audio listener is a component that listens to all audio playing in the scene and transfers it to the computer speakers; all heard audio is with respect to the audio listener's positioning, and by default only one audio listener should be in the scene attached to the camera.

61/S5/F6.text: Unity audio filters are components that modify the output of an audio source or the intake of an audio listener to generate various sound effects, and each filter is provided as its own component.

62/S0/F0.text: In the Unity development environment, built-in support gives a good-quality experience that is only what the system provides, so to obtain a more customized experience according to the programmer's expectations and needs, the programmer must write scripts or small pieces of code to change the built-in support.

62/S0/F1.text: Unity's scripting environment is set up automatically when the Unity package is installed, Unity supports integrated development environments (IDEs) such as Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code, and JetBrains Rider, and on Windows and Mac the default Unity installation also installs Visual Studio, which can be used to develop and compile scripts.

62/S0/F2.text: The scripting language supported by Unity is C#, which is an object-oriented programming language created by Microsoft.

62/S0/F3.text: In Unity, a C# script can be attached as a component to a game object to control the behavior or activities of that object, and creating a C# script is essentially creating a new type of component that can be attached to game objects, providing a component that behaves as desired rather than according to the built-in support provided by the environment.

62/S0/F4.text: Once a C# script is attached as a component to a game object in Unity as part of the design or development, it starts working whenever the game is executed, and it allows the developer to trigger game events, modify component properties over time, and respond to user input in any way the developer wants.

62/S0/F5.text: Unlike most other assets, C# scripts in Unity are usually created directly within Unity, using the interface provided by the integrated development environment (IDE), by choosing Assets, then Create, then C# Script from the main menu, and the new script is created in the folder selected in the project panel when the project is started.

62/S1/F0.text: A Unity C-sharp (C#) script file begins with a namespace component, with using statements such as using Unity engine and using system.collections, and defines a public class, typically inherited from MonoBehaviour, whose name is the same as the file name.

62/S1/F1.text: A Unity script contains a Start function that is called whenever the script is called, as the starting point, and an Update function that is called in each frame and is invoked whenever the script executes and some change happens.

62/S1/F2.text: In a Unity script, the Vector3 data type represents the position of a three-dimensional (3D) point by storing three coordinates as three elements of a vector.

62/S1/F3.text: In Unity, a developer can see the code in a script file by double-clicking the script asset and can check variable values in the Inspector interface on the Unity Hub editor.

62/S1/F4.text: In a Unity script, the Debug.Log function prints a message to the console output, which can be seen after running the game or application or after the script has been executed.

62/S2/F0.text: In Unity's scripting environment, the Destroy function, which comes under the MonoBehaviour class, destroys a game object from the scene after a specified delay, typically in seconds; for example, Destroy(gameObject, 5f) makes the game object no longer visible in the scene five seconds after the function is called.

62/S2/F1.text: Unity scripts use prebuilt functions that are critical for making a script work, and user-defined functions, which are defined by the user and are typically part of a good script.

62/S2/F2.text: An event function in Unity is a function that Unity activates in response to an event that occurs during gameplay, and when the event happens, Unity passes control to the event function, its body executes, and then control is passed back to Unity.

62/S2/F3.text: Common Unity gameplay events and their event functions include regular update events, such as the Update, FixedUpdate, and LateUpdate functions; initialization events, such as the Start and Awake functions; graphical user interface (GUI) events, such as the OnGUI, OnMouseOver, and OnMouseDown functions; physics events, such as the OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit functions, which relate to contact being made or broken; and other physics-related events, such as the OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit functions, which are called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

62/S2/F4.text: Unity's event functions can be used to impose realistic behavior, such as physical behavior in physics-event functions and interactive behavior in graphical user interface (GUI) event functions.

62/S3/F0.text: To instantiate a prefab at runtime, the script being written needs a reference to that prefab.

62/S3/F1.text: In the editor interface, a prefab is attached for runtime instantiation by creating a new script, creating an empty game object, adding the script to the game object as a component, creating a prefab, and dragging that prefab from the project window into the script component's My Prefab field.

62/S3/F2.text: The scripting environment supports standard conditional if-else statements.

62/S3/F3.text: Loops in the scripting environment can be entry-controlled or exit-controlled: for and while loops are entry-controlled because the loop condition is checked before the loop body executes, and a do-while loop is exit-controlled because the loop body executes at least once and the condition is checked after the loop body executes.

62/S3/F4.text: A for each (foreach) loop can be used for arrays or collections of homogeneous data types, allowing the programmer to work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types.

62/S4/F0.text: The transform property attached to every game object in a scene stores the object's position, rotation, and scale, and it can be modified programmatically through a script, for example in the update function by using transform.Translate, rotation values, and local scale values, to make the object behave as desired.

62/S4/F1.text: A coroutine in Unity is a method that allows a developer to spread tasks across several frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off on the following frame.

62/S4/F2.text: Coroutines are not threads and are not designed to behave like threads; synchronous operations within a coroutine still execute on the main thread, and coroutine execution does not spawn individual threads.

62/S4/F3.text: A gradual opacity fade of an object is visible only when its alpha or opacity value is reduced over a sequence of frames so that Unity renders the intermediate values; a fade function called only once is not perceivable, so the fade must be defined as a coroutine and started so that the change is spread frame by frame.

62/S4/F4.text: InvokeRepeating invokes a method after a specified initial delay and then repeatedly at a specified interval; it takes a function name and two times in seconds, the first for the initial start time and the second for the repeat interval.

62/S5/F0.text: In Unity, scripting supports user interaction with input devices through inbuilt handling of inputs such as the mouse, keyboard, and buttons; for other device-specific inputs, imported software development kit (SDK) input support may be needed and it extends Unity's inbuilt support.

62/S5/F1.text: In the Unity development environment, after the script is written and the system is built, the last stage is to publish or deploy the system, and the editor's Build Settings window, reached by going to File Build Settings, contains all settings and options to publish the build.

62/S5/F2.text: In the Unity development environment's editor, the Build Settings window's Scenes in Build panel manages which scenes are included in the build, its platform section selects the platform to which the system is deployed, and the Build or Build and Run button begins the build process.

62/S6/F0.text: If a system is to be deployed on a specified hardware platform, head-mounted display (HMD), or smart glasses, and that platform provides features or functions not included in the built-in support provided by the Unity environment, the developer imports software development kits (SDKs) or packages to access and use those platform-specific functions.

62/S6/F1.text: In the Unity layered architecture, the application is the top layer, and the software development kit (SDK) layer, which is positioned on top of the Unity layer, is treated as part of the installed Unity package whose application programming interfaces (APIs) are used.

62/S6/F2.text: Vuforia is an augmented reality (AR) software development kit (SDK) primarily meant to help developers deal with object recognition or computer vision issues, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking.

62/S6/F3.text: Unity's built-in support for object recognition or computer vision operations, such as object detection, recognition, and tracking, is not extensive and not very good, so seamless and efficient performance of these operations requires external packages.

62/S6/F4.text: The basic steps for integrating a software development kit (SDK) into the Unity development environment are to install Unity Hub, import the SDK package into the Unity environment, use the functions of both Unity and the SDK, and then compile, build, and deploy.

62/S7/F0.text: Vuforia is a software development kit (SDK) specifically developed for augmented reality (AR) that supports advanced computer vision functionality for recognizing images and objects and interacting with spaces in the real world.

62/S7/F1.text: Vuforia is a cross-platform software development kit (SDK) that supports multiple platforms, including Unity, Android, and iOS, and using it requires a license, with a developer's license available.

62/S7/F2.text: To install Vuforia in Unity, a new Unity project is created using the universal 3D template or an empty project, and the Vuforia engine is added to the project assets either by downloading the Vuforia SDK for Unity from developer.vuforia.com or by manually importing the package as a custom package, after which it can be used directly in the Unity editor.

62/S7/F3.text: The Vuforia configuration requires a Vuforia account and license, and the license is added to the Unity project from that Vuforia account.

62/S7/F4.text: Vuforia setup requires creating a new database on the Vuforia website, adding the images or markers to be tracked to that database so the Vuforia engine can recognize them, and downloading the database package file and importing it into the project as a custom package because the database is required for recognition.

62/S7/F5.text: In the Unity sample scene, the main camera is removed, the Vuforia augmented reality (AR) camera and image target are selected, image targets and models folders are created in assets, the target image is placed in the image targets folder, a three-dimensional (3D) model downloaded from sketchfab.com is placed in the models folder, the target image asset is assigned to the image target component, the 3D model is assigned to the image target component in the sample scene, and the 3D model is scaled to the desired dimensions in the inspector.

62/S7/F6.text: An image target behavior script is attached to or used to modify the behavior of a Vuforia image target, and it performs the operations after the Vuforia engine recognizes the marker.

62/S7/F7.text: For this sample project, the Unity player settings are configured under Edit > Project Settings > Player > Other by removing Vulkan and adding the Open Graphics Library (OpenGL) application programming interface (API), unchecking AutoGraphics API, unchecking Advanced RISC Machines (ARM) version 7, checking ARM 64, using the IL2CPP scripting backend, and ensuring the minimum API level is greater than 7; these settings are application-specific and may not work for other projects or platforms.

62/S7/F8.text: For the Android platform, the build is created by following File > Build Settings > Android > Switch Platform, connecting the Android device through a universal serial bus (USB) cable with USB debugging enabled, and selecting Build and Run, which creates an Android package (APK) file and deploys it directly to the device; alternatively, the Android package (APK) file can be developed first and then transferred and installed separately.

62/S7/F9.text: In the sample marker-based augmented reality (AR) application, the Earth image is the marker, and when a device running the Android package (APK) file captures a matching colored image on a mobile screen, desk, or paper, the Vuforia engine recognizes the marker and displays a three-dimensional (3D) model in place of the marker; the displayed image must match the original image in color, shape, and size.

62/S7/F10.text: In the Unity development environment, installing a software development kit (SDK) extends the built-in environment, as shown by Vuforia adding image-recognition functionality and device-specific SDKs being used to access device-specific sensory or input data.

62/S8/F0.text: Building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems are primarily programming tasks, with the amount of programming depending on the required functionality: a basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment (IDE) support, whereas a customized experience requires scripting, which involves more programming.

62/S8/F1.text: Software development kits (SDKs) provide device-specific support for virtual and augmented reality systems and are imported when the required functionalities exceed the support provided by the Unity development environment.

62/S8/F2.text: The Programmer's Manual and Developer's Manual, available on the respective websites, provide further details on building and deploying virtual and augmented reality systems and writing code.

63/S1/F0.text: Computer vision is an enabling technology with huge potential for building better applications in augmented reality (AR) and mixed reality (MR).

63/S1/F1.text: Cloud and edge computing concepts are relevant for scalable and affordable extended reality systems and for addressing resource optimization concerns.

63/S1/F2.text: Machine learning and deep learning concepts are currently ubiquitous for building better experiences and more intelligent systems in extended reality.

63/S1/F3.text: Large language models (LLMs) or generative artificial intelligence (AI) can be used for enhanced interactivity in extended reality applications.

63/S1/F4.text: Internet of Things (IoT), robotics, and blockchain technology are relevant technologies for extended reality applications.
